assumptions_latex: Each encoding \(E\) represents the same Boolean relation on a fixed original-variable set \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Encoding regimes are compared by the attainable triples \((C(E),L(E),A(E;X))\) and their Pareto order.
review_flags: Relevant SAT-encoding source locator is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes size tradeoffs as a multiobjective comparison among equally faithful encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Associate with each faithful encoding \(E\) of a fixed relation on \(X\) the cost vector
\[
\kappa(E):=\bigl(C(E),L(E),A(E;X)\bigr).
\]
Encoding \(E_1\) dominates \(E_2\) when every component of \(\kappa(E_1)\) is at most the corresponding component of \(\kappa(E_2)\), with at least one strict inequality. A size-auxiliary tradeoff regime is the set of nondominated attainable vectors under a fixed fidelity requirement and encoding class; no scalar ordering exists without specified weights or constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Size-auxiliary tradeoffs compare equally faithful encodings by nondominated clause, literal, and auxiliary-variable costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Size–Auxiliary Tradeoff Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto formulation is coherent and fits a tradeoff-regime leaf, but it is a substantive chosen formalization that requires an explicit source or clearly marked standard-field rationale.

children.title: Unit-Propagation Strength
children.top_down_role: Consequences exposed by unit propagation on the encoded instance.

assumptions_latex: The CNF formula \(E\) and partial assignment \(\alpha\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unit propagation derives the closure obtained by repeatedly satisfying unit clauses, or derives contradiction from an empty clause.
review_flags: Relevant SAT-specific source locator is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the unit-resolution closure used to assess propagation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a CNF formula \(E\) and partial assignment \(\alpha\), initialize \(\rho:=\alpha\). While \(E|_\rho\) contains a unit clause \((\ell)\), extend \(\rho\) so that \(\ell\) is true and simplify again. Stop with conflict if an empty clause appears; otherwise stop when no unit clause remains and output \(\operatorname{UP}(E,\alpha):=\rho\). The propagation strength of \(E\) is evaluated by which semantically implied literals or conflicts this procedure derives under admissible partial assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit propagation repeatedly assigns forced unit literals until reaching a fixed point or an empty-clause conflict; strength records which consequences it detects.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Propagation Strength

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-propagation procedure is standard, but no SAT-specific citation is provided. The algorithm kind describes the procedure while the terminal title concerns propagation strength; the sourced revision should define the comparison criterion more explicitly.

children.title: Domain-Consistency Targets
children.top_down_role: Finite-domain pruning guarantees sought from Boolean encodings.

assumptions_latex: A finite-domain constraint \(C\) is encoded using Boolean literals that represent admissible variable-value pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target is to delete every value lacking support in any solution extending the current domains.
review_flags: Relevant constraint-encoding source locator is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses generalized arc consistency as the finite-domain propagation target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a constraint on variables \(V=\operatorname{var}(C)\) with current finite domains \(D(x)\). A value \(a\in D(x)\) is supported when there exists a tuple \(t\in C\) such that \(t(x)=a\) and \(t(y)\in D(y)\) for every \(y\in V\). Domain consistency requires every remaining \(a\in D(x)\) to be supported. A CNF encoding reaches this target when unit propagation under the domain-literal assignment removes every unsupported value and detects inconsistency when no satisfying tuple remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain consistency keeps exactly values that participate in some constraint-satisfying tuple compatible with all current domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Consistency Targets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support definition matches domain consistency, but the claim connecting unit propagation to value deletion requires a source and a precise domain-literal convention, including the polarity representing removal.

children.title: Propagation-Complete Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encoding families designed to expose all relevant forced literals within a selected scope.

assumptions_latex: The CNF formula \(E\\) is finite and \(\alpha\) is any partial assignment to its variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every literal semantically forced by \(E\wedge\alpha\), and every semantic conflict, is derived by unit propagation.
review_flags: Relevant SAT-specific source locator is missing.
Check notation escaping for the CNF symbol before promotion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines propagation completeness for all partial assignments over the formula's variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite CNF formula \(E\) is propagation complete if, for every partial assignment \(\alpha\), both conditions hold:
\[
E\wedge\alpha\models\bot\;\Longrightarrow\;E\wedge\alpha\vdash_{\mathrm{UP}}\bot,
\]
and, for every unassigned literal \(\ell\),
\[
E\wedge\alpha\models\ell\;\Longrightarrow\;E\wedge\alpha\vdash_{\mathrm{UP}}\ell.
\]
Thus unit propagation detects every inconsistency and every forced literal arising after any partial assignment. Variants restricting \(\alpha\) or \(\ell\) to designated input variables are weaker notions and must be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagation-complete CNF lets unit propagation derive every forced literal and detect every conflict under every partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-Complete Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated full-variable notion of propagation completeness is mathematically plausible and fits the definition leaf, but it needs an authoritative locator. The assumptions contain the malformed token \(E\\\), which must be repaired before promotion.

children.title: Strength–Consistency Separation
children.top_down_role: Cases where clause-level propagation and source-level consistency provide different guarantees.

assumptions_latex: Propagation properties are compared only for encodings of the same represented relation and under the same class of partial assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Logical fidelity alone neither implies nor is characterized by a chosen propagation-consistency level.
review_flags: Relevant SAT-encoding source locator is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates semantic correctness from inference strength under unit propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Encoding fidelity and propagation consistency are distinct. For example, let \(F=(x)\) and introduce \(z\). The CNF
\[
E=(x\lor z)\land(x\lor\neg z)
\]
is logically equivalent to \(F\) after existentially forgetting \(z\), yet unit propagation from the empty assignment derives neither \(x\) nor a conflict, although \(E\models x\). By contrast, the equivalent CNF \((x)\) immediately derives \(x\). Hence equal represented model sets do not imply equal unit-propagation strength; propagation guarantees require additional syntactic or structural conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semantically equivalent encodings can propagate differently: an encoding may imply a literal without unit propagation deriving it.
knowledge_statements.title: Strength–Consistency Separation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly demonstrates weaker unit propagation despite equivalent projection onto the original variable, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. A source is still required, and “logically equivalent after existentially forgetting z” should be identified explicitly as projected or existential equivalence rather than ordinary same-variable logical equivalence.

children.title: Original-Variable Model Projection
children.top_down_role: Removal of auxiliary assignments to recover models over the source variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Original-Variable Model Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection semantics for CNF encodings with original and auxiliary Boolean variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be disjoint finite sets of Boolean variables, let \(F(X)\) be the original constraint, and let \(E(X,Y)\) be its CNF encoding. Exact original-variable model projection means
\[
\operatorname{Mod}(F)=\{\alpha|_X:\alpha\in\operatorname{Mod}(E)\},
\]
equivalently, for every assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^{X}\),
\[
a\models F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists b\in\{0,1\}^{Y}: (a,b)\models E.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The original models are exactly the restrictions to original variables of encoded models, or equivalently the assignments admitting an auxiliary extension.
assumptions_latex: \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\).
\(F\) and \(E\) are interpreted over Boolean assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Mod}(F)=\{\alpha|_X:\alpha\models E\}\).

notation.meaning: set of satisfying assignments of formula G

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: existential projection is the standard fidelity condition for auxiliary-variable CNF encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically precise and matches the leaf, but no inspectable SAT-encoding source supports the existential-projection fidelity condition.

children.title: Auxiliary-Witness Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of extension-variable values from a source-level assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Witness Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstructing definitional auxiliary variables from an original-variable model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input an assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^{X}\) and an acyclic sequence of auxiliary definitions \(y_i\leftrightarrow\phi_i(X,y_1,\ldots,y_{i-1})\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Initialize \(b\) empty and, in increasing order, set
\[
b(y_i):=\phi_i(a,b(y_1),\ldots,b(y_{i-1})).
\]
Output \((a,b)\). Accept the reconstruction precisely when every clause of \(E(X,Y)\) evaluates to true; otherwise report that the supplied definitions or original assignment are inconsistent with \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate acyclic auxiliary definitions in dependency order, then accept the reconstructed extension only if it satisfies every encoding clause.
assumptions_latex: \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\).
Each auxiliary definition depends only on \(X\) and earlier auxiliary variables.
\(a\models F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((a,b)\models E\) whenever the definitional encoding is correct for \(F\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: topological evaluation is standard for definitional Tseitin-style encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the reconstruction leaf, but the condition that the definitional encoding is “correct for F” requires a precise sourced relationship between the definitions, E, and F.

children.title: Nonunique Extension Regimes
children.top_down_role: Encodings permitting multiple auxiliary completions for one projected source model.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Extension Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of encoded models having multiple auxiliary witnesses for one original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an encoding \(E(X,Y)\) and original assignment \(a\), define its extension fiber by
\[
W_E(a):=\{b\in\{0,1\}^{Y}:(a,b)\models E\}.
\]
The encoding has a nonunique extension at \(a\) exactly when \(|W_E(a)|>1\). It is globally extension-unique when \(|W_E(a)|=1\) for every \(a\models F\). Exact model projection requires only \(W_E(a)\neq\varnothing\) for satisfying \(a\), and therefore does not imply extension uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An original model has nonunique extensions when at least two auxiliary assignments satisfy the encoding; exact projection alone guarantees existence, not uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite disjoint Boolean-variable sets.
\(E\) has exact original-variable model projection for \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) has nonunique extensions if and only if \(|W_E(a)|>1\).

notation.meaning: fiber of auxiliary witnesses extending a

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: witness fibers directly characterize uniqueness of existential extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fiber characterization and content kind fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the encoding-fidelity and extension-uniqueness terminology.

children.title: Reconstruction Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks connecting reconstructed witnesses with encoded constraints and source-level models.

knowledge_statements.title: Reconstruction Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clause-level validation certificate for a reconstructed encoded model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(E=C_1\land\cdots\land C_m\) over \(X\cup Y\), an original assignment \(a\), and reconstructed witness \(b\), the pair \((a,b)\) is a reconstruction certificate when
\[
(a,b)\models C_i\quad\text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
A checker validates the certificate by evaluating each literal and confirming at least one true literal in every clause. If exact projection holds, acceptance also certifies \(a\models F\); rejection identifies an unsatisfied clause and invalidates the proposed reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reconstructed witness is valid exactly when its combined assignment satisfies every encoding clause; under exact projection this also certifies the original model.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) has exact original-variable model projection for \(F\).
\(a\) and \(b\) assign every variable of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((a,b)\models E\), and hence \(a\models F\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a total satisfying assignment is checkable by a linear clause scan

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental-Encoding Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic condition for extending a CNF encoding without invalidating prior clauses or assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An encoding sequence \((E_t)_{t=0}^{T}\), with original constraints \((F_t)_{t=0}^{T}\), is incrementally compatible when \(E_{t+1}=E_t\land\Delta_t\) and, for every \(t\) and assignment \(a\) to the active original variables,
\[
a\models F_t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists b:(a,b)\models E_t.
\]
Variables and clauses already exposed to the solver retain their meanings, while deactivation is represented by explicit selector assumptions rather than clause deletion or reinterpretation. Thus learned clauses remain consequences of the persistent clause database under the corresponding assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible incremental encodings extend a persistent CNF monotonically, preserve projection at every stage, and use selectors when constraints must be activated or deactivated.
assumptions_latex: Each \(E_t\) is a Boolean CNF encoding.
Previously introduced variable meanings are immutable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_{t+1}=E_t\land\Delta_t\) and every stage preserves the intended existential projection.

notation.meaning: intended original constraint at stage t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the topic, but the stage-specific original and auxiliary variable domains are not defined, and the claims about selectors, persistence, and learned clauses require a precise incremental-SAT source.

children.title: Encoding-Induced Solver Hardness
children.top_down_role: Search difficulty caused or amplified by a chosen Boolean representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Induced Solver Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative solver hardness created by the chosen encoding rather than the represented instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a deterministic SAT solver \(S\) and a family of Boolean constraints \((F_n)\). Two polynomial-size, projection-correct encodings \(E_n\) and \(E'_n\) exhibit encoding-induced solver hardness for \(S\) when there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[
T_S(E'_n)\le p(n)
\]
for all \(n\), but \(T_S(E_n)\) is superpolynomial for infinitely many \(n\), using the same resource measure and solver configuration. This separation attributes the observed asymptotic difficulty to representation relative to \(S\), not merely to satisfiability preservation or encoding size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver hardness is encoding-induced when equivalent polynomial-size encodings cause polynomial versus superpolynomial resource use by the same fixed solver.
assumptions_latex: \(E_n\) and \(E'_n\) exactly project to \(F_n\).
Both encoding families have size polynomial in \(n\).
The solver and resource measure are fixed across both families.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_S(E'_n)\) is polynomially bounded while \(T_S(E_n)\) is superpolynomial infinitely often.

notation.meaning: chosen solver resource on formula G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but “superpolynomial for infinitely many n” and the solver resource measure need sourced formal definitions before the claimed asymptotic separation is reliable.

children.title: Encoding-Induced Proof Hardness
children.top_down_role: Certificate size or derivation difficulty caused by encoding structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Induced Proof Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proof-complexity separation between equivalent encodings in a fixed refutation system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a propositional proof system \(P\), an unsatisfiable constraint family \((F_n)\), and polynomial-size encodings \(E_n,E'_n\) that are equisatisfiable with \(F_n\). Encoding-induced proof hardness occurs when the minimum \(P\)-refutation lengths satisfy
\[
L_P(E'_n)\le p(n)
\]
for some polynomial \(p\), whereas \(L_P(E_n)\) is superpolynomial for infinitely many \(n\). The boundary is proof-system relative: changing \(P\), adding extension variables, or admitting stronger inference rules may remove the separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof hardness is encoding-induced when equivalent polynomial-size unsatisfiable encodings require polynomial versus superpolynomial shortest refutations in one fixed proof system.
assumptions_latex: Every \(F_n\), \(E_n\), and \(E'_n\) is unsatisfiable.
Both encoding families have polynomial size.
The proof system \(P\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_P(E'_n)\) is polynomially bounded but \(L_P(E_n)\) is superpolynomial infinitely often.

notation.meaning: minimum length of a P-refutation of G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record matches proof hardness conceptually, but the asymptotic condition and proof-length measure require alignment with a specified proof-complexity source.

children.title: Solver–Proof Hardness Mismatches
children.top_down_role: Cases where operational solver difficulty diverges from proof-system difficulty.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver–Proof Hardness Mismatches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic mismatch between solver resources and shortest proofs in an associated proof system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a SAT solver whose runs on unsatisfiable CNFs produce refutations in a proof system \(P\). A family \((E_n)\) has a solver–proof hardness mismatch when either
\[
L_P(E_n)\le \operatorname{poly}(n)\quad\text{and}\quad T_S(E_n)\not\le\operatorname{poly}(n),
\]
or
\[
T_S(E_n)\le\operatorname{poly}(n)\quad\text{and}\quad L_Q(E_n)\not\le\operatorname{poly}(n)
\]
for a separately specified weaker system \(Q\). The first case separates proof existence from proof search; the second separates solver power from the weaker proof model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mismatch occurs when short proofs exist but a solver searches superpolynomially, or a polynomial solver run escapes a specified weaker proof system.
assumptions_latex: Each \(E_n\) is an unsatisfiable CNF.
Solver time and proof length use fixed encodings and size parameters.
The solver-to-proof correspondence is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial proof length and polynomial solver resources need not coincide across the chosen models.

notation.meaning: solver resource on the n-th encoding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two displayed regimes compare different proof systems and require an explicit simulation model connecting solver runs to P and Q; without such a source, the proposed mismatch definition is unreliable.

children.title: Hardness-Preserving Translation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which translations retain, reduce, or amplify structural hardness.

knowledge_statements.title: Hardness-Preserving Translation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial simulation condition delimiting when CNF translations preserve proof hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For proof systems \(P\) and \(Q\), a translation \(\tau\) from formulas to CNFs preserves refutation hardness up to polynomial factors when \(|\tau(F)|\le p(|F|)\) and there are polynomials \(q,r\) such that
\[
L_Q(\tau(F))\le q(L_P(F),|F|)
\quad\text{and}\quad
L_P(F)\le r(L_Q(\tau(F)),|F|)
\]
for every unsatisfiable \(F\) in the translation domain. If either simulation fails, polynomial-size translation and equisatisfiability alone do not transfer lower or upper proof-length bounds across the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A translation preserves proof hardness only when source and target refutations polynomially simulate one another; polynomial size and equisatisfiability alone are insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau(F)\) is equisatisfiable with \(F\).
\(P\) and \(Q\) are fixed refutation systems.
\(F\) ranges over the specified unsatisfiable domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_P(F)\) and \(L_Q(\tau(F))\) are polynomially related.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Mutual polynomial simulation is a suitable sufficient condition, but failure of either direction does not uniformly block every upper- or lower-bound transfer. A sourced directional formulation is required.

children.title: Complete SAT Solving
children.top_down_role: Complete elimination, splitting, clause-learning, look-ahead, exact-exponential, hybrid, and parallel search families.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolution-Based Variable Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Davis–Putnam elimination of one Boolean variable by resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a CNF \(F\) and variable \(x\). Partition clauses containing \(x\) as \(x\lor A_i\), clauses containing \(\neg x\) as \(\neg x\lor B_j\), and clauses omitting \(x\) as \(R\). Form every non-tautological resolvent \(A_i\lor B_j\), discard duplicates, and output
\[
\operatorname{DP}_x(F):=R\land\bigwedge_{i,j}(A_i\lor B_j).
\]
Repeatedly choose and eliminate variables; stop when the empty clause appears or no variables remain. The transformation satisfies \(\operatorname{DP}_x(F)\equiv\exists x\,F\), hence preserves satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete clauses containing a variable, add all non-tautological resolvents across its two polarities, and repeat; each step performs existential elimination.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite propositional CNF.
Tautological resolvents are discarded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{DP}_x(F)\equiv\exists x\,F\).

notation.meaning: clauses not containing the eliminated variable

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Davis–Putnam elimination is existential quantification implemented by exhaustive resolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and existential-elimination conclusion match the leaf, but the clause partition is ambiguous if input clauses contain both polarities of x. A source-backed convention excluding or preprocessing tautological input clauses is needed.

children.title: Variable-Elimination Orders
children.top_down_role: Order choices governing the sequence and structural impact of variable elimination.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Elimination Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered Davis–Putnam elimination and its order-dependent intermediate size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a CNF \(F_0\) and an ordering \(\pi=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) of variables to eliminate. For \(t=1,\ldots,k\), set
\[
F_t:=\operatorname{DP}_{x_t}(F_{t-1}),
\]
using all non-tautological resolvents and optionally deleting duplicate or subsumed clauses. Output \(F_k\). Although
\[
F_k\equiv\exists x_1\cdots\exists x_k\,F_0
\]
is independent of the order up to logical equivalence, the intermediate clause counts, widths, and computation required can depend strongly on \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate variables in a chosen order. The final existential projection is order-independent, but intermediate clause count, width, and work can vary greatly.
assumptions_latex: \(F_0\) is a finite propositional CNF.
\(x_1,\ldots,x_k\) are distinct variables of \(F_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_k\equiv\exists x_1\cdots\exists x_k\,F_0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: existential quantifiers commute while elimination intermediates depend on order

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordered-elimination algorithm and order-dependent intermediate growth match the leaf, but no inspectable elimination-order source is supplied.

children.title: Intermediate Clause Growth
children.top_down_role: Clause proliferation and width expansion during elimination.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate Clause Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step clause-growth bound for resolution-based variable elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a CNF \(F\) has \(m\) clauses, exactly \(p\) clauses containing \(x\), and exactly \(q\) clauses containing \(\neg x\). Eliminating \(x\) deletes those \(p+q\) clauses and generates at most \(pq\) candidate resolvents. Therefore, before optional subsumption and after discarding tautologies and duplicates,
\[
|\operatorname{DP}_x(F)|\le m-p-q+pq.
\]
Constructing the candidates requires at most \(pq\) resolution operations. Repetition can cause exponential intermediate growth because the multiplicative term may recur across elimination steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating a variable occurring positively in p clauses and negatively in q clauses creates at most pq resolvents and at most m−p−q+pq clauses.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF with \(m\) clauses.
Clause generation uses pairwise resolution on \(x\).
Tautologies and duplicates are not retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\operatorname{DP}_x(F)|\le m-p-q+pq\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: every positive occurrence clause pairs with every negative occurrence clause

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-step bound is correct under the intended pairwise-resolution and clause-count conventions, but those conventions and the exponential-growth claim lack an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Width-Guided Elimination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Order-selection regimes informed by graph width or related structural parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Width-Guided Elimination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clause-space bound for Davis–Putnam elimination ordered by induced primal-graph width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a CNF formula on \(n\) variables, and let \(\pi\) be an elimination order of induced width \(w\) in the primal graph. At each elimination step, discard tautological and duplicate resolvents. Every retained clause produced while eliminating a variable has its remaining variables in that variable's later-neighbor bag, whose size is at most \(w\). Hence each bucket contains at most \(3^{w+1}\) distinct non-tautological clauses, and the complete elimination run stores or generates at most \(O(n3^{w+1})\) distinct bucket clauses. Thus Davis–Putnam elimination is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to induced width, up to polynomial bookkeeping factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elimination order of induced width w limits every bucket to exponentially many clauses in w, giving an overall fixed-parameter bound proportional to n times 3^(w+1).
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
\(\pi\) has induced primal-graph width \(w\).
Tautological and duplicate resolvents are discarded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{clauses}}=O(n3^{w+1})\).

notation.meaning: number of distinct bucket clauses generated or stored

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard induced-width analysis of bucket-style Davis–Putnam elimination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits the width-regime leaf, but no inspectable SAT source supports the precise bucket-clause count or the resulting fixed-parameter tractability claim. The supplied local inventory is unrelated to Davis–Putnam induced-width analysis.

children.title: Elimination Blowup Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instance structures separating controlled elimination from prohibitive intermediate growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Elimination Blowup Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit quadratic one-step growth under unrestricted Davis–Putnam elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(p,q\geq 1\), let \(F_{p,q}\) contain the clauses \((x\lor a_i)\) for \(1\leq i\leq p\) and \((\neg x\lor b_j)\) for \(1\leq j\leq q\), where all \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) are distinct positive literals. Eliminating \(x\) by Davis–Putnam resolution produces every clause \((a_i\lor b_j)\). These \(pq\) resolvents are distinct, non-tautological, and pairwise non-subsuming. Consequently, eliminating one variable with \(p\) positive and \(q\) negative occurrences can increase the clause set quadratically; repeated unrestricted eliminations can therefore cause exponential intermediate growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable occurring positively p times and negatively q times can generate pq indispensable resolvents, establishing the local boundary behind elimination blowup.
assumptions_latex: All literals \(a_i,b_j\) use distinct variables and occur positively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{DP}_x(F_{p,q})=\{a_i\lor b_j:1\leq i\leq p,\ 1\leq j\leq q\}\), so exactly \(pq\) resolvents remain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit cross-product family fits this blowup-boundary leaf and the counterexample content kind. A relevant source is still required, particularly because quadratic growth in one elimination step does not by itself establish the additional claim that repeated eliminations can cause exponential intermediate growth.

children.title: Unit-Clause Reasoning
children.top_down_role: Forced-assignment reasoning triggered by unit clauses.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Clause Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive unit propagation on a finite CNF formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a CNF formula \(F\). While \(F\) contains a unit clause \((\ell)\), assign \(\ell=1\), delete every clause containing \(\ell\), and delete \(\neg\ell\) from every remaining clause. Stop with conflict if the empty clause appears, and otherwise stop when no unit clause remains. The transformation preserves satisfiability under the accumulated assignment: the original formula is satisfiable exactly when the reduced formula is satisfiable together with all propagated literals. Output either conflict or the reduced formula and propagated partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly satisfy unit clauses, simplify the CNF, and stop at an empty clause or a unit-free residual formula; the process preserves satisfiability under its assignments.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is satisfiable}\iff F'\land\bigwedge_{\ell\in U}\ell\text{ is satisfiable}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical unit-propagation rule for CNF

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm accurately describes exhaustive unit propagation and fits the terminal container, but it has no relevant citation with a specific locator. None of the inventoried sources supports this SAT rule.

children.title: Pure-Literal Reasoning
children.top_down_role: Polarity-based simplification for variables occurring with only one sign.

knowledge_statements.title: Pure-Literal Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Satisfiability-preserving elimination of pure literals from CNF.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a CNF formula \(F\). A literal \(\ell\) is pure in the current formula when \(\ell\) occurs and \(\neg\ell\) does not. While a pure literal exists, assign \(\ell=1\) and delete every clause containing \(\ell\); no clause requires deletion of \(\neg\ell\). Stop when no pure literal remains, and output the residual formula \(F'\) with the pure assignments \(P\). Every satisfying assignment of \(F'\) extends by these assignments to one of \(F\), and every satisfying assignment of \(F\) implies that \(F'\) is satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each currently pure literal true and remove its clauses. The resulting formula is equisatisfiable, and any residual model extends to an original model.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is satisfiable}\iff F'\text{ is satisfiable}\).

notation.meaning: a literal pure in the current formula

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and equisatisfiability claim fit pure-literal reasoning, but no inspectable SAT source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Propagation Closure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point behavior under repeated local simplification.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Closure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed points of repeated unit and pure-literal reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) repeatedly apply unit-clause reduction and pure-literal reduction to a finite CNF formula until conflict or until neither rule applies. Every terminating nonconflicting result \((F',\alpha)\) is a propagation closure: \(F'\) has neither a unit clause nor a pure literal, and \(F\) is satisfiable exactly when \(F'\) is satisfiable under extension by \(\alpha\). Termination follows because each nontrivial reduction removes a variable occurrence or a clause. Different rule orders may yield different residual syntax, but each terminal residual is equisatisfiable with \(F\) under its accumulated assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhaustive unit and pure-literal reductions terminate at conflict or a rule-closed residual; all terminal residuals preserve satisfiability, though their syntax may depend on rule order.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
Each step applies a currently valid unit or pure-literal rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'\text{ contains no applicable reduction, and }F\text{ is satisfiable}\iff F'\text{ is satisfiable}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite fixed-point closure of standard CNF reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits propagation closure, and the record avoids claiming confluence. A relevant source is nevertheless needed for the combined closure, termination measure, equisatisfiability statement, and rule-order dependence claim.

children.title: Pure-Literal Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instances or proof contexts where polarity simplification is absent, weak, or unsuitable.

assumptions_latex: Pure-literal reasoning is used without branching, resolution, or another complete inference rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is unsatisfiable, but no pure-literal reduction applies to }G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure-literal elimination is satisfiability-preserving but incomplete for deciding CNF satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(x\lor y)\land(x\lor
eg y)\land(
eg x\lor y)\land(
eg x\lor
eg y)\). Both polarities of each variable occur in \(G\), so no pure-literal reduction applies. The formula \(G\) is unsatisfiable. Thus pure-literal closure alone does not decide CNF satisfiability. Pure-literal elimination also preserves satisfiability rather than the complete set of satisfying assignments: fixing a pure literal may exclude original satisfying assignments that give its variable the opposite value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displayed unsatisfiable four-clause formula has no pure literal, so pure-literal closure does not decide SAT. Pure-literal elimination preserves existence of a model, not the complete original model set.
knowledge_statements.title: Pure-Literal Failure Boundaries

children.title: Case-Splitting Structure
children.top_down_role: Decomposition of SAT search into complementary assignment cases.

knowledge_statements.title: Case-Splitting Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary Shannon-style case split underlying DPLL branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a CNF formula and let \(x\) be an unassigned variable. Write \(F[x=b]\) for simplification after assigning \(x=b\), where satisfied clauses are deleted and falsified literals are removed. Every total assignment chooses exactly one value of \(x\); therefore \(F\) is satisfiable exactly when at least one of \(F[x=0]\) and \(F[x=1]\) is satisfiable. Equivalently, \(F\) is unsatisfiable exactly when both branches are unsatisfiable. This equivalence justifies complete binary branching after deterministic propagation reaches a nonterminal fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting on an unassigned variable is complete: the original formula is satisfiable iff at least one Boolean branch is satisfiable.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
\(x\) is unassigned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SAT}(F)\iff\operatorname{SAT}(F[x=0])\lor\operatorname{SAT}(F[x=1])\).

notation.meaning: CNF simplified under x assigned b

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Boolean case distinction and CNF restriction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Boolean case-splitting principle is precise and fits the leaf, but it lacks a relevant authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Branching-Variable Selection
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria for choosing the next variable or literal.

assumptions_latex: \(F\bigr|_\alpha\) is a reduced, nonterminal finite CNF formula.
The score \(s(x;F,\alpha)\) is defined for every variable \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)\).
Both truth-value branches of the selected variable are eventually explored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\notin\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)}s(x;F,\alpha)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic complete score-based DPLL selection scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic deterministic score-based variable choice at a DPLL decision node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a reduced, nonterminal finite CNF formula \(F\bigr|_\alpha\) and a deterministic score function \(s(x;F,\alpha)\) defined for every unassigned variable \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)\). Compute all scores and choose \(x^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\notin\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)}s(x;F,\alpha)\), resolving ties by a fixed variable order. Output \(x^*\) as the next decision variable, after which DPLL explores both restrictions \(x^*=0\) and \(x^*=1\). Provided both values are eventually explored, the score changes search order and tree size but not soundness or completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an unassigned variable maximizing a deterministic heuristic score, break ties by a fixed order, and branch eventually on both values. The selection affects efficiency but not completeness.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Variable Selection

children.title: Branching-Polarity Selection
children.top_down_role: Policies controlling which truth-value branch receives priority.

assumptions_latex: \(F\bigr|_\alpha\) is a reduced finite CNF formula.
\(x\notin\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)\) is the selected decision variable.
The score \(p(b;x,F,\alpha)\) is defined for both \(b\in\{0,1\}\).
The nonpreferred branch remains available for subsequent exploration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{b\in\{0,1\}}p(b;x,F,\alpha)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic two-polarity DPLL traversal rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic ordering of the two truth values at a DPLL decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a reduced finite CNF formula \(F\bigr|_\alpha\), a selected unassigned variable \(x\), and a deterministic polarity score \(p(b;x,F,\alpha)\) for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Choose \(b^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{b\in\{0,1\}}p(b;x,F,\alpha)\), using a fixed tie rule. Explore the restriction with \(x=b^*\) first and retain the restriction with \(x=1-b^*\) as the alternative branch if the first branch does not produce a final satisfying assignment. Polarity selection changes only traversal order when both alternatives remain available; omitting the second alternative can destroy completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Score both truth values, explore the preferred value first, and retain the opposite value for backtracking. Ordering can affect runtime, while retaining both alternatives preserves completeness.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Polarity Selection

children.title: Branch-Balance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search behavior arising from balanced versus highly asymmetric subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Balance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search-tree bounds from guaranteed progress in the two DPLL branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(F)\) be a nonnegative integer measure that becomes zero at terminal DPLL nodes. Suppose every nonterminal branch produces children whose measures decrease by at least \(a\) and \(b\), where \(a,b\geq 1\). If \(T(m)\) is the maximum number of nodes below a state of measure \(m\), then \(T(m)\leq T(m-a)+T(m-b)+1\). Let \(\rho>1\) be the unique positive root of \(\rho^{-a}+\rho^{-b}=1\). Then \(T(m)=O(\rho^m)\). More balanced decreases reduce \(\rho\); highly asymmetric branches approach the slower exponential regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the two branches reduce a measure by a and b, search size is exponential with base determined by rho^(-a)+rho^(-b)=1; balanced progress improves the base.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) is integer-valued, nonnegative, and terminal at zero.
Every branch decreases \(m\) by at least \(a\) and \(b\), with \(a,b\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(m)=O(\rho^m)\), where \(\rho^{-a}+\rho^{-b}=1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The branching-recurrence complexity bound fits the branch-balance leaf. A source is required for the recurrence solution and for the qualitative assertion that more balanced decreases reduce the branching number, which needs an explicit comparison regime such as fixed total decrease.

knowledge_statements.title: Chronological Backtracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth-first DPLL recovery to the most recent unresolved decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a CNF formula \(F\), an ordered assignment trail, and for each decision a record of tried polarities. Propagate deterministic consequences after every decision. On conflict, erase all assignments following the most recent decision whose opposite polarity is untried, replace that decision by its opposite polarity, mark both polarities tried, and resume propagation. If both polarities of the latest decision are exhausted, remove it and continue backward chronologically. Stop with satisfiable when every clause is satisfied, returning the trail; stop with unsatisfiable when conflict occurs and no unresolved decision remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After conflict, undo to the newest decision with an untried opposite value, flip it, and continue; exhaustion of every decision proves unsatisfiability.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
Each decision records which polarities have been explored.
Propagation is sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{output is either a satisfying assignment of }F\text{ or }\mathrm{UNSAT}\text{ after both branches of every decision are exhausted}.\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical chronological depth-first DPLL backtracking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm describes classical chronological DPLL backtracking and fits the topic container, but no relevant authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: DPLL Search Trees
children.top_down_role: Branching-tree views containing satisfiable, contradictory, or unresolved search regions.

knowledge_statements.title: DPLL Search Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted-tree representation of a complete DPLL execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DPLL search tree for a CNF formula \(F\) is a rooted binary tree whose root carries the empty assignment. Each node carries a consistent partial assignment \(\alpha\) and the propagated restriction \(F\bigr|_\alpha\). A nonterminal internal node selects an unassigned variable \(x\) and has children corresponding to \(x=0\) and \(x=1\), followed by deterministic propagation. A leaf is successful when its assignment satisfies every clause and conflicting when its restriction contains the empty clause. The tree is complete when every nonterminal leaf is expanded; then \(F\) is satisfiable exactly when the tree has a successful leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DPLL execution is a binary tree of propagated partial assignments; a successful leaf gives a model, while a complete tree with only conflict leaves proves unsatisfiability.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
Every propagation step is sound.
Both children of each required case split are represented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is satisfiable}\iff\text{the complete DPLL search tree has a successful leaf}.\)

notation.meaning: formula restricted and propagated under alpha
decision variable at an internal node

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard rooted-tree semantics of complete DPLL search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind correctly fits DPLL search trees, and the search-tree semantics are internally coherent. The record nevertheless lacks a relevant citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: DPLL Refutation Trees
children.top_down_role: Closed branching trees serving as unsatisfiability evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: DPLL Refutation Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed binary DPLL trees as certificates of CNF unsatisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite CNF formula. A DPLL refutation tree for \(F\) is a rooted binary tree whose root carries the empty assignment. Each internal node carrying a consistent partial assignment \(\alpha\) selects an unassigned variable \(x\), and its children carry \(\alpha\cup\{x=0\}\) and \(\alpha\cup\{x=1\}\), optionally extended by sound unit propagation. Every leaf assignment falsifies some clause of \(F\). The tree certifies that every total assignment extending the root reaches a leaf falsifying \(F\), hence that \(F\) is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed DPLL branching tree certifies unsatisfiability when every leaf’s partial assignment falsifies an input clause.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
Every propagation step is logically implied by the current residual formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ has a DPLL refutation tree}\Rightarrow F\text{ is unsatisfiable}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the leaf and the statement is mathematically plausible under the stated sound-propagation convention. However, no citation or inspectable locator supports the precise refutation-tree convention, especially the treatment of propagated extensions and leaf closure.

children.title: Search–Refutation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural relationship between exhaustive DPLL search and tree-like refutations.

knowledge_statements.title: Search–Refutation Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence for chronological DPLL without clause learning or restarts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite unsatisfiable CNF formula \(F\), every closed chronological DPLL search tree can be transformed into a tree-like resolution refutation of \(F\): label each leaf by an input clause falsified there and eliminate branch variables upward by resolution, allowing weakening when necessary. Conversely, a tree-like resolution refutation can be traversed as a branching search whose leaves expose falsified initial clauses. Under standard size measures, each transformation increases size by at most a polynomial factor; exact equality depends on conventions concerning weakening, unit propagation, and repeated variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed chronological DPLL searches and tree-like resolution refutations represent the same unsatisfiability reasoning up to conventional polynomial overhead.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite unsatisfiable CNF formula.
DPLL is chronological and uses neither clause learning nor restarts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ has a closed DPLL tree}\Longleftrightarrow F\text{ has a tree-like resolution refutation}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role is defensible for this correspondence leaf, but the converse construction and polynomial-overhead assertion depend on exact DPLL, weakening, and tree-like resolution conventions. No source with a specific locator is supplied, so the claimed size correspondence cannot be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Tree-Size Complexity
children.top_down_role: Search or refutation difficulty measured through branching-tree size and shape.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Size Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity measured by nodes or leaves in a DPLL search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a DPLL search tree for a CNF formula \(F\), and let \(|T|\) denote its number of nodes. With residual clauses and unit propagation maintained in polynomial time per visited node, the run uses \(|T|-1\) branch edges, at most \(|T|\) node visits, and time \(O(|T|\,p(|F|))\) for some implementation-dependent polynomial \(p\). For a full binary tree with \(L(T)\) leaves, \(|T|=2L(T)-1\). Thus node count, leaf count, and tree-like refutation size agree up to constant or polynomial factors under standard encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DPLL running time is polynomial per tree node, and full binary tree node and leaf counts differ only by a constant factor.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
Each visited node is processed in time polynomial in \(|F|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{time}(T)=O(|T|p(|F|))\) and, for full binary \(T\), \(|T|=2L(T)-1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf. The full-binary-tree identity is precise, but the runtime and comparison with tree-like refutation size rely on an unspecified implementation and encoding cost model. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: DPLL Completeness Scope
children.top_down_role: Problem classes, branching assumptions, and termination settings covered by DPLL completeness.

knowledge_statements.title: DPLL Completeness Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination and completeness for finite propositional CNF under exhaustive branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite propositional CNF formula. Suppose DPLL applies only satisfiability-preserving simplifications, performs sound unit propagation, branches on an unassigned variable into both truth values whenever no terminal condition holds, and never permanently omits a branch. Then every branch has depth at most the number of variables. The procedure terminates: it returns SAT with a total satisfying extension exactly when one exists, and otherwise exhausts all branches and returns UNSAT with a closed refutation tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhaustive DPLL with sound simplification terminates and correctly decides every finite propositional CNF formula.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has finitely many propositional variables.
Branching explores both values of an unassigned variable.
All simplification and propagation rules preserve satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{DPLL}(F)=\mathrm{SAT}\Longleftrightarrow F\text{ is satisfiable}\), and otherwise \(\mathrm{DPLL}(F)=\mathrm{UNSAT}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and finite propositional scope fit the leaf. The statement is plausible for exhaustive DPLL, but no cited source supports the exact simplification, fairness, termination, and certificate formulation.

children.title: Exponential Search Families
children.top_down_role: Instance families exhibiting worst-case branching-tree growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Search Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case exponential size for chronological DPLL via tree-like resolution lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist constants \(c>0\) and unsatisfiable CNF families \((F_n)_{n\ge 1}\), with \(|F_n|\) polynomial in \(n\), such that every chronological DPLL refutation tree for \(F_n\) has at least \(2^{cn}\) leaves. Standard examples arise from appropriately encoded pigeonhole or Tseitin contradictions. Through the correspondence with tree-like resolution, an exponential lower bound on every tree-like resolution refutation of \(F_n\) yields the same exponential lower bound on DPLL search, independently of the branching heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Some polynomial-size unsatisfiable CNF families force every chronological DPLL branching heuristic to construct an exponentially large tree.
assumptions_latex: DPLL is chronological and uses neither clause learning nor restarts.
\((F_n)\) is a family having exponential tree-like resolution lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(T_n)\ge 2^{cn}\) for every DPLL refutation tree \(T_n\) of \(F_n\).

notation.meaning: a DPLL refutation tree for the nth instance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf, but the quantified exponential lower bound needs an explicitly defined CNF family and a cited theorem fixing the size parameter and DPLL/tree-like-resolution conventions. Merely naming pigeonhole or Tseitin contradictions is insufficient support.

children.title: Branching Lower-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings supporting large DPLL search or refutation trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Lower-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract adversary criterion forcing binary branching depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be an unsatisfiable CNF formula and \(d\ge 0\). Suppose that, for every residual formula reachable before depth \(d\) and every variable eligible for branching, both truth-value branches remain nonterminal and belong to the same lower-bound class. Then every closed binary DPLL refutation tree for \(F\) has at least \(2^d\) leaves and at least \(2^{d+1}-1\) nodes. More generally, if every admissible root branch produces residual instances with respective minimum leaf requirements \(a\) and \(b\), the parent requires at least \(a+b\) leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If neither side of any admissible branch can terminate for d levels, every DPLL refutation needs at least 2^d leaves.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an unsatisfiable finite CNF formula.
Both children of every eligible node before depth \(d\) remain nonterminal lower-bound instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(T)\ge 2^d\) and \(|T|\ge 2^{d+1}-1\) for every closed binary DPLL tree \(T\).

notation.meaning: number of leaves of the DPLL tree

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, and the binary-tree counting conclusion is plausible. However, the phrase "same lower-bound class" is not formally defined, and no cited source fixes the residual-instance invariant needed to validate the quantified claim.

children.title: Parameterized DPLL Regimes
children.top_down_role: Worst-case behavior organized by width, backdoor size, occurrence, or related parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized DPLL Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DPLL parameterized by a strong backdoor into a tractable CNF class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a class of CNF formulas closed under partial assignments and decidable in time \(q(n)\). If \(F\) has a strong \(\mathcal C\)-backdoor \(B\) of size \(k\), meaning \(F\mathbin{|}\tau\in\mathcal C\) for every total assignment \(\tau:B\to\{0,1\}\), then DPLL branching first on the variables of \(B\) creates at most \(2^k\) leaves. Solving each residual formula in \(\mathcal C\) decides \(F\) in time \(O(2^k q(|F|)+2^k|F|)\), assuming \(B\) is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a size-k strong backdoor to a tractable class, DPLL decides the formula using at most 2^k residual subproblems.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is closed under partial assignments and decidable in polynomial time.
A strong \(\mathcal C\)-backdoor \(B\) of size \(k\) is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(T)\le 2^k\) and \(\operatorname{time}=O(2^k(q(|F|)+|F|))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the parameterized-regime leaf. The supplied-backdoor leaf bound is plausible, but the exact runtime depends on the residual encoding size, the meaning of q, and whether the tractable-class solver is part of the DPLL procedure. These conventions require a specific authoritative citation.

children.title: Assignment Trail State
children.top_down_role: Trail ordering, assignment status, propagation boundaries, and backtracking visibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Trail State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered CDCL trail containing decisions and propagated literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a CNF formula \(F\), an assignment trail is a finite sequence \(M=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_t)\) of pairwise variable-distinct literals, each annotated as either a decision or a propagation. It induces the partial assignment making every \(\ell_i\) true. The order records the temporal dependency of propagation and backtracking. A literal may be appended only if its variable is unassigned; backtracking to a decision level removes a suffix of \(M\). The trail is conflicting exactly when it falsifies every literal of some clause in the active clause database.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The CDCL trail is an ordered, consistent sequence of decision and propagated literals whose suffix structure supports backtracking.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
No variable occurs twice on the trail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) induces a well-defined partial assignment, and backtracking removes a suffix of \(M\).

notation.meaning: assigned literal at trail position i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the state-component leaf, and the trail description is internally coherent. No source or locator supports the exact trail, conflict, and backtracking conventions.

children.title: Reason-Clause State
children.top_down_role: Antecedent records, reason availability, and explanation ownership for propagated literals.

knowledge_statements.title: Reason-Clause State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antecedent clauses explaining propagated trail literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_t)\) be a CDCL trail over an active clause database \(D\). A reason map \(R\) assigns to every propagated literal \(\ell_i\) a clause \(R(\ell_i)\in D\) such that \(\ell_i\in R(\ell_i)\) and every other literal of \(R(\ell_i)\) is false under the prefix \((\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_{i-1})\). Decision literals have no reason clause. Consequently, each propagation is locally checkable as unit-clause inference from the earlier trail state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each propagated literal stores a clause that became unit before the literal was appended; decisions have no such reason.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is an ordered, variable-consistent trail.
\(D\) is the active clause database.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\ell_i)\setminus\{\ell_i\}\) is falsified by the trail prefix before \(\ell_i\).

notation.meaning: partial map from propagated literals to reason clauses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, and the prefix-based reason condition precisely expresses unit propagation. A specific CDCL source is still required to support the active-database and antecedent conventions.

children.title: Decision-Level State
children.top_down_role: Level attribution, decision boundaries, and conflict-level organization.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is an ordered trail whose literals are marked as decisions or propagations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lev}(\ell_i)=|\{j\le i:\ell_j\text{ is a decision}\}|\), and backtracking to \(b\) removes levels greater than \(b\).

notation.meaning: decision level of an assigned literal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-level annotations partitioning the CDCL trail into eras.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a CDCL trail \(M=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_t)\), the decision level \(\operatorname{lev}(\ell_i)\) is the number of decision literals in the prefix ending at \(\ell_i\). A propagated literal receives the current level when appended, and assignments made before the first decision have level \(0\). The current level \(d\) is the number of decisions on \(M\). Backtracking to level \(b<d\) deletes precisely the maximal suffix containing literals whose levels exceed \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A literal's decision level counts preceding decisions; backtracking removes the trail suffix above the chosen level.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Level State

children.title: Cross-State Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency obligations linking trail positions, reasons, and decision levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-State Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency invariant linking trail order, reasons, levels, and clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A CDCL state \((D,M,R,\operatorname{lev})\) is cross-state consistent when: \(M\) assigns each variable at most once; every reason \(R(\ell_i)\) belongs to \(D\), contains \(\ell_i\), and has all other literals falsified by the preceding trail prefix; decision literals have no reason; levels are nondecreasing along \(M\); and each propagated literal has the current level at its insertion. If a conflict clause \(C\in D\) is recorded, every literal of \(C\) must be false under \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid CDCL state aligns unique trail assignments, antecedent clauses, decision levels, and any reported conflict.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is an active clause database.
\(M\), \(R\), and \(\operatorname{lev}\) have the stated CDCL state types.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((D,M,R,\operatorname{lev})\) satisfies the trail, reason, level, and conflict invariants simultaneously.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role exactly fits the invariant leaf. The listed trail, reason, level, and conflict requirements are coherent, but no cited source establishes that this is the intended complete state-consistency convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Watched-Literal Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-watched-literal representation for incremental unit propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every active clause \(C\) with at least two literals, store two distinct watched literals \(w_1(C),w_2(C)\in C\). Maintain the invariant that, whenever one watch is false under the current trail, either the other watch is not false or the false watch can be moved to another nonfalse literal of \(C\). When an assignment falsifies a watched literal, scan only clauses watching it: move that watch if possible; otherwise propagate the other watch if unassigned, or report conflict if it is false. Unit clauses are handled separately as immediate propagations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two watched literals let propagation revisit only clauses whose watched literal just became false, while preserving unit and conflict detection.
assumptions_latex: The active formula is represented as finite clauses.
Watch lists are updated whenever a watched literal becomes false.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ unit or conflicting under the trail}\Rightarrow\) processing a falsified watch detects the required propagation or conflict.

notation.meaning: two distinct watched literals of a nonunit clause

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the topic. The operational description is plausible, but watched-literal invariants have convention-sensitive formulations, and the detection conclusion depends on initialization and watch-list update details. No source with a specific locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite CNF formula \(F\) with a consistent partial assignment represented by a trail \(M\).
Every propagated literal records the clause that implied it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure either extends \(M\) to a unit-propagation fixpoint or returns a clause falsified by \(M\).

notation.meaning: literal made true by the trail

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialized unit propagation for binary and ternary clauses within a CDCL propagation interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F\) and \(M\), maintain a queue of newly true literals. When \(p\) is dequeued, every binary clause \((\neg p\lor q)\) directly yields a conflict if \(q\) is false and otherwise enqueues \(q\) if it is unassigned. For every ternary clause \((\neg p\lor q\lor r)\), inspect \(q\) and \(r\): report conflict when both are false, enqueue either unassigned literal when the other is false, and take no action otherwise. Record the triggering clause as the reason for each enqueued literal. Stop when the queue is empty or a conflict is found.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process short clauses touched by each new assignment, propagating their sole remaining literal and stopping at either a fixpoint or a falsified clause.
knowledge_statements.title: Short-Clause Propagation Paths

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No SAT source is cited. Moreover, the procedure inspects only binary and ternary clauses, so its conclusion must specify a fixpoint relative to those clauses unless propagation over longer clauses is also defined.

assumptions_latex: The trail \(M\) was produced by decisions and reason-annotated unit propagations from a CNF formula \(F\).
A conflict clause is falsified by the current trail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cuts separating decision vertices from \(\bot\) yield clauses entailed by \(F\) and falsified by the current trail.

notation.meaning: reason clause for an implied literal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard implication graph for one conflicting CDCL trail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The implication graph \(G_M\) has one vertex for each true trail literal and a distinguished conflict vertex \( ot\). If \(q\) was propagated by \(R(q)=(q\lor 
eg p_1\lor\cdots\lor
eg p_k)\), add arcs \(p_i	o q\) for all \(i\). For a falsified conflict clause \((
eg r_1\lor\cdots\lor
eg r_s)\), add arcs \(r_j	o ot\). Decision literals have no incoming arcs. Resolving the conflict clause successively with reason clauses corresponds to moving a cut backward through \(G_M\); the negations of the true literals crossing the cut form the associated learned clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph links assignments to the propagations and conflict they caused; graph cuts correspond to resolution-derived learned clauses.
knowledge_statements.title: Implication-Graph Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and cut-based learning claim are standard in broad form, but no inspectable SAT reference supports the precise graph and cut convention used here.

assumptions_latex: The current CDCL trail ends in a conflict at decision level \(d>0\).
Every nondecision literal at level \(d\) has a recorded reason clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output clause is entailed by \(F\), falsified by the current trail, and contains exactly one literal assigned at level \(d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-UIP learning using reverse trail order and resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(C\) to the falsified conflict clause. While \(C\) contains at least two literals whose complements occur on the trail at level \(d\), choose the latest such propagated trail literal \(q\) and replace \(C\) by the non-tautological resolvent of \(C\) and \(R(q)\) on \(q\). Stop when exactly one literal of \(C\) belongs to level \(d\). That literal is the first unique implication point encountered by reverse analysis. Return \(C\), optionally together with the maximum decision level among its remaining literals as the backjump level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolve backward from the conflict until the learned clause has one current-level literal, identifying the first unique implication point.
knowledge_statements.title: UIP Learning Schemes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The first-UIP algorithm is plausible and fits the container, but its resolution convention and first-UIP characterization require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Learned-Clause Minimization
children.top_down_role: Literal-removal strategies applied to newly learned clauses.

assumptions_latex: The clause database \(F\) entails an initial learned clause \(C\).
Unit propagation is performed against the current permanent clause database, not merely the current trail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned clause \(C'\subseteq C\) is entailed by \(F\).

notation.meaning: candidate clause after deleting a literal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion-based learned-clause minimization certified by reverse unit propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each selected literal \(l\in C\), form \(C'=C\setminus\{l\}\). Temporarily assume every complement of a literal in \(C'\), and compute \(\operatorname{UP}(F\land\bigwedge_{q\in C'}\neg q)\). If unit propagation derives a conflict, replace \(C\) by \(C'\); otherwise retain \(l\). Repeat according to a fixed literal order until no tested deletion succeeds, then output the resulting clause. Each accepted reverse-unit-propagation test certifies \(F\models C'\), so accepted deletions preserve the learned clause's logical consequence status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete a learned-clause literal only when reverse unit propagation certifies that the smaller clause is still implied by the database.
knowledge_statements.title: Learned-Clause Minimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reverse-unit-propagation deletion test is mathematically plausible, but no cited source supports this exact minimization procedure or its database assumptions.

children.title: Learned-Clause Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Clause-tightening transformations beyond basic literal minimization.

assumptions_latex: The database contains clauses \(C=(l\lor A)\) and \(D=(\neg l\lor B)\).
The side-literal sets satisfy \(B\subseteq A\), and neither clause is tautological.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(C\) by \(A\) while retaining \(D\) preserves the models of the database.

notation.meaning: resolvent obtained after removing the pivot

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-subsuming resolution as a sound learned-clause strengthening rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(l\lor A)\) and \(D=(\neg l\lor B)\) be clauses with \(B\subseteq A\). Their resolvent on \(l\) is \(A\lor B=A\), which strictly subsumes \(C\) when \(l\notin A\). Consequently, within any database containing and retaining \(D\), the conjunction \(C\land D\) may be replaced by \(A\land D\). Thus self-subsuming resolution strengthens \(C\) by deleting \(l\) without changing the satisfying assignments of the complete database.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting clause can justify deleting a pivot literal when the resulting resolvent subsumes the clause being strengthened.
knowledge_statements.title: Learned-Clause Strengthening

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The self-subsuming-resolution condition and model-preservation claim appear correct, but they have no relevant citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Refinement Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Runtime, propagation value, and clause-quality tradeoffs of learned-clause refinement.

assumptions_latex: A refinement traverses a reason subgraph \(H=(V_H,E_H)\) reachable from literals of a learned clause.
Adjacency lists and literal marks support constant-time edge visits and membership checks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A full traversal costs \(O(|V_H|+|E_H|)\) time and \(O(|V_H|)\) auxiliary space, while any clause-size reduction is instance dependent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case graph-processing cost versus instance-dependent reduction in learned-clause size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A depth-first or breadth-first learned-clause refinement that examines each reachable reason vertex and each incident reason edge at most once runs in \(O(|V_H|+|E_H|)\) time and uses \(O(|V_H|)\) marks or stack space. Its output has at most the original number of literals, but the guaranteed reduction is zero: an irredundant learned clause may survive unchanged. Hence additional refinement has a linear worst-case analysis cost in the explored implication region, whereas its benefit in clause length, propagation, or later search is not guaranteed by the traversal bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reason-graph refinement is linear in the explored subgraph, but may remove no literals and offers no guaranteed search reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Refinement Cost Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-traversal bound follows under the stated visit assumptions, but the record does not identify a specific refinement algorithm for which those assumptions and the claimed tradeoff are documented.

children.title: Refinement Soundness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting safe minimization or strengthening during conflict processing.

assumptions_latex: A CNF formula \(F\) entails a learned clause \(C\).
A proposed refinement deletes literals to produce \(C'\subseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The refinement is sound exactly when \(F\models C'\); validity only under the current trail is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary separating globally valid refinement from trail-dependent simplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing \(C\) by a subclause \(C'\subseteq C\) is sound as permanent learning only if \(F\models C'\), established by a valid inference or certificate. Satisfaction or redundancy observed solely under the current trail does not suffice. For example, with \(F=(x\lor y)\), the clause \(C=(x\lor y)\) is entailed, and a trail setting \(x\) true may make deletion of \(y\) appear harmless; nevertheless \(F\not\models(x)\), since \(x\) false and \(y\) true satisfies \(F\). Permanently replacing \(C\) by \((x)\) therefore removes models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permanent refinement must be globally implied by the database; a deletion justified only by the current trail can remove valid models.
knowledge_statements.title: Refinement Soundness Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global-entailment boundary and counterexample are coherent and fit a failure-boundary container, but no relevant source is supplied.

assumptions_latex: A learned clause \(C\) is falsified by the current trail and has exactly one literal assigned at the current level \(d\).
Decision levels of trail literals are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After backtracking to \(b\), the clause \(C\) is unit unless \(b=0\) and \(C\) is empty, in which case unsatisfiability is detected.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backjumping induced by an asserting learned clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) be the unique literal of \(C\) whose complement is assigned at level \(d\). Set \(b\) to the maximum decision level among complements of literals in \(C\setminus\{u\}\), using \(b=0\) when this set is empty. Erase every trail assignment above level \(b\), retain \(C\) in the database, and propagate \(u\) with reason \(C\). Because \(b\) may be smaller than \(d-1\), this is nonchronological. If conflict analysis produces the empty clause at level zero, terminate with an unsatisfiability result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jump to the highest level occurring among the learned clause's nonasserting literals, then propagate its sole remaining literal.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonchronological Backjumping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asserting-clause backjump rule is standard, but it lacks a citation. The empty-clause exception in the conclusion lies outside the assumption that the learned clause has exactly one current-level literal and should be stated as a separate level-zero case.

children.title: VSIDS Branching
children.top_down_role: Variable selection driven by decaying conflict activity.

assumptions_latex: The formula has a finite set of variables, and decisions are made only on unassigned variables.
Each conflict identifies a finite set of variables eligible for activity bumps.
