knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter tuned on source instances transfers when its target success probability is within epsilon of the best target-tuned probability.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a nonempty admissible parameter set.
All expectations use the same search budget \(T\) and success criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_s\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-transferable to }D_t\iff\sup_{p\in\mathcal P}J_{D_t}(p)-J_{D_t}(p_s)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Expected finite-budget success probability under instance distribution D.

review_flags: No supplied source identifies the intended transfer metric.
The regret-based definition is precise but requires domain-specific confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The target-regret formulation is precise but uncited and not uniquely determined by the title. The assumptions also do not ensure that the displayed source argmax is nonempty; existence of a maximizing source parameter must be assumed or established.

children.title: Parameter-Transfer Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instance shifts under which previously effective parameter settings cease to transfer.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Transfer Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Target-regret boundary beyond which a source-tuned SAT parameter fails to transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the cross-instance transfer convention, define the target regret of a source-selected parameter by \[R_{s\to t}(p_s)=\sup_{p\in\mathcal P}J_{D_t}(p)-J_{D_t}(p_s).\] For tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), transfer succeeds exactly when \(R_{s\to t}(p_s)\le\varepsilon\) and fails when \(R_{s\to t}(p_s)>\varepsilon\). Consequently, the level set \(R_{s\to t}(p_s)=\varepsilon\) is the parameter-transfer failure boundary relative to the chosen distributions, budget, parameter family, and performance criterion; changing any of these may move the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transfer fails when the target regret of the source-tuned parameter exceeds tolerance. Equality with the tolerance defines the failure boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(p_s\) is selected using the source distribution \(D_s\).
Target performance is evaluated using the same budget and success criterion as source performance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{s\to t}(p_s)>\varepsilon\Rightarrow p_s\text{ is not }\varepsilon\text{-transferable to }D_t\).

notation.meaning: Target regret of the source-selected parameter.

review_flags: No supplied source supports this particular regret boundary.
Definition depends on the provisional cross-instance transfer convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is internally consistent with the preceding regret convention and the content kind fits, but that convention is provisional and no source supports this particular boundary.

children.title: Frozen-Variable Structure
children.top_down_role: Variables whose values remain fixed across relevant solution clusters or search regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Frozen-Variable Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variables fixed throughout a connected cluster of satisfying assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a satisfiable CNF formula and let \(C\) be a nonempty cluster of satisfying assignments, with connectivity taken in a specified solution graph. A variable \(v\in V\) is frozen in \(C\) when \[a(v)=b(v)\quad\text{for all }a,b\in C.\] Its common value is the frozen value. The frozen-variable set is \(\operatorname{Fr}(C)=\{v\in V:(\forall a,b\in C)\ a(v)=b(v)\}\). Variables outside \(\operatorname{Fr}(C)\) are unfrozen relative to \(C\), even if changing them individually would leave the cluster.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable is frozen in a solution cluster when it has the same truth value in every assignment of that cluster.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite satisfiable CNF formula.
\(C\) is a nonempty cluster under a specified solution-graph adjacency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\operatorname{Fr}(C)\iff(\forall a,b\in C)\ a(v)=b(v)\).

notation.meaning: Set of variables constant across cluster C.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard cluster-relative definition of a frozen variable
A source specifying the solution-graph adjacency is requested.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cluster-relative frozen-variable definition is standard and fits the leaf, but the solution graph and its adjacency are left abstract and no cited source identifies the intended SAT cluster convention.

children.title: Cluster Barriers
children.top_down_role: Separations between assignment clusters that impede local transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax unsatisfied-clause elevation separating two assignment clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,C_2\) be disjoint sets of assignments for a CNF formula \(F\). For a one-flip path \(\gamma=(a_0,\ldots,a_m)\) with \(a_0\in C_1\) and \(a_m\in C_2\), define its elevation above \(C_1\) as \(\max_i E_F(a_i)-\min_{a\in C_1}E_F(a)\). The cluster barrier from \(C_1\) to \(C_2\) is \[B_F(C_1,C_2)=\min_{\gamma:C_1\leadsto C_2}\left(\max_{0\le i\le m}E_F(a_i)-\min_{a\in C_1}E_F(a)\right).\] A positive value means every connecting one-flip path must temporarily worsen the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The barrier between clusters is the smallest unavoidable rise in unsatisfied clauses along any one-flip path connecting them.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has finitely many variables.
At least one one-flip path connects \(C_1\) to \(C_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_F(C_1,C_2)>0\Rightarrow\text{every one-flip path from }C_1\text{ to }C_2\text{ exceeds the baseline energy}.\)

notation.meaning: Directed minimax energy barrier from cluster C1 to cluster C2.
A finite path of single-variable flips.

review_flags: The supplied sources do not establish the intended SAT cluster-barrier normalization.
Directed and symmetric barrier conventions coexist.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source selects the directed baseline normalization. For arbitrary assignment sets, a positive value only guarantees elevation above the minimum energy in C1; it need not represent a temporary worsening relative to the chosen starting assignment. That interpretation becomes valid under additional conditions such as a zero-energy solution cluster.

children.title: Barrier-Crossing Difficulty
children.top_down_role: Local-search limitations arising from frozen coordinates and separated clusters.

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier-Crossing Difficulty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-budget failure criterion defined by the hitting time of a barrier-separated target cluster.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((A_t)_{t\ge0}\) be a stochastic one-flip search initialized in cluster \(C_1\), and let \(\tau_{C_2}=\inf\{t\ge0:A_t\in C_2\}\) be the first hitting time of a target cluster \(C_2\). For budget \(T\) and failure tolerance \(\eta\in[0,1]\), the barrier is difficult to cross when \[\Pr(\tau_{C_2}\le T)\le\eta.\] The associated finite-budget failure boundary is \(\Pr(\tau_{C_2}\le T)=\eta\). Barrier height alone does not determine this probability; the transition kernel, initialization within \(C_1\), plateau geometry, and accepted worsening moves also matter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossing is difficult when the probability of reaching the target cluster within the search budget is at most a prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic search has a specified transition kernel on assignments.
Initialization is supported on \(C_1\), and \(C_2\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\tau_{C_2}\le T)\le\eta\Rightarrow\text{the }C_1\text{-to-}C_2\text{ crossing is difficult at budget }T.\)

notation.meaning: First time the search reaches target cluster C2.

review_flags: No supplied source selects this hitting-probability notion of difficulty.
A quantitative barrier-height-to-runtime theorem would require a specified transition kernel.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hitting-probability threshold is mathematically well-defined and the failure-boundary kind is plausible, but no source establishes that this is the intended meaning of barrier-crossing difficulty or connects it to the preceding barrier notion.

knowledge_statements.title: Absence of Unsatisfiability Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why unsuccessful stochastic local search alone cannot certify that a CNF formula is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a stochastic SAT local-search run inspect assignments \(a_0,\ldots,a_T\) and terminate without finding a satisfying assignment. Its transcript establishes only \[F(a_t)=0\quad\text{for }0\le t\le T.\] Unless the inspected assignments exhaust \(\{0,1\}^{V}\) or the output includes an independently checkable sound refutation, this observation does not imply \((\forall a\in\{0,1\}^{V})\ F(a)=0\). Thus finding a satisfying assignment is a verifiable positive certificate, whereas finite failure to find one is not an unsatisfiability certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite unsuccessful local-search run rules out only visited assignments. It certifies unsatisfiability only with exhaustive coverage or a separate sound refutation.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
The reported output contains only the local-search transcript and no independent refutation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall t\le T)\ F(a_t)=0\not\Rightarrow(\forall a\in\{0,1\}^{V})\ F(a)=0\).

notation.meaning: Assignments inspected during the finite search run.
Truth value of formula F under assignment a.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite nonexhaustive search failure is logically weaker than universal falsity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logical limitation is correct and fits the failure-regime topic: a nonexhaustive unsuccessful run is not an unsatisfiability certificate. An authoritative SAT certification or proof-systems source with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: SAT Proof-Theoretic Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Abstract refutation systems, solver correspondence, correctness obligations, proof-resource measures, and canonical hardness families.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7: Proof Complexity and SAT Solving; proof-system sections of the unsatisfiability-proof treatment

children.title: Tree-Like Resolution
children.top_down_role: Resolution derivations without reuse of previously derived clauses.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Like Resolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolution refutations in which every derived clause occurrence is used at most once.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree-like resolution refutation of an unsatisfiable CNF formula \(F\) is a rooted binary tree whose leaves are clauses of \(F\), whose root is the empty clause \(\bot\), and whose internal node labeled \(C\lor D\) has children labeled \(C\lor x\) and \(D\lor\neg x\) for some variable \(x\). Each internal label is therefore the resolvent of its children. Because the proof object is a tree, every derived clause occurrence has at most one parent and cannot be shared between distinct later inferences; repeated use requires repeated derivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree-like resolution refutation is a binary inference tree ending in the empty clause, with no sharing of derived clause occurrences.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an unsatisfiable finite CNF formula.
Tautological details and clause weakening are omitted from the resolution rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\vdash_{\mathrm{tree\text{-}res}}\bot\iff\text{such a rooted resolution tree exists}.\)

notation.meaning: Parent clauses resolved on pivot variable x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard proof-complexity representation of tree-like resolution
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is a standard tree-like resolution refutation and correctly captures the absence of shared derived-clause occurrences, but no resolution-specific source or locator is supplied.

children.title: DAG Resolution
children.top_down_role: Resolution derivations permitting shared reuse of derived clauses.

knowledge_statements.title: DAG Resolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolution refutations permitting shared reuse of previously derived clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DAG resolution refutation of an unsatisfiable CNF formula \(F\) is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are labeled by clauses of \(F\), whose unique designated sink is labeled by the empty clause \(\bot\), and whose nonsource node has two incoming predecessors labeled \(C\lor x\) and \(D\lor\neg x\) and is labeled by their resolvent \(C\lor D\). A derived-clause node may have several outgoing edges, so the same derivation can support multiple subsequent inferences. The proof size is commonly counted by nodes or inference nodes, with the convention stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DAG resolution refutation derives the empty clause in an acyclic inference graph and permits derived clauses to be reused by multiple later steps.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an unsatisfiable finite CNF formula.
Every nonsource node applies the binary resolution rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\vdash_{\mathrm{DAG\text{-}res}}\bot\iff\text{such an acyclic resolution graph exists}.\)

notation.meaning: Resolvent obtained after eliminating pivot x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard proof-complexity representation of general DAG resolution
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The DAG representation and reuse interpretation are standard and fit the leaf, but no resolution-specific citation with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Tree-to-DAG Sharing Gap
children.top_down_role: Proof-resource differences attributable to derivation reuse.

assumptions_latex: Proof size is the number of derived-clause occurrences for trees and the number of distinct clause nodes for DAGs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a polynomial-versus-exponential separation between DAG-like and tree-like resolution size.

notation.meaning: Minimum tree-like resolution refutation size of F
Minimum DAG-like resolution refutation size of F

review_flags: Exact separating family and authoritative proof-complexity locator are missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential proof-size separation under the standard clause-count measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every resolution tree, identifying nodes carrying identical derived clauses produces a resolution DAG and cannot increase size, so \(S_{\mathrm{DAG}}(F)\leq S_{\mathrm{tree}}(F)\). Moreover, there exists a family of unsatisfiable CNF formulas \((F_n)_{n\geq 1}\) and constants \(c,k>0\) such that \(S_{\mathrm{DAG}}(F_n)\leq n^k\) while \(S_{\mathrm{tree}}(F_n)\geq 2^{cn}\). Thus reuse of a derived clause can yield an exponential advantage over duplicating its derivation at every use.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DAG resolution never exceeds tree-like resolution in size, and some unsatisfiable formula families have polynomial DAG refutations but require exponentially large tree-like refutations.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-to-DAG Sharing Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits this leaf, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the exponential separation. The node-identification justification is also unsafe as stated: indiscriminately merging equal-labeled nodes can create dependency issues; the basic inequality follows directly because every tree-like proof is a DAG-like proof. An authoritative source must specify the separating family, size parameter, and bounds.

children.title: Regular Resolution
children.top_down_role: Resolution derivations constrained by regularity along inference paths.

assumptions_latex: Clauses are finite sets of literals and tautological resolvents may be discarded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regular resolution is the subclass of resolution satisfying the pathwise no-repeated-pivot condition.

notation.meaning: Pivot variable of a resolution inference

review_flags: A proof-complexity source explicitly defining regular resolution is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard pathwise regularity for DAG-like resolution derivations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A resolution derivation \(\Pi\) is regular if, on every directed path from an initial clause to the final clause, no variable is used as a resolution pivot more than once. Equivalently, whenever a path contains an inference \(C\lor p,\ D\lor\neg p\vdash C\lor D\), every later inference on that path must pivot on a variable different from \(p\). A regular resolution refutation is a regular derivation whose final clause is the empty clause \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resolution proof is regular when no variable is resolved upon twice along any path from an input clause to the conclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Resolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind match the regular-resolution leaf, and the pathwise pivot condition is standard. No source or specific locator is supplied, however, so the exact DAG orientation and regularity convention cannot be checked against evidence.

children.title: General Resolution
children.top_down_role: Unrestricted resolution derivations within the standard proof system.

assumptions_latex: Clauses are finite sets of literals over a fixed finite variable set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A derivation ending in \(\bot\) is a general resolution refutation.

notation.meaning: Input CNF viewed as a set of clauses

review_flags: A directly relevant resolution source and locator are missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DAG-like propositional resolution without regularity or premise restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A general resolution derivation from a CNF formula \(F\) is a finite directed acyclic graph whose leaves are clauses of \(F\) and whose nonleaf nodes are obtained by weakening or by the resolution rule
\[ (C\lor x),\ (D\lor\neg x)\ \vdash\ C\lor D, \]
where \(x\) is a variable and neither \(C\) nor \(D\) contains \(x\) or \(\neg x\). There is no restriction on reusing derived clauses or on resolving repeatedly upon a variable along a path. The derivation refutes \(F\) when its unique sink is \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General resolution derives clauses in a DAG by resolving complementary literals, permits unrestricted reuse and pivots, and refutes a CNF by deriving the empty clause.
knowledge_statements.title: General Resolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but the selected general-resolution system explicitly includes weakening and imposes a unique-sink convention. These variant choices require a directly relevant source and locator; none is supplied.

children.title: Regularity Cost
children.top_down_role: Proof-complexity separations caused by the regularity restriction.

assumptions_latex: Proof size counts clause nodes in a resolution DAG.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enforcing regularity can cause an exponential proof-size increase.

notation.meaning: Minimum regular resolution refutation size of F
Minimum unrestricted resolution refutation size of F

review_flags: Exact separating family and quantitative locator are missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential separation between regular and unrestricted DAG resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because every regular refutation is a general resolution refutation, \(S_{\mathrm{gen}}(F)\leq S_{\mathrm{reg}}(F)\) for every unsatisfiable CNF formula \(F\). There nevertheless exists a family \((F_n)_{n\geq 1}\) of unsatisfiable CNF formulas and constants \(c,k>0\) for which \(S_{\mathrm{gen}}(F_n)\leq n^k\) but \(S_{\mathrm{reg}}(F_n)\geq 2^{cn}\). Hence the pathwise prohibition against reusing a pivot may impose exponential cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular resolution is no stronger than general resolution, and known formula families exhibit polynomial general refutations but exponential regular refutations.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is the correct role for the regularity-cost leaf, but the claimed polynomial-versus-exponential separation requires an identified formula family, parameter convention, proof-size measure, and authoritative theorem locator. None is provided.

children.title: Input Resolution
children.top_down_role: Resolution derivations restricted by the participation of input clauses.

assumptions_latex: A designated set \(F\) contains the initial clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Input resolution requires an original input clause as a parent of every resolution inference.
review_flags: A directly relevant source defining the immediate-parent convention is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immediate-parent definition of input resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An input-resolution derivation from \(F\) is a resolution derivation in which every inference \(C_1,C_2\vdash R\) has at least one immediate parent in \(F\), meaning \(C_1\in F\) or \(C_2\in F\). Derived clauses may be reused, but an inference between two previously derived clauses is forbidden. An input-resolution refutation is such a derivation with final clause \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Input resolution requires every resolution step to use at least one original input clause; resolving two derived clauses is forbidden.
knowledge_statements.title: Input Resolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the immediate-parent sense of input resolution and fits the leaf. A source with a definition-level locator is still required because input-resolution conventions can differ and no citation is present.

children.title: Unit Resolution
children.top_down_role: Resolution derivations centered on unit-clause inferences.

assumptions_latex: A unit clause contains exactly one literal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unit resolution restricts every inference to have a unit-clause parent.

notation.meaning: A literal used as a unit premise

review_flags: A directly relevant unit-resolution source and locator are missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic unit-premise restriction, allowing derived unit clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A unit-resolution derivation is a resolution derivation in which every resolution inference has a unit clause as an immediate parent. Its inference rule therefore has the form
\[ \{\ell\},\ C\lor\neg\ell\ \vdash\ C, \]
where \(\ell\) is a literal and \(C\) contains neither \(\ell\) nor \(\neg\ell\). The unit parent may be initial or previously derived. A unit-resolution refutation derives \(\bot\), equivalently producing complementary forced units or reducing a clause to the empty clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit resolution repeatedly uses a one-literal clause to delete its complement from another clause, and refutes when it derives the empty clause.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit Resolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and unit-parent definition fit the leaf, including allowance for derived unit clauses. No cited source or specific locator supports the selected convention or the stated refutation characterization.

children.title: Input–Unit Strength Relations
children.top_down_role: Relative expressive power and refutation reach of the two restricted systems.

assumptions_latex: Input and unit restrictions are imposed on immediate inference parents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither syntactic proof class contains the other, although both are contained in general resolution.
review_flags: The comparison depends on immediate-parent and proof-transformation conventions.
A source treating input-unit simulation or refutation equivalences is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares derivations syntactically, not formula classes after transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the immediate-parent definitions, \(\mathsf{IR}\subseteq\mathsf{R}\) and \(\mathsf{UR}\subseteq\mathsf{R}\), but \(\mathsf{IR}\) and \(\mathsf{UR}\) are incomparable. Resolving the two input clauses \(x\lor a\) and \(\neg x\lor b\) is an input step but not a unit step. Conversely, a unit step may resolve a derived unit \(\{u\}\) with a derived clause \(\neg u\lor v\); it is then a unit step but not an input step. Claims about equality of refutation power require additional conventions and are not implied by these inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With immediate-parent restrictions, input and unit resolution are incomparable syntactic subclasses of general resolution; transformations may yield different refutation-level comparisons.
knowledge_statements.title: Input–Unit Strength Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits this comparison leaf, and the examples plausibly distinguish the two immediate-parent restrictions. The incomparability claim depends on the precise universe of derivations and reuse conventions, so it requires a source treating these exact syntactic classes and a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: Each extension variable is fresh when introduced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extended resolution is resolution augmented by satisfiability-preserving definitional extensions.
review_flags: A proof-complexity source fixing the allowed extension basis is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-disjunction extension rule; other finite Boolean bases are polynomially equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An extended-resolution derivation may introduce a fresh variable \(y\) abbreviating \(\ell_1\lor\ell_2\), where \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) use previously available variables. The definition is encoded by the extension clauses
\[ (
eg y\lor\ell_1\lor\ell_2)\land(y\lor
eg\ell_1)\land(y\lor
eg\ell_2), \]
which express \(y\leftrightarrow(\ell_1\lor\ell_2)\). Ordinary resolution may then use both input and extension clauses. An extended-resolution refutation of \(F\) is a derivation of \( ot\) from \(F\) together with finitely many such acyclic definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended resolution introduces fresh variables for previously expressible formulas through definitional clauses, then applies ordinary resolution to the enlarged clause set.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended Resolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definitional clauses correctly encode the displayed binary-disjunction extension, and definition is an appropriate content kind. A proof-complexity source must nevertheless fix the extension rule, freshness and acyclicity requirements, and allowed basis; no citation is supplied.

assumptions_latex: Every propagated literal has an antecedent clause that became unit under the current assignment.
A conflict clause is falsified by the current assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The learned clause has a resolution derivation from the conflict and antecedent clauses and is entailed by the database.
review_flags: The polarity of the literal eliminated during conflict analysis has been corrected.
A CDCL source specifying the conflict-analysis scheme and resolution correspondence is still required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolution interpretation of implication-graph conflict analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with the falsified conflict clause \(C_0\). If \(C_i\) contains \(\neg\ell\), where \(\ell\) is a propagated literal selected for elimination, and the antecedent of \(\ell\) is \(A_\ell=\ell\lor D\), resolve \(C_i\) with \(A_\ell\) on the variable of \(\ell\) to obtain \(C_{i+1}\). Continue until the chosen conflict-analysis stopping condition is met, and output \(L=C_t\). Every antecedent clause \(A_\ell\) belongs to the current database \(F\), so the sequence is a resolution derivation and \(F\models L\). For first-UIP learning, the stopping condition leaves exactly one literal in \(L\) whose variable is assigned at the current decision level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conflict analysis resolves each negated propagated literal in the conflict clause against the antecedent that implied that literal. The terminal resolvent is an entailed learned clause; first-UIP learning leaves exactly one literal from the current decision level.
knowledge_statements.title: Learned-Clause Derivation View

assumptions_latex: CDCL uses asserting clause learning, retains learned clauses, and may restart after conflicts.
Branching choices may be selected to realize a prescribed simulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Idealized CDCL polynomially simulates general resolution, while each learned clause is resolution derivable.

notation.meaning: Size of a general resolution refutation

review_flags: The exact polynomial depends on the CDCL, learning, restart, and size conventions.
Authoritative simulation theorem and locator are required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idealized nondeterministic CDCL with learning, retention, and unrestricted restarts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be an unsatisfiable CNF formula on \(n\) variables having a general resolution refutation of size \(s\). Under the stated idealized CDCL model, there is a choice of decisions, conflict analyses, and restarts that derives unsatisfiability using \(\operatorname{poly}(n,s)\) decisions, propagations, conflicts, and learned clauses. Conversely, every clause learned by conflict analysis has a resolution derivation from clauses present in the database at that conflict. Thus this CDCL model and general resolution simulate one another with polynomial overhead under compatible proof encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Idealized CDCL with asserting learning, clause retention, and unrestricted restarts polynomially simulates general resolution, and its learned clauses possess resolution derivations.
knowledge_statements.title: CDCL–Resolution Simulation Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the simulation-relations leaf, but the polynomial simulation depends on exact learning, restart, branching, deletion, proof-encoding, and cost conventions. The learned-clause derivability observation alone does not establish the full converse simulation bound. A precise theorem citation and locator are required.

children.title: CDCL Restart Regimes
children.top_down_role: Restart availability and scheduling within CDCL proof search.

assumptions_latex: A restart preserves the clause database but erases the current partial assignment and decision stack.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A restart regime is determined by its trigger sequence and its clause-retention policy.

notation.meaning: Cumulative conflict counts at restart times

review_flags: A standard SAT reference defining restart schedules and retention variants is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract restart schedules separated from branching and learning choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A CDCL restart regime consists of a strictly increasing sequence \((r_i)_{i\geq1}\) of conflict counts, or an adaptive rule producing such counts, together with a learned-clause retention policy. At conflict count \(r_i\), the solver cancels all decision assignments, returns to decision level zero, performs root-level propagation, and continues with database \(F_i\). A regime is restart-free if the sequence is empty, bounded-restart if it is finite, and unrestricted if no a priori bound is placed on the number or spacing of restarts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CDCL restart regime specifies when the assignment is cleared and which learned clauses survive; it may be restart-free, finitely bounded, or unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.title: CDCL Restart Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the appropriate role for this leaf, and the schedule categories are internally coherent. No source or locator is supplied for the asserted restart semantics, root-level behavior, or treatment of clause retention as part of the regime.

children.title: Restart-Induced Proof Strength
children.top_down_role: Effects of restarts on the resolution derivations reachable by CDCL.

assumptions_latex: CDCL uses asserting learning and retains the clauses required by the simulation.
Restarts and branching decisions are unrestricted and nondeterministically selectable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restarts permit polynomial simulation of DAG-like general resolution by reusing learned clauses across independent search episodes.

notation.meaning: Size of a general resolution refutation

review_flags: The content kind has been corrected from principle to complexity_bound.
Strength depends materially on learning, deletion, branching, restart, proof-encoding, and cost conventions.
A precise restart-based simulation theorem and polynomial-bound locator are still required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proof-complexity role of unrestricted restarts in idealized CDCL.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an unsatisfiable CNF formula \(F\) has a general resolution refutation of size \(s\). In the stated idealized model, a CDCL run can learn clauses corresponding to successive nodes of that resolution DAG, restart to discard assignments that served only to derive the current clause, and retain the learned clause for later reuse. With suitable decisions and conflict analyses, this yields a refutation using \(\operatorname{poly}(s,|F|)\) solver steps. The claim does not extend automatically to restart-free runs or to policies that delete clauses needed later.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unrestricted restarts let idealized CDCL separate clause derivations while retaining their results, enabling a polynomial-size simulation of DAG-like general resolution under the stated policies.
knowledge_statements.title: Restart-Induced Proof Strength

children.title: Restart-Free Simulation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on proof simulation when restarts are absent or restricted.

assumptions_latex: The input is a CNF formula \(F\), and every learned clause is derived by sound conflict analysis.
Backjumping is conflict-driven; no voluntary operation resets a nonempty trail to decision level \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The corresponding proof trace is restricted to clauses obtainable along one uninterrupted sequence of decisions, propagations, conflicts, and forced backjumps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational boundary for CDCL runs without voluntary restarts; no stronger proof-complexity equivalence is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restart-free CDCL run on \(F\) is a sequence of trails \(T\) changed only by decisions, unit propagation, conflict analysis, and the backjump prescribed by a detected conflict. It contains no voluntary transition from a consistent nonempty trail to the empty trail. Consequently, any clause used later must have been learned earlier on this uninterrupted run and retained, or must be an original clause. This restriction defines the restart-free simulation boundary; it does not by itself identify the resulting traces with all unrestricted resolution refutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without restarts, the trail changes only through decisions, propagation, conflict analysis, and forced backjumping; learned clauses must arise and remain available within that uninterrupted run.
knowledge_statements.title: Restart-Free Simulation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The operational description is plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the claimed proof-trace restriction and its precise simulation significance require a SAT proof-complexity source with a specific locator.

children.title: Learning-Scheme Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Constraints on which conflict-derived clauses may be learned.

assumptions_latex: The active database is a CNF formula \(F\), and conflict analysis produces a candidate clause \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only clauses satisfying the selected learning predicate may enter the active database.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract admissibility condition covering asserting, conflict-graph, and bounded-width learning schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A learning scheme is a predicate \(L(F,C)\) governing clause admission. It is sound when \(L(F,C)\) implies \(F\models C\). A conflict-graph restriction additionally requires \(C\) to be obtainable by resolving the conflict clause with reason clauses from the current implication graph. An asserting restriction requires that, after the prescribed backjump, unit propagation on the retained database makes \(C\) unit. Width, length, or variable restrictions may be conjoined with these conditions but cannot replace semantic soundness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learning scheme admits only entailed clauses meeting its syntactic or operational restrictions, such as conflict-graph derivability, asserting behavior, or bounded width.
knowledge_statements.title: Learning-Scheme Restrictions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits, but the conflict-graph and asserting restrictions require authoritative definitions. In particular, the retained database and whether it already contains C must be clarified in the asserting condition.

children.title: Clause-Forgetting Policies
children.top_down_role: Retention and deletion choices for learned clauses.

assumptions_latex: The active database \(F_t\) contains original clauses and currently retained learned clauses.
A deletion policy never deletes an original clause required by the chosen solver convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deletion changes future propagation and available antecedents but does not constitute a logical inference.

notation.meaning: active clause database at time t
set of learned clauses selected for deletion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic learned-clause deletion algorithm, independent of a particular activity or quality score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a deletion event, compute a removable set \(D_t\subseteq F_t\) using the policy's scores and protection rules, then update \(F_{t+1}=F_t\setminus D_t\). Clauses currently serving as locked reason clauses may be protected until unlocked. Subsequent propagation, conflict analysis, and redundancy checks use only \(F_{t+1}\). If a deleted clause is needed later, it must be learned again or rederived. The policy stops deleting when its database-size or score threshold is met and outputs the reduced active database.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forgetting policy removes selected learned clauses, preserves protected clauses, and makes all later propagation and conflict analysis use only the reduced database.
knowledge_statements.title: Clause-Forgetting Policies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits this policy leaf, but protection of locked clauses, stopping criteria, and database-update semantics are implementation-dependent and have no cited support.

children.title: Retention–Strength Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Proof-strength limits induced by restricted learning or aggressive forgetting.

assumptions_latex: Every learned clause is sound for the original CNF formula.
A clause may be used as an antecedent only while it is retained in the active database.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Retention cannot affect refutation soundness, but restricted retention can increase proof length or prevent a prescribed simulation.

notation.meaning: active retained database at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates semantic soundness from proof-size strength under learned-clause retention restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because every active learned clause \(C\) satisfies \(F_0\models C\), replacing \(F_t\) by any subdatabase containing \(F_0\) preserves semantic soundness. Proof strength is nevertheless retention-sensitive: a later inference may use \(C\) only if \(C\in F_t\), unless \(C\) is rederived. Thus unrestricted retention can realize traces whose reuse pattern is unavailable under bounded-memory or mandatory-forgetting policies; any claimed proof-system simulation must account for the cost of such rederivations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forgetting sound learned clauses preserves correctness, but it can destroy clause reuse, enlarge refutations, or invalidate simulations that assume unrestricted retention.
knowledge_statements.title: Retention–Strength Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits. Semantic soundness under deletion is plausible, but the proof-length and simulation consequences require a specifically located proof-complexity source.

children.title: RUP System
children.top_down_role: Proof records based on reverse unit propagation checks.

assumptions_latex: The active formula \(F\) and candidate \(C\) are clauses over finitely many Boolean variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A RUP refutation is locally checkable by unit propagation and certifies that the initial formula is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard reverse-unit-propagation addition rule and refutation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A clause \(C\) has the reverse unit propagation property with respect to \(F\) when \(F\land\bigwedge_{\ell\in C}\neg\ell\vdash_1\bot\). A RUP derivation from \(F_0\) is a sequence \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) such that each \(C_i\) is RUP with respect to \(F_{i-1}=F_0\cup\{C_1,\ldots,C_{i-1}\}\). It is a RUP refutation when \(C_m=\varnothing\). Each addition is entailed by the current database, and the final empty clause certifies unsatisfiability of \(F_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clause is RUP when assuming all its literals false makes unit propagation conflict. A sequence of such additions ending with the empty clause certifies unsatisfiability.
knowledge_statements.title: RUP System

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind and RUP formulation are mathematically standard, but no citation or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: DRUP System
children.top_down_role: RUP proof records extended with clause-deletion information.

assumptions_latex: The input \(F_0\) is a finite CNF formula.
Additions are checked against the currently active database.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A DRUP trace ending by addition of \(\varnothing\) certifies unsatisfiability of \(F_0\).

notation.meaning: active clause database after step i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard deletion reverse-unit-propagation trace semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DRUP derivation is a sequence of addition and deletion steps starting from \(F_0\). An addition of \(C_i\) is valid only if \(F_{i-1}\land\bigwedge_{\ell\in C_i}\neg\ell\vdash_1\bot\), after which \(F_i=F_{i-1}\cup\{C_i\}\). A deletion of an active clause \(C_i\) sets \(F_i=F_{i-1}\setminus\{C_i\}\) and requires no redundancy test. The derivation is a refutation when a valid addition introduces \(\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DRUP extends RUP traces with unchecked clause deletions. Every addition is RUP against the active database, and adding the empty clause certifies unsatisfiability.
knowledge_statements.title: DRUP System

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits and the trace semantics are plausible, but the definition lacks an authoritative format or proof-system citation with a specific locator.

children.title: DRUP Deletion Semantics
children.top_down_role: Consequences of deletion records for proof maintenance and validation.

assumptions_latex: Every added clause is RUP with respect to the active database at its addition step.
Deletion removes only an occurrence currently represented in the database.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing all deletion commands yields a sound RUP derivation, so deletion affects checking resources but not logical validity.

notation.meaning: active database immediately before an addition
database obtained by retaining previously deleted clauses

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical meaning of DRUP deletion, apart from format-specific duplicate-clause conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DRUP deletion asserts no consequence and needs no redundancy justification; it only removes a clause from the active checking database. If an addition \(C\) is RUP with respect to \(F\), then it remains RUP with respect to every superset \(F'\supseteq F\), because the same unit-propagation conflict remains available. Therefore erasing deletion commands preserves validity of all subsequent additions. Deletions can reduce memory and propagation work, but they cannot strengthen the logical certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DRUP deletion only changes the active checker database. Erasing deletions leaves a valid RUP derivation because RUP remains valid when clauses are restored.
knowledge_statements.title: DRUP Deletion Semantics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits. Monotonicity supports erasing deletions under set semantics, but duplicate-clause and occurrence-deletion conventions must be fixed and sourced.

assumptions_latex: The active database \(F\) is CNF, \(C\) is a candidate clause, and \(p\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adding a RAT clause preserves satisfiability and is checkable through finitely many RUP tests.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard resolution-asymmetric-tautology condition with one designated pivot literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clause is RAT on a pivot when every resolvent against a clause containing the opposite pivot is tautological or RUP. RAT addition preserves satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.title: RAT Redundancy System

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits and the pivoted RAT predicate is plausible, but its equisatisfiability claim and the pivot-free rule used to add the empty clause require an authoritative locator.

assumptions_latex: The candidate clause \(C\) is nonempty, and \(\alpha_C\) is the partial assignment falsifying every literal of \(C\).
Formula restriction by a partial assignment removes satisfied clauses and falsified literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A PR addition is accepted when its witness makes every restricted target clause derivable by unit propagation from the falsifying restriction.

notation.meaning: restriction of F by an assignment rho

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Witness-based propagation-redundancy predicate; conventions vary for restrictions and tautological clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A clause \(C\) is propagation redundant with respect to \(F\) if there exists a partial assignment \(\omega\) satisfying \(C\) such that every clause \(D\in F\vert_\omega\) is RUP from \(F\vert_{\alpha_C}\); equivalently, \((F\vert_{\alpha_C})\land\bigwedge_{\ell\in D}\neg\ell\vdash_1\bot\) for each such \(D\). The assignment \(\omega\) is a checkable redundancy witness. A propagation-redundancy proof system admits these additions, optional deletions, and certifies unsatisfiability by deriving \(\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation redundancy uses an assignment satisfying the candidate clause as a witness; unit propagation must derive every witness-restricted clause from the restriction falsifying the candidate.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-Redundancy Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits, but propagation-redundancy definitions depend on exact restriction, witness, implication, and tautology conventions. The stated formulation cannot be confirmed without a specific authoritative source.

children.title: Clausal Redundancy Strength
children.top_down_role: Proof power available through clausal redundancy additions.

assumptions_latex: Two clausal proof systems are compared by the number of literal occurrences in their encoded traces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(P\)'s admissibility predicate implies \(Q\)'s predicate stepwise, then \(Q\) simulates \(P\) with no increase in trace length.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stepwise criterion for comparing clausal redundancy systems; specific strict separations are not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every addition admitted by \(P\) against any active database is also admitted by \(Q\) against that database, and both systems give deletions the same semantics. Then every \(P\)-refutation \(\pi\) is already a \(Q\)-refutation, with unchanged clause sequence and \(s_Q(\pi)=s_P(\pi)\). Thus inclusion of local redundancy predicates yields simulation of proof systems. The converse need not follow, because a global polynomial simulation may replace one source step by many target steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inclusion of clause-admission predicates gives a step-for-step simulation. General polynomial simulation may still exist without such local inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Clausal Redundancy Strength

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind is suitable. The stepwise-inclusion argument is plausible, but its applicability requires formally defined systems, identical deletion semantics, and a cited size convention.

children.title: Extended-Resolution Strength
children.top_down_role: Proof power available through extension variables and extended-resolution reasoning.

assumptions_latex: The initial formula \(F\) is CNF over variables \(X\).
Each fresh extension variable is introduced once and does not occur in earlier clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extended resolution measures refutation size after allowing conservative definitional extensions followed by ordinary resolution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-disjunction presentation of extended resolution; other bounded-fan-in extension bases are polynomially interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An extended-resolution derivation may introduce a fresh variable \(x\) abbreviating \(a\lor b\) by adding the definitional clauses \((
eg x\lor a\lor b)\), \((x\lor
eg a)\), and \((x\lor
eg b)\). It may then apply ordinary resolution and weakening to original, extension, and derived clauses. An extended-resolution refutation derives \(\varnothing\). Its size counts the encoded extension clauses and resolution derivation, so strength comparisons must include both definition introduction and subsequent inference cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended resolution augments resolution with fresh variables defined by small formulas, then derives the empty clause using the original and extension clauses.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Resolution Strength

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a standard-looking definition of extended resolution, but the leaf concerns strength and the statement also fixes weakening and a size measure. These conventions and the intended terminal role require a specific proof-complexity source.

children.title: Redundancy–Extension Simulations
children.top_down_role: Simulation and separation relations between redundancy systems and extended resolution.

assumptions_latex: Proof size is the encoded number of literal occurrences, and translations must be computable in polynomial time.
RAT traces permit fresh variables and the standard deletion semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under standard encodings, extended resolution and RAT-based clausal redundancy proofs polynomially simulate one another.

notation.meaning: proof of F in system P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial simulation claim for standard ER and RAT encodings, not for every restricted implementation format.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For standard encodings there exist polynomials \(p\) and \(q\) such that every \(ER\)-refutation \(\pi_{ER}(F)\) can be translated into a \(RAT\)-refutation of size at most \(p(|\pi_{ER}(F)|)\), and every \(RAT\)-refutation \(\pi_{RAT}(F)\) can be translated into an \(ER\)-refutation of size at most \(q(|\pi_{RAT}(F)|)\). In the forward direction, RAT additions encode extension definitions; the reverse direction replaces satisfiability-preserving RAT steps by extension variables and resolution derivations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With standard encodings and fresh variables, RAT-based redundancy proofs and extended resolution admit polynomial-size translations in both directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy–Extension Simulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bidirectional polynomial-simulation assertion is a theorem rather than a duality. Its validity depends on the exact RAT system, fresh-variable permissions, deletion rules, encodings, and size measure, none of which is supported by a cited locator.

children.title: Propagation Soundness
children.top_down_role: Validity obligations for implications produced by Boolean propagation.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
\(\alpha\) is a consistent partial assignment.
Every propagation step applies the unit-clause rule to the current restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\land\alpha\models \ell\) for every propagated literal \(\ell\); a derived empty clause implies that no total model of \(F\) extends \(\alpha\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses SAT unit propagation; an authoritative SAT reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit propagation under a consistent partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite CNF formula and \(\alpha\) a consistent partial assignment. If a clause of \(F\) restricted by the current assignment has exactly one unassigned literal \(\ell\) and all its other literals are false, extending the assignment by \(\ell\) preserves every total model extending the current assignment. Consequently, every literal obtained by iterated unit propagation satisfies \(F\land\alpha\models\ell\). If propagation produces the empty clause, then \(F\land\alpha\) is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit propagation derives only literals forced by the formula and current assignment; a propagation conflict certifies that the assignment has no satisfying extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Soundness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-propagation soundness claim is mathematically precise and fits the leaf, but no inspectable SAT source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Learned-Clause Soundness
children.top_down_role: Validity obligations for clauses derived from conflicts.

knowledge_statements.title: Learned-Clause Soundness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolution-based conflict clauses in CDCL.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a CNF formula. Suppose conflict analysis derives a clause \(C\) from clauses \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), where \(F\models C_i\) for every \(i\), using only resolution and deletion of duplicate literals. Since each resolution resolvent is entailed by its premises, the derivation certifies \(F\models C\). Therefore adding \(C\) preserves the model set: \(\operatorname{Mod}(F\land C)=\operatorname{Mod}(F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clause learned by sound conflict resolution is entailed by the original formula, so adding it cannot create or remove satisfying assignments.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a CNF formula.
Each premise used in conflict analysis is entailed by \(F\).
The learned clause \(C\) is obtained by sound resolution steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\models C\), and hence \(F\) and \(F\land C\) have exactly the same models.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports resolution-based clause learning; an authoritative CDCL or proof-complexity reference is required.

children.title: Propagation–Learning Interaction
children.top_down_role: Soundness dependencies linking propagated implications to learned clauses.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
Every clause in the learned database \(L\) is entailed by \(F\).
Propagation uses only clauses of \(F\cup L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Propagation from \(F\land L\land\alpha\) remains sound relative to \(F\land\alpha\), and learning preserves \(\operatorname{Mod}(F)\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses the CDCL propagation-learning invariant; an authoritative SAT reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic invariant coupling propagation and clause learning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite CNF formula and \(L\) a learned-clause database satisfying \(F\models D\) for every \(D\in L\). Then \(F\land L\) is equivalent to \(F\). For any consistent partial assignment \(\alpha\), every literal propagated from \(F\land L\land\alpha\) is therefore entailed by \(F\land\alpha\). If conflict analysis subsequently learns \(C\) with \(F\models C\), replacing \(L\) by \(L\cup\{C\}\) preserves this invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entailed learned clauses may strengthen propagation without changing the models, and each soundly learned clause preserves that invariant for later propagation.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation–Learning Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The propagation–learning invariant is coherent and appropriately classified as a principle, but it has no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Complete-Search Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage requirements for exhaustive satisfiability search.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a CNF formula over a finite variable set \(V\).
Search branches on an unassigned variable into both truth values.
Every branch is eventually explored unless propagation closes it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search returns a model of \(F\) or closes every total assignment and correctly declares \(F\) unsatisfiable.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses DPLL search completeness; an authoritative SAT reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive binary DPLL search on finitely many variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A search has complete-search coverage for a CNF formula \(F\) over finite \(V\) when every open node labeled by a partial assignment \(\alpha\) either is extended to a model, is closed by a sound conflict, or is split on some \(x\in V\setminus\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)\) into \(\alpha\cup\{x=0\}\) and \(\alpha\cup\{x=1\}\), with both children eventually processed. Under these conditions, failure to find a model after all leaves close implies that \(F\) is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete SAT search either finds a model or soundly closes both branches for every assignment choice, thereby covering all total assignments.
knowledge_statements.title: Complete-Search Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite exhaustive-search coverage condition is precise and locally appropriate, but no DPLL completeness source is cited.

children.title: Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solver configurations under which finite completion is supported.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) has a finite variable set \(V\).
Branching assigns a previously unassigned variable.
The control policy cannot postpone an open finite-depth branch forever.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search processes only finitely many distinct partial assignments and terminates with either a model or exhaustive closure.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports SAT termination regimes, especially policies with restarts; a dedicated reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient termination conditions for finite exhaustive search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) use \(n=|V|<\infty\) variables. A chronological exhaustive search terminates if every descent assigns a previously unassigned variable and every unresolved sibling is eventually visited, because its search tree has depth at most \(n\) and at most \(2^{n+1}-1\) nodes. More generally, a restart-enabled regime terminates when it permits only finitely many restarts or otherwise guarantees permanent progress through a finite set of search obligations; sound inference alone does not guarantee this control property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-variable search terminates when each descent makes assignment progress and scheduling eventually processes every open branch; unrestricted restarts require an additional progress guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Termination Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated termination regimes are plausible, but the restart-enabled progress condition requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Completeness Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Restrictions or policies that can undermine exhaustive search guarantees.

assumptions_latex:
\(F=(x\lor y)\land(x\lor
eg y)\land(
eg x\lor y)\land(
eg x\lor
eg y)\).
The solver restarts immediately after every first decision.
No clause is learned before each restart.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure may run forever although \(F\) is unsatisfiable, so local inference soundness does not imply search completeness.
review_flags: The concrete boundary is elementary but no supplied source locator addresses restart-induced incompleteness; external support is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nontermination caused by restarts without persistent progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(F=(x\lor y)\land(x\lor
eg y)\land(
eg x\lor y)\land(
eg x\lor
eg y)\). The formula is unsatisfiable, but root-level unit propagation derives nothing. A procedure that repeatedly decides only \(x\), restarts before deciding \(y\), and retains no learned clause repeats forever without reaching a conflict. Thus removing fairness or persistent progress permits an inference-sound procedure to be incomplete as a decision procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsatisfiable two-variable formula can make an always-restarting solver loop forever when restarts occur before conflicts and preserve no search progress.
knowledge_statements.title: Completeness Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon fits the container, but the policy must be sourced and clarified to restart before post-decision propagation; otherwise deciding x triggers unit propagation and a conflict in the displayed formula.

children.title: Restart Safety
children.top_down_role: Preservation of valid solver state and search guarantees across restarts.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the original CNF formula.
Every retained learned clause is entailed by \(F\).
A restart removes decision and propagated assignments but retains \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After restart the active clause database remains equivalent to \(F\), and no model or valid refutation is lost semantically.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses CDCL restart safety; an authoritative SAT reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic safety of discarding the CDCL assignment trail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the active database be \(F\land\bigwedge_{C\in L}C\), where \(F\models C\) for every retained learned clause \(C\). A restart replaces the current trail \(\alpha\) by the empty trail without modifying \(F\) or introducing a non-entailed clause. Since the trail is search state rather than a permanent constraint, this operation leaves the active database equivalent to \(F\). It may change future search order, but it cannot change satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discarding the current assignment trail is semantically safe when the original formula and only entailed learned clauses remain active.
knowledge_statements.title: Restart Safety

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic restart-safety property is correctly scoped, but no authoritative CDCL restart reference or locator is supplied.

children.title: Clause-Deletion Safety
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which learned clauses may be discarded safely.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the original CNF formula.
Every learned clause in \(L\) is entailed by \(F\).
Deletion chooses an arbitrary subset \(D\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\land\bigwedge_{C\in L\setminus D}C\equiv F\), so deleting such clauses preserves satisfiability and models.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports learned-clause deletion safety; an authoritative CDCL reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic deletion of redundant learned clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the immutable original CNF and let \(L\) contain only clauses \(C\) satisfying \(F\models C\). For any deletion set \(D\subseteq L\), the remaining database satisfies \(F\land\bigwedge_{C\in L\setminus D}C\equiv F\). Hence deleting clauses from \(L\) cannot alter the models or satisfiability of \(F\). This condition does not authorize deletion of original clauses unless their redundancy is separately certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any subset of learned clauses entailed by the original formula may be deleted without changing its models; original-clause deletion needs separate justification.
knowledge_statements.title: Clause-Deletion Safety

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated entailment condition correctly supports deletion safety, but it lacks an inspectable CDCL source.

children.title: Restart–Deletion Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined effects of state resets and learned-clause removal on solver guarantees.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the immutable original CNF.
Every retained learned clause is entailed by \(F\).
Restarts discard only the trail, while deletion removes only eligible learned clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every interleaving leaves the active clause database equivalent to \(F\), although completeness additionally requires a progress policy.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses the combined restart-deletion invariant; an authoritative SAT reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant under interleaved CDCL restarts and learned-clause deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At time \(t\), let the solver state contain trail \(\alpha_t\) and learned clauses \(L_t\), with \(F\models C\) for every \(C\in L_t\). Any interleaving of operations that either resets \(\alpha_t\) or replaces \(L_t\) by a subset preserves \(F\land\bigwedge_{C\in L_t}C\equiv F\). Thus restarts and eligible deletions compose semantically. Nevertheless, deleting all progress-bearing clauses while restarting indefinitely can destroy termination or completeness without violating satisfiability preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safe restarts and safe learned-clause deletions remain satisfiability preserving when interleaved, but an aggressive policy can still eliminate progress and prevent termination.
knowledge_statements.title: Restart–Deletion Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The combined semantic invariant and its separation from progress are appropriate, but no source supports the interleaved restart–deletion claim.

children.title: Preprocessing Satisfiability Preservation
children.top_down_role: Preservation of satisfiability status across preprocessing transformations.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) maps CNF formulas to CNF formulas.
The transformation may introduce or eliminate variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Preprocessing is satisfiability preserving exactly when \(F\in\mathrm{SAT}\iff F'\in\mathrm{SAT}\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses SAT preprocessing or equisatisfiability; an authoritative preprocessing reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equisatisfiability, not necessarily logical equivalence over identical variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a preprocessing transformation \(P\) and input CNF formula \(F\), write \(F'=P(F)\). The transformation is satisfiability preserving when \(F\) has a total satisfying assignment if and only if \(F'\) has one: \(F\in\mathrm{SAT}\iff F'\in\mathrm{SAT}\). This obligation is equisatisfiability rather than literal formula equivalence; \(P\) may add auxiliary variables, eliminate original variables, or change the model set projected onto variables not designated for reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A SAT preprocessor is satisfiability preserving when its output is satisfiable exactly when its input is, even if variables and individual models change.
knowledge_statements.title: Preprocessing Satisfiability Preservation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equisatisfiability condition is precise and correctly distinguished from logical equivalence, but no SAT-preprocessing citation is supplied.

children.title: Preprocessing Model Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of original-instance models from simplified-instance models.

knowledge_statements.title: Preprocessing Model Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-based lifting of a simplified-formula model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a preprocessing trace \(T=(t_1,\ldots,t_k)\) for \(F'=P(F)\) and a total assignment \(\beta\models F'\). Initialize \(\alpha_k:=\beta\). For \(i=k,k-1,\ldots,1\), apply the inverse model-extension rule recorded by \(t_i\), obtaining \(\alpha_{i-1}\) from \(\alpha_i\). Stop after \(t_1\) and output \(\alpha:=\alpha_0\) restricted to the variables of \(F\). Correct reconstruction requires every inverse rule to ensure that satisfaction after step \(i\) extends to satisfaction before that step, yielding \(\alpha\models F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replay preprocessing records backward, extending the simplified model at each step, then output its restriction as a model of the original formula.
assumptions_latex: \(F'=P(F)\) is the preprocessed CNF.
\(T\) is reconstruction information emitted by preprocessing.
\(\beta\models F'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstruction procedure returns \(R(T,\beta)=\alpha\) with \(\alpha\models F\).

notation.meaning: Reconstructed model of the original formula

review_flags: The exact reconstruction rules depend on preprocessing techniques, and no relevant source locator was supplied.

children.title: Preprocessing Proof Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery or elaboration of proof evidence across preprocessing transformations.

assumptions_latex: \(F'=P(F)\) is produced with a checkable preprocessing trace \(T\).
\(\pi'\) is a refutation of \(F'\).
Each recorded transformation has a sound proof-lifting rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstructed object \(R_{\mathrm{proof}}(T,\pi')=\pi\) is a checkable refutation of \(F\).

notation.meaning: Reconstructed refutation of the original formula

review_flags: Proof reconstruction depends on the chosen proof system and preprocessing rules; no relevant source locator was supplied.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-based lifting of an UNSAT proof through preprocessing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let preprocessing transform \(F\) into \(F'\) while emitting a trace \(T=(t_1,\ldots,t_k)\). Given a checkable refutation \(\pi'\) of \(F'\), process \(T\) in reverse order and apply the proof-lifting rule associated with each \(t_i\). If every lifting rule converts a refutation after its transformation into a refutation before it, the resulting object \(\pi=R_{\mathrm{proof}}(T,\pi')\) derives the empty clause from \(F\) in the designated proof system and is independently checkable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse the preprocessing trace and lift the simplified formula's refutation step by step to obtain a checkable refutation of the original formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Preprocessing Proof Reconstruction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional lifting claim fits proof reconstruction, but its validity depends on the designated proof system and transformation-specific lifting rules, for which no source is supplied.

assumptions_latex: The proof system \(P\) has a polynomial-time checker \(V_P\).
The solver starts from a CNF formula \(F_0\) and may replace it by formulas \(F_1,\ldots,F_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Checker acceptance of the emitted and reconstructed proof certifies that \(F_0\) is unsatisfiable.

notation.meaning: proof checker for the proof system
reconstruction map associated with transformation step \(i\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A reconstruction-based preservation condition for proof-producing SAT solvers with preprocessing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Proof emission is preserved when every transformation \(F_{i-1}\mapsto F_i\) has a computable reconstruction map \(R_i\) such that, for every \(P\)-refutation \(\pi_i\) of \(F_i\), the object \(R_i(\pi_i)\) is a \(P\)-refutation of \(F_{i-1}\), and every emitted search inference is accepted by \(V_P\). Consequently, if \(\pi_k\) refutes \(F_k\), then \(R_1(R_2(\cdots R_k(\pi_k)\cdots))\) is accepted as a refutation of \(F_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof emission is preserved when every transformation supports checked backward reconstruction, so an accepted final trace yields a refutation of the original formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Emission Preservation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the Proof-Emission Preservation container and is mathematically plausible, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the reconstruction obligation, checker assumptions, or certification conclusion. Source uncertainty is material because preservation requirements depend on the proof format and transformation framework.

children.title: Proof Size
children.top_down_role: Aggregate representation cost of a proof.

assumptions_latex: A proof \(\pi=(C_1,\ldots,C_L)\) is written as a sequence of clauses.
The encoding size \(|C_i|_{\mathrm{enc}}\) counts symbols in the fixed clause encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proof size is \(S(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{L}|C_i|_{\mathrm{enc}}\).

notation.meaning: encoded symbol size of a clause

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic size of a sequential clause proof under a fixed reasonable encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a clause proof \(\pi=(C_1,\\ldots,C_L)\) in a fixed proof system and encoding, its proof size is the total encoded size of all proof lines: \[S(\pi):=\sum_{i=1}^{L}|C_i|_{\mathrm{enc}}.\] If literals and separators have constant encoding cost, then \(S(\pi)\) is within constant factors of the total number of literal occurrences plus clause delimiters and inference annotations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof size is the total encoded symbol count of all clauses and required annotations appearing in the proof.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof Size

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Proof Size, but no cited proof-complexity source fixes the encoding convention or supports the constant-factor comparison. The displayed proof tuple also appears to contain a doubled backslash before ldots and should be checked when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Proof Length
children.top_down_role: Number of inference or record units in a proof.

assumptions_latex: A proof \(\pi=(C_1,\ldots,C_L)\) is represented as an ordered sequence of derived or downloaded clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proof length is \(L(\pi)=L\), the number of clause occurrences in the sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Line-count length for sequential clause proofs; repeated clauses are counted repeatedly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequential clause proof \(\pi=(C_1,\ldots,C_L)\), its proof length is \[L(\pi):=L.\] Every occurrence of an axiom download or derived clause counts as one line. If deletion instructions are represented separately, they are excluded from this clause-line convention unless the proof format explicitly declares them to be proof lines.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof length counts clause lines, including repeated downloads or derivations, under a stated convention for deletion instructions.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof Length

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The line-count definition fits Proof Length and clearly states its deletion convention, but it has no source reference or inspectable locator. A source is needed because conventions differ on whether axioms, downloads, deletions, and other commands count as proof lines.

children.title: Size–Length Relations
children.top_down_role: Correspondence and separation between aggregate size and inference count.

assumptions_latex: Every proof line has positive encoded size.
The maximum encoded line size is \(M(\pi):=\max_i |C_i|_{\mathrm{enc}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extent measures satisfy \(L(\pi)\leq S(\pi)\leq M(\pi)L(\pi)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary comparison under the local sequential-proof and positive line-size conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\pi=(C_1,\ldots,C_L)\), let \(S(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{L}|C_i|_{\mathrm{enc}}\) and \(M(\pi)=\max_{1\leq i\leq L}|C_i|_{\mathrm{enc}}\). If \(|C_i|_{\mathrm{enc}}\geq 1\) for every line, then \[L(\pi)\leq S(\pi)\leq M(\pi)L(\pi).\] Thus length and size are polynomially equivalent on proof families whose maximum line size is polynomially bounded in the relevant input parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Size lies between length and length times the largest line size; bounded line size therefore makes the two measures comparable.
knowledge_statements.title: Size–Length Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary inequalities fit Size–Length Relations under the stated positive line-size convention, but no citation supports the adopted size and length conventions or the concluding family-level comparison. An authoritative proof-complexity source with a specific locator is required.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an unsatisfiable CNF formula.
\(\pi\) is a resolution refutation of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resolution width is \(W(\pi)=\max_{C\in\pi}|C|\), and \(W(F\vdash\bot)=\min_{\pi}W(\pi)\).
