knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum clause width, including input clauses, in a resolution refutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The width of a clause \(C\) is its number of literals \(|C|\). The width of a resolution refutation \(\pi\) is \[W(\pi):=\max\{|C|:C\text{ occurs in }\pi\}.\] The resolution width required to refute an unsatisfiable CNF formula \(F\) is \[W(F\vdash\bot):=\min\{W(\pi):\pi\text{ is a resolution refutation of }F\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolution width is the largest clause width in a refutation; formula width is the minimum such maximum over all refutations.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolution Width

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and formulas fit Resolution Width, including input clauses, but the record supplies no source or locator. A resolution-complexity reference is required to confirm the precise proof and formula-level conventions.

children.title: Clause Space
children.top_down_role: Maximum number of clauses retained simultaneously during a proof.

assumptions_latex: A refutation is presented as configurations \(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_T\).
Each transition downloads, derives, or erases clauses according to the proof system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clause space is \(\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{cl}}=\max_t|\mathcal C_t|\).

notation.meaning: set or multiset of clauses simultaneously retained at time \(t\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blackboard clause space for configuration-style clause derivations with explicit erasure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a configuration derivation \(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_T\), where \(\mathcal C_t\) contains the clauses retained after step \(t\), its clause space is \[\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{cl}}(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_T):=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}|\mathcal C_t|.\] The clause space of refuting \(F\) is the minimum of this quantity over all legal configuration refutations of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clause space is the maximum number of clauses simultaneously retained during a configuration refutation, minimized over refutations for a formula measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Clause Space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The blackboard/configuration definition fits Clause Space, but no source supports the legal transition model, set-versus-multiset convention, or minimization over refutations. These convention-sensitive details require an authoritative source and specific locator.

children.title: Total Space
children.top_down_role: Aggregate simultaneous storage measured across retained proof objects.

assumptions_latex: A configuration \(\mathcal C_t\) consists of clauses retained simultaneously.
Clause size is measured by literal occurrences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total space is \(\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{tot}}=\max_t\sum_{C\in\mathcal C_t}|C|\).

notation.meaning: number of literal occurrences in clause \(C\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Literal-occurrence total space; representation overhead is omitted up to conventional additive terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a configuration derivation \(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_T\), its total space is \[\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_T):=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\sum_{C\in\mathcal C_t}|C|.\] Under this convention, each simultaneously stored literal occurrence contributes one unit. The total space required to refute \(F\) is the minimum total-space cost over all legal configuration refutations of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total space is the maximum simultaneous number of stored literal occurrences, minimized over legal refutations when used as a formula measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Total Space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The literal-occurrence definition fits Total Space, but the record has no citation or locator. A source is needed to establish that this is the intended total-space convention and to clarify treatment of clause and representation overhead.

children.title: Clause-to-Total Space Separation
children.top_down_role: Differences between clause-count memory and aggregate storage requirements.

assumptions_latex: At every time \(t\), all retained clauses have width at most \(W\).
Empty clauses contribute zero literal occurrences under the stated convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every configuration, \(\sum_{C\in\mathcal C_t}|C|\leq W|\mathcal C_t|\), while no width-free converse bounds total space by clause space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instantaneous separation showing why clause space alone does not control literal-occurrence space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every configuration \(\mathcal C_t\) of clauses of width at most \(W\), \[|\mathcal C_t|\leq \sum_{C\in\mathcal C_t}\max\{1,|C|\}\leq W|\mathcal C_t|\] when all clauses are nonempty. Without a width bound, bounded clause space does not bound total space: the singleton configuration \(\mathcal C=\{x_1\lor\cdots\lor x_n\}\) has clause space \(1\) and total space \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Width controls the gap between clause and total space; one arbitrarily wide stored clause already separates the two measures.
knowledge_statements.title: Clause-to-Total Space Separation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate for Clause-to-Total Space Separation, and the singleton wide-clause example is plausible. However, no source supports the claimed separation, and the assumptions mention empty clauses while the statement's lower bound is restricted to nonempty clauses; the width bound also needs an explicit positive-width convention. A sourced, convention-consistent formulation is required.

children.title: Proof Depth
children.top_down_role: Longest dependency-chain depth within a proof.

assumptions_latex: \(G_\pi\) is a rooted acyclic proof graph whose edges point from premises to conclusions.
Sources are axioms and the unique sink is the final conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proof depth is the maximum number of inference edges on an axiom-to-conclusion path in \(G_\pi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inference depth in a rooted proof DAG, measured in edges from axioms to the conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_\pi\) be the directed acyclic graph of a proof \(\pi\), with an edge from each premise occurrence to the inference using it. The proof depth is \[D(\pi):=\max\{\text{number of inference edges on }P:P\text{ is an axiom-to-conclusion path in }G_\pi\}.\] A proof consisting only of an axiom conclusion therefore has depth \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof depth is the longest number of inference steps along any dependency path from an axiom to the final conclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof Depth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Proof Depth and consistently uses edge depth with an axiom-only proof at depth zero. It nevertheless lacks any citation or inspectable locator establishing this convention for proof DAGs.

children.title: Proof Tree Structure
children.top_down_role: Branching, reuse, and dependency shape of proof derivations.

assumptions_latex: Each proof-line occurrence is either an axiom or the conclusion of an inference.
Dependencies are directed from premise occurrences to their conclusion occurrence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proof is represented by a rooted DAG; duplicating shared subderivations yields its tree unfolding.

notation.meaning: tree unfolding of the proof graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency-DAG representation and its canonical unfolding into a tree-like proof.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proof \(\pi\) has a dependency representation \(G_\pi=(V,E)\): vertices are proof-line occurrences, and \((u,v)\in E\) exactly when line \(u\) is used as an immediate premise in deriving line \(v\). A tree-like proof is one in which every derived occurrence is used at most once. Any proof DAG has a tree unfolding \(T_\pi\), obtained by copying a shared subderivation once for each outgoing use, with the same root conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proof forms a dependency DAG; copying every reused subderivation produces an equivalent tree-like unfolding with the same conclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof Tree Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind fits Proof Tree Structure, and the DAG-to-tree unfolding is standard in form. No source or locator supports the precise occurrence-based graph model, tree-like use condition, or preservation claim, so authoritative sourcing is required.

children.title: Depth–Structure Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relations between dependency depth and derivation shape.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a rooted proof tree with at most two premises per inference.
Its depth \(d\) is the largest root-to-leaf edge count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(N=|V(T)|\), then \(N\leq 2^{d+1}-1\) and \(d\geq\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial depth-size relation for proof trees with inference fan-in at most two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a rooted proof tree in which every inference vertex has at most two children, and let \(d\) be its maximum root-to-leaf distance. Then the number \(N\) of vertices satisfies \[N\leq 1+2+\cdots+2^d=2^{d+1}-1.\] Equivalently, every such tree with \(N\) vertices has \[d\geq \lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil-1.\] Shared subderivations can invalidate this tree-size conclusion when size is measured in the unexpanded proof DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary proof tree of depth d has at most exponentially many nodes; DAG sharing can avoid the corresponding tree-size cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Depth–Structure Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary-tree depth-size property fits Depth–Structure Tradeoffs and is internally consistent for the stated rooted-tree convention. It has no cited source or locator, however, and the proof-tree interpretation and DAG-sharing boundary require authoritative support.

assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) is a sequential clause refutation of length \(L\) and maximum width \(W\).
The same derivation is viewed as configurations \(\mathcal C_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its literal size and spaces obey \(L\leq S\leq O(WL)\) and \(\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{cl}}\leq \operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{tot}}\leq W\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{cl}}\), subject to encoding conventions.

notation.meaning: maximum clause width in the derivation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary per-proof comparisons, not stronger formula-level resolution tradeoff theorems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a clause refutation \(\pi\) of length \(L\) and width at most \(W\), constant-cost literal encoding gives \[L\leq S(\pi)\leq O((W+1)L).\] For every nonempty-clause configuration in the same derivation, \[|\mathcal C_t|\leq\sum_{C\in\mathcal C_t}|C|\leq W|\mathcal C_t|,\] and hence \[\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{cl}}(\pi)\leq\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{tot}}(\pi)\leq W\operatorname{Sp}_{\mathrm{cl}}(\pi).\] These inequalities compare one fixed proof; independently minimizing different measures need not preserve a common optimizing proof.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed bounded-width proof, width bounds both symbol size per line and total literal space per stored clause.
knowledge_statements.title: Size–Width–Space Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits Size–Width–Space Tradeoffs, but no source supports the encoding-dependent size bound or the space comparison. Moreover, the pointwise lower bound is stated only for nonempty-clause configurations, while a refutation normally reaches the empty clause; the derived whole-proof inequality therefore needs a convention such as charging at least one unit per stored clause. A sourced correction is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Pigeonhole-Principle Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard unary CNF encoding of the functional pigeonhole principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For integers \(m>n\ge 1\), introduce \(x_{i,j}\) for pigeon \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and hole \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The functional pigeonhole CNF is \[\operatorname{FPHP}_{m}^{n}= igwedge_{i=1}^{m}\left( igvee_{j=1}^{n}x_{i,j}ight)\wedge igwedge_{i=1}^{m} igwedge_{1\le j<k\le n}(
eg x_{i,j}\vee
eg x_{i,k})\wedge igwedge_{j=1}^{n} igwedge_{1\le i<k\le m}(
eg x_{i,j}\vee
eg x_{k,j}).\] Its clauses respectively require every pigeon to occupy a hole, forbid a pigeon from occupying two holes, and forbid two pigeons from sharing a hole. Consequently, \(\operatorname{FPHP}_{m}^{n}\) is unsatisfiable when \(m>n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unary functional encoding assigns every pigeon exactly one hole and prevents collisions; it is unsatisfiable whenever there are more pigeons than holes.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(m>n\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{FPHP}_{m}^{n}\) is an unsatisfiable CNF representation of an injection from \(m\) pigeons into \(n\) holes.

notation.meaning: Pigeon i is assigned to hole j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no cited source supports the encoding convention or unsatisfiability claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Tseitin Contradictions on Expanders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolution lower bound for inconsistent parity charges on bounded-degree expanders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a bounded-degree graph with edge expansion at least \(h>0\), and let \(b:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfy \(\bigoplus_{v\in V}b(v)=1\). Encode, by constant-width CNF clauses, each parity equation \(\bigoplus_{e\ni v}x_e=b(v)\). The resulting Tseitin formula \(T(G,b)\) is unsatisfiable. For every fixed degree bound and \(h>0\), there exists \(c>0\) such that every resolution refutation of \(T(G,b)\) has length at least \(2^{c|V|}\); equivalently, the family requires exponential resolution size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd total charge makes the Tseitin parity constraints inconsistent, and bounded-degree expansion forces every resolution refutation to have exponential size.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has uniformly bounded degree and edge expansion at least a fixed \(h>0\).
\(\bigoplus_{v\in V}b(v)=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(G,b)\) is unsatisfiable and every resolution refutation has size \(2^{\Omega(|V|)}\).

notation.meaning: CNF encoding of the charged vertex-parity equations.
Boolean variable associated with edge e.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, but the precise expansion assumptions, CNF encoding convention, and exponential resolution lower bound require an authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-CNF Refutation Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability resolution lower bound in a constant-density random \(k\)-CNF regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(k\ge 3\). There exist constants \(\Delta_k,c_k>0\) such that, if \(F_{n,m}^{(k)}\) is formed by independently sampling \(m=\lceil\Delta n\rceil\) uniformly random non-tautological \(k\)-clauses with \(\Delta\ge\Delta_k\), then, with probability tending to one as \(n\to\infty\), \(F_{n,m}^{(k)}\) is unsatisfiable and every resolution refutation of it contains at least \(2^{c_kn}\) clauses. Thus the relevant random formulas almost surely have exponential resolution-refutation size, despite possessing short probabilistically checkable descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At sufficiently large constant clause density, random k-CNFs are almost surely unsatisfiable and require exponentially large resolution refutations.
assumptions_latex: \(k\ge 3\) is fixed.
\(m=\lceil\Delta n\rceil\) with sufficiently large constant \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With high probability, \(F_{n,m}^{(k)}\) is unsatisfiable and has resolution size \(2^{\Omega(n)}\).

notation.meaning: Random k-CNF on n variables with m sampled clauses.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim depends on the exact random-clause distribution and density regime. No source is supplied for the asserted high-probability exponential resolution bound.

children.title: Variable-Ordering Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Proof or solver difficulty induced by variable and constraint ordering choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Ordering Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering dependence of ordered decision or proof representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a CNF over variables \(X\), let \(\Pi(X)\) be the set of total variable orders, and let \(S(F,\pi)\) denote the minimum size of a fixed-order representation or refutation of \(F\) respecting \(\pi\). The ordering sensitivity of \(F\) is \[\operatorname{OS}(F)=\frac{\max_{\pi\in\Pi(X)}S(F,\pi)}{\min_{\pi\in\Pi(X)}S(F,\pi)}.\] A family \((F_n)\) is exponentially ordering-sensitive when \(\operatorname{OS}(F_n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\). This predicate requires the representation or proof system defining \(S\) to be fixed before orders are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordering sensitivity is the ratio between worst- and best-order representation sizes; exponential sensitivity means that this ratio grows exponentially.
assumptions_latex: A single fixed-order representation or proof system and one size measure are used throughout.
\(S(F,\pi)\) is finite and positive for every compared order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OS}(F)\) quantifies the multiplicative effect of variable ordering on the chosen representation.

notation.meaning: Set of total orders of the variables X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits, but S ranges ambiguously over ordered representations or refutations. A particular proof or representation system and a source establishing this sensitivity measure are required.

children.title: Encoding Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Difficulty variation across logically related propositional encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity variation among projection-equivalent encodings of one Boolean constraint family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n(\bar{x})\) be a Boolean constraint and let \(\mathcal{E}(P_n)\) be a specified class of CNF encodings \(E(\bar{x},\bar{y})\) satisfying \(P_n(\bar{x})=1\) if and only if \(\exists\bar{y}\,E(\bar{x},\bar{y})=1\). For a fixed proof or representation system with positive size measure \(S\), define \[\operatorname{ES}(P_n)=\frac{\max_{E\in\mathcal{E}(P_n)}S(E)}{\min_{E\in\mathcal{E}(P_n)}S(E)}.\] The family is exponentially encoding-sensitive when \(\operatorname{ES}(P_n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\). Comparisons are meaningful only after fixing the admissible auxiliary variables, projection semantics, proof or representation system, and size measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding sensitivity measures the worst-to-best complexity ratio among CNF encodings with the same projected satisfying assignments, after fixing the admissible encoding class and complexity measure.
assumptions_latex: \(P_n\) is a Boolean constraint on the primary-variable vector \(\bar{x}\).
Every \(E\in\mathcal{E}(P_n)\) uses the same projection semantics on \(\bar{x}\).
The admissible encoding class, proof or representation system, and positive size measure \(S\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ES}(P_n)\) quantifies complexity variation within the specified class of projection-equivalent encodings.

notation.meaning: Specified admissible class of CNF encodings of P_n.

children.title: Ordering–Encoding Interactions
children.top_down_role: Coupled effects of representation choice and ordering choice on resolution hardness.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering–Encoding Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison reversals showing joint dependence of ordered complexity on encoding and variable order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) be projection-equivalent CNF encodings, possibly with different auxiliary variables, and let \(U=\operatorname{Var}(E_1)\cup\operatorname{Var}(E_2)\). For a total order \(\pi\) on \(U\), let \(S(E_i,\pi|_{\operatorname{Var}(E_i)})>0\) be the minimum size in one fixed ordered proof or representation system. Encoding and ordering exhibit a comparison reversal when there are total orders \(\pi\) and \(\rho\) on \(U\) such that \[S(E_1,\pi|_{\operatorname{Var}(E_1)})<S(E_2,\pi|_{\operatorname{Var}(E_2)})\quad\text{and}\quad S(E_1,\rho|_{\operatorname{Var}(E_1)})>S(E_2,\rho|_{\operatorname{Var}(E_2)}).\] Such a reversal precludes an order-independent ranking of these two encodings that agrees with both comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding and ordering interact through a comparison reversal when two equivalent encodings exchange which has smaller ordered complexity under two orders on their common variable universe.
assumptions_latex: \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) encode the same projected Boolean constraint.
\(U=\operatorname{Var}(E_1)\cup\operatorname{Var}(E_2)\), and compared orders are total orders on \(U\).
One ordered proof or representation system and one positive size measure are used throughout.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A comparison reversal demonstrates that the relative size of \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) depends on the variable order.

notation.meaning: Union of the variable sets of the two encodings.
Restriction of the common order to variables occurring in encoding E_i.
Minimum ordered size of encoding E_i under the restricted order.

children.title: SAT Certificate Verification System
children.top_down_role: Satisfying witnesses, practical refutation formats, proof elaboration, certified checking, proof-derived artifacts, and trust boundaries.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: The DRAT Format and DRAT-trim Checker
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: DRAT syntax, RUP and RAT checking, deletion, and trimming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: The DRAT Format and DRAT-trim Checker

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: LRAT hints and certified Coq and ACL2 checking

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Flexible Proof Format for SAT Solver-Elaborator Communication
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Flexible Proof Format for SAT Solver-Elaborator Communication

knowledge_statements.title: Total Assignment Witnesses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct satisfiability certificate for a propositional CNF formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}C_i\) be a finite CNF over variables \(X\). A total-assignment witness is a map \(\alpha:X\to\{0,1\}\). It certifies satisfiability precisely when \[\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\},\quad \exists\ell\in C_i\text{ such that }\alpha(\ell)=1,\] where \(\alpha(\neg x)=1-\alpha(x)\). Verification scans every clause and accepts if and only if each contains a true literal; with constant-time assignment lookup, its running time is linear in the total number of literal occurrences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A total Boolean assignment certifies satisfiability exactly when every clause contains a literal made true by that assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF over \(X\).
\(\alpha:X\to\{0,1\}\) assigns every variable occurring in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The verifier accepts \(\alpha\) if and only if \(\alpha\models F\).

children.title: Partial-Model Certificates
children.top_down_role: Satisfiability witnesses that specify only a subset of variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Model Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Satisfiability certificate consisting of a partial assignment plus a verifiable completion condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a CNF \(F\) over \(X\), a partial assignment is a map \(\tau:D\to\{0,1\}\) with \(D\subseteq X\). It is a partial-model certificate relative to a specified completion procedure \(K\) when \(K(F,\tau)\) returns a total assignment \(\alpha:X\to\{0,1\}\), \(\alpha|_D=	au\), and direct clause evaluation establishes \(\alpha\models F\). Equivalently, without relying on \(K\), completion exists exactly when the restricted formula \(F|_\tau\) is satisfiable. The certificate is efficiently verifiable only when the completion or an independently checkable completion trace is supplied or efficiently derivable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial assignment certifies satisfiability only with a checked procedure or trace that extends it to a total satisfying assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF over \(X\).
The completion procedure and its acceptance conditions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance yields a total extension \(\alpha\supseteq\tau\) satisfying \(F\).

notation.meaning: Formula obtained by restricting F with partial assignment tau.
Domain assigned by the partial certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role and mathematical boundary are coherent, but the completion procedure or trace format is not tied to an authoritative specification with a locator.

children.title: Model Completion
children.top_down_role: Extension of partial witnesses to assignments covering the required formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Model Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completion by restriction, propagation, and residual SAT search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a CNF \(F\) over \(X\) and a consistent partial assignment \(\tau\). Initialize \(\sigma\leftarrow\tau\) and repeatedly assign every unit literal of \(F|_\sigma\); reject if an empty clause appears. If the residual formula has no clauses, assign arbitrary values to remaining variables and output the resulting total \(\alpha\). Otherwise invoke a complete SAT search on \(F|_\sigma\). If it returns a satisfying residual assignment \(\beta\), output \(\alpha=\sigma\cup\beta\), assigning arbitrary values to unused variables; otherwise report that \(\tau\) has no satisfying extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict by the partial assignment, propagate units, and solve the residual formula; output the combined total model or report that no extension exists.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF over \(X\).
\(\tau\) is a consistent partial Boolean assignment.
The residual SAT search is complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(\alpha\supseteq\tau\) with \(\alpha\models F\), or correctly reports that no such extension exists.

notation.meaning: Residual CNF under the current assignment.
Satisfying assignment of the residual formula.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is sound at the stated level and fits the leaf, but no source supports the completion procedure or its stated correctness guarantee.

children.title: Completion Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where omitted assignments cannot be recovered without additional information.

knowledge_statements.title: Completion Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary between extendible and nonextendible partial assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a CNF and \(	au\) a consistent partial assignment. A satisfying completion of \(	au\) exists if and only if the restricted formula \(F|_	au\) is satisfiable. Unit propagation detecting an empty clause is sufficient to prove nonextendibility, but failure to derive an empty clause is not sufficient to prove extendibility. For example, with empty \(	au\), the formula \[(x\vee y)\wedge(x\vee
eg y)\wedge(
eg x\vee y)\wedge(
eg x\vee
eg y)\] is unsatisfiable and contains no unit clause. Thus propagation-only completion can stall on a nonextendible certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Completion exists exactly when the residual formula is satisfiable; unit propagation may stall even though no completion exists.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF.
\(\tau\) is a consistent partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absence of a unit-propagation conflict does not certify that \(\tau\) has a satisfying extension.

notation.meaning: Partial Boolean assignment to be completed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-satisfiability boundary and counterexample are mathematically coherent and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the record has no supporting source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Preprocessing Model Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse reconstruction of an original SAT model from a preprocessed model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let preprocessing transform \(F_0\) through \(F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_t\), recording for each step a reconstruction map \(R_i\) such that every model \(\alpha_i\models F_i\) is mapped to a model \(R_i(\alpha_i)\models F_{i-1}\). Given \(\alpha_t\models F_t\), initialize \(\alpha\leftarrow\alpha_t\), then apply \(\alpha\leftarrow R_i(\alpha)\) for \(i=t,t-1,\ldots,1\). Output \(\alpha_0\) only after directly checking \(\alpha_0\models F_0\). If any inverse record is absent, inconsistent, or fails its local condition, reconstruction fails rather than certifying satisfiability of \(F_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply recorded inverse preprocessing steps in reverse order, then validate the reconstructed assignment against the original formula.
assumptions_latex: Each preprocessing step supplies a sound reconstruction map.
A total model \(\alpha_t\models F_t\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful reverse application and final validation produce \(\alpha_0\models F_0\).

notation.meaning: Model-reconstruction map for preprocessing step i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reverse-reconstruction algorithm fits the leaf, but the reconstruction-map contract and trace semantics require an authoritative preprocessing or certificate specification.

children.title: RUP Redundancy in DRAT
children.top_down_role: DRAT additions validated through reverse unit propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: RUP Redundancy in DRAT
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-unit-propagation condition for adding a clause to a DRAT proof.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a CNF and \(C\) a clause. The clause \(C\) has the reverse unit propagation property with respect to \(F\) precisely when unit propagation on \[F\wedge\bigwedge_{\ell\in C}\neg\ell\] derives the empty clause. Equivalently, assigning every literal of \(C\) false makes \(F\) unit-inconsistent. A DRAT checker may therefore accept addition of \(C\) as a RUP step. Because unit propagation establishes \(F\models C\), adding \(C\) preserves both satisfiability and unsatisfiability of the active clause database.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clause is RUP when assuming all its literals false makes unit propagation derive conflict; adding such a clause preserves satisfiability.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the active finite CNF clause database.
\(C\) is a finite clause interpreted as a disjunction of literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If unit propagation refutes \(F\wedge\bigwedge_{\ell\in C}\neg\ell\), then \(F\models C\) and the addition \(F\leftarrow F\wedge C\) is redundant.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The RUP condition is stated coherently and has the correct content kind, but acceptance as a DRAT step and the exact unit-propagation convention require a DRAT-format or proof-checking specification with a precise locator.

children.title: RAT Redundancy in DRAT
children.top_down_role: DRAT additions validated through resolution asymmetric tautology.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula and \(C\) is a clause.
\(p\in C\) is the designated pivot literal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is a satisfiability-preserving DRAT addition to \(F\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of clauses C and D on pivot p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard clause-addition form of the resolution asymmetric tautology condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The clause \(C\) has resolution asymmetric tautology (RAT) redundancy with pivot \(p\) relative to \(F\) if, for every clause \(D\in F\) containing \(\neg p\), either the resolvent \(R=C\mathbin{\otimes_p}D\) is tautological or \(R\) has RUP relative to \(F\). The latter means that unit propagation on \(F\) under the assumptions \(\{\neg r:r\in R\}\) derives the empty clause. Under this condition, adding \(C\) preserves satisfiability: \(F\) is satisfiable if and only if \(F\land C\) is satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clause is RAT-redundant when every non-tautological pivot resolvent is refutable by unit propagation; adding such a clause preserves satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.title: RAT Redundancy in DRAT

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The RAT condition is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no cited source supports the exact definition or satisfiability-preservation conclusion.

children.title: RUP-to-RAT Coverage
children.top_down_role: Relative coverage of admissible clause additions under the two redundancy criteria.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
\(C\neq\varnothing\) has RUP relative to \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(p\in C\), the clause \(C\) has RAT with pivot \(p\) relative to \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the inclusion of nonempty RUP additions within RAT additions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) have RUP relative to \(F\), meaning unit propagation refutes \(F\land igwedge_{c\in C}
eg c\). Fix any \(p\in C\) and any \(D\in F\) with \(
eg p\in D\). If the pivot resolvent is non-tautological, assumptions falsifying all its literals make \(D\) unit and force \(
eg p\); consequently every literal of \(C\) is false, and the original RUP conflict follows. Thus every required pivot resolvent has RUP, so \(C\) has RAT on \(p\). Hence DRAT's RAT rule covers every nonempty RUP addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty RUP clause is also a RAT clause, with any of its literals usable as the pivot.
knowledge_statements.title: RUP-to-RAT Coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The RUP-to-RAT inclusion is plausible, but it lacks evidence and the statement contains proof-style reasoning that must be removed after the claim is sourced.

children.title: DRAT Clause-Addition Records
children.top_down_role: Proof records introducing clauses subject to DRAT redundancy checks.

assumptions_latex: \(F_0\) is the initial CNF formula.
Records are processed sequentially against the current formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted addition transforms \(F_i\) into \(F_{i+1}=F_i\cup\{C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the semantic effect of a DRAT addition record, independently of textual or binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DRAT clause-addition record carries an ordered clause \(C=(p,c_2,\ldots,c_k)\), whose first literal \(p\) is the RAT pivot when a RAT check is needed. At state \(F_i\), the checker accepts the record if \(C\) has RUP relative to \(F_i\), or otherwise has RAT on \(p\) relative to \(F_i\). Upon acceptance, the state becomes \(F_{i+1}=F_i\cup\{C\}\). An accepted empty-clause addition \(C=\varnothing\) terminates a refutation because its presence makes the current CNF unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An addition record supplies a clause, validates it by RUP or RAT against the current formula, and then inserts it.
knowledge_statements.title: DRAT Clause-Addition Records

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the record-taxonomy leaf, but the ordered-clause, pivot, acceptance, and empty-clause conventions require a DRAT format source.

children.title: DRAT Clause-Deletion Records
children.top_down_role: Proof records removing clauses from the active checking database.

assumptions_latex: \(F_i\) is the current clause multiset.
\(C\) is the clause named by the deletion record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deletion transforms \(F_i\) into \(F_{i+1}=F_i\setminus\{C\}\) without itself proving redundancy.

notation.meaning: One matching occurrence removed from the multiset

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses multiset semantics so repeated clauses and deletion matching are explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DRAT clause-deletion record names a clause \(C\) to be removed from the current active clause multiset \(F_i\). If a matching active occurrence exists, the update is \(F_{i+1}=F_i\setminus\{C\}\), removing one occurrence; a checker may treat deletion of an absent clause according to its declared format convention. No RUP or RAT condition is imposed on a deletion. Deletion cannot establish the final contradiction: it serves only to reduce clauses available to later redundancy checks, so every subsequent addition must be validated against the resulting active state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deletion record removes a matching active clause without a redundancy test; later additions must be checked against the reduced formula.
knowledge_statements.title: DRAT Clause-Deletion Records

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic role is appropriate, but one-occurrence multiset deletion and absent-clause behavior are format-specific and unsupported.

children.title: Binary DRAT Representation
children.top_down_role: Compact binary serialization of DRAT proof records.

assumptions_latex: Variables are indexed by positive integers.
Each clause is terminated by the code \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decoding the byte stream recovers the same ordered sequence of DRAT additions and deletions.

notation.meaning: Unsigned code assigned to a signed literal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the usual signed-literal mapping; exact marker and variable-byte conventions require format confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary DRAT representation serializes each proof record as a record-kind marker followed by the literals of its clause and a zero terminator. Under the signed-literal mapping \(u(\ell)=2|\ell|+\mathbf{1}_{\{\ell<0\}}\), each positive code \(u(\ell)\) is written with the format's variable-length unsigned-integer encoding. The marker distinguishes clause addition from clause deletion, while literal order is retained because the first literal of an addition may designate its RAT pivot. Concatenating these self-delimiting records represents exactly the ordered DRAT state transitions obtained after decoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary DRAT encodes each marked addition or deletion as variable-length signed-literal codes followed by zero, preserving clause and pivot order.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary DRAT Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the record markers, literal mapping, variable-length encoding, terminator, and ordering conventions need an authoritative binary-DRAT specification.

children.title: DRAT Proof Trimming
children.top_down_role: Removal of proof records irrelevant to the final contradiction.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)\) is an accepted DRAT refutation of \(F_0\).
The final required addition is the empty clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output subsequence \(P'\) remains a DRAT refutation of \(F_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes dependency-based trimming followed by mandatory revalidation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the required set with the final empty-clause addition. Scan \(P\) backward while reconstructing the active clause state. Whenever a required addition is reached, retain it and mark every earlier clause occurrence actually used by its RUP chain or RAT-resolvent checks as required; retain deletion information needed to reconstruct those active states. Discard an unrequired addition only when no retained validation depends on it. Reverse the retained records to obtain \(P'\), then check \(P'\) forward from \(F_0\). Output \(P'\) only if every retained addition is valid in its newly induced state and the empty clause is derived.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof trimming traces dependencies backward from the empty clause, removes unused records, and outputs the subsequence only after forward revalidation.
knowledge_statements.title: DRAT Proof Trimming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the trimming leaf, but dependency extraction, deletion retention, and the claimed subsequence property depend on an unspecified trimming procedure.

children.title: DRAT Backward Validation
children.top_down_role: Reverse traversal focused on records needed by the contradiction.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)\) is a DRAT record sequence.
The final target is an empty-clause addition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The backward pass identifies a candidate dependency slice but does not alone certify that slice.

notation.meaning: Set of currently required clause occurrences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates reverse dependency discovery from the final forward certificate check.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First obtain the active state after all records, then scan indices \(i=m,m-1,\ldots,1\), undoing each record to reconstruct \(F_i\). Initialize \(Q\) with the final empty clause. If an addition of \(C\) is not in \(Q\), mark it removable. If it is in \(Q\), validate or reconstruct its RUP or RAT justification in \(F_i\), remove \(C\) from \(Q\), and insert the antecedent clause occurrences used by that justification. Reverse processing of deletions restores the removed occurrences needed for earlier states. The retained indices form a candidate trimmed proof requiring forward validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backward validation reconstructs earlier formula states and traces antecedents from the empty clause to identify records needed by the refutation.
knowledge_statements.title: DRAT Backward Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits, but the reverse state reconstruction and antecedent-selection conventions require a precise checker or trimming-algorithm source.

children.title: Trimmed-Proof Validation
children.top_down_role: Checking considerations for reduced DRAT proof traces.

assumptions_latex: \(P'=(r'_1,\ldots,r'_t)\) is a trimmed DRAT record sequence.
Checking begins from the original formula \(F_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies that \(F_0\) is unsatisfiable.

notation.meaning: Active formula before trimmed record j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward validation is required because trimming changes the active formulas used by later checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(G_0=F_0\) and process \(P'\) in forward order. For every addition of a clause \(C\), verify that \(C\) has RUP relative to the current \(G_j\), or has RAT on its recorded pivot relative to \(G_j\), before setting \(G_{j+1}=G_j\cup\{C\}\). For every deletion, apply the declared clause-matching rule to update the active state. Accept the trimmed certificate only if all records are well formed, all additions pass in their actual trimmed states, and an accepted addition derives \(C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trimmed proof is certified by replaying it forward, checking every addition in its actual active state, and finally accepting the empty clause.
knowledge_statements.title: Trimmed-Proof Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward-checking claim needs a source, and the leaf describes a validation procedure or acceptance condition rather than a certificate object; the content kind should be reconsidered after sourcing.

assumptions_latex: The proof has \(L\) addition records.
Every active formula contains at most \(N\) literal occurrences.
Unit propagation is implemented by a linear scan costing \(O(N)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Naive checking costs \(O(LN^2)\) time and \(O(N)\) active-formula space, excluding proof storage.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A coarse worst-case bound for explicit scans, not a claim about optimized watched-literal checkers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For one RUP test, scanning an active formula with at most \(N\) literal occurrences during unit propagation costs \(O(N)\) in the stipulated model. A RAT test may inspect \(O(N)\) clauses containing the complementary pivot and perform one RUP test for each corresponding resolvent, giving \(O(N^2)\) time per addition. Therefore a proof with \(L\) additions has the coarse worst-case checking bound \(O(LN^2)\). Maintaining the active clause database uses \(O(N)\) space apart from storage for the proof stream and implementation indexes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under naive scanning, RUP costs linear time and RAT may invoke linearly many RUP checks, yielding a coarse quadratic-per-addition bound.
knowledge_statements.title: DRAT Checking-Cost Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the cost-regime topic and the bound follows the stipulated coarse model, but neither that model nor the resulting time and space bounds are cited.

children.title: LRAT Antecedent Hints
children.top_down_role: References identifying clauses relevant to a checked derivation.

assumptions_latex: Every active clause has a unique positive identifier.
A new LRAT clause has identifier \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Antecedent hints restrict validation to explicitly identified earlier clauses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines antecedents semantically; exact LRAT signed-identifier grammar remains source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An LRAT antecedent hint for a clause addition with identifier \(i\) is an ordered reference to active clauses having identifiers smaller than \(i\). For a RUP addition, the referenced clauses are precisely the candidate antecedents used by the directed unit-propagation check. For a RAT addition, antecedent data additionally associates each relevant clause containing the complementary pivot with an ordered chain intended to refute the corresponding resolvent assumptions. Antecedent identifiers are references rather than trusted conclusions: the checker retrieves each clause and independently verifies that its stated propagation or resolvent role is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LRAT antecedent hints name earlier active clauses intended to justify a new clause, while the checker independently verifies every named dependency.
knowledge_statements.title: LRAT Antecedent Hints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the hint-system leaf, but LRAT antecedent ordering, identifier restrictions, and RAT subcheck organization are format-specific and need a specification.

children.title: LRAT Propagation Hints
children.top_down_role: Ordered guidance supporting efficient propagation-based validation.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the clause being checked.
\((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) references earlier active clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid propagation hint sequence yields a unit-propagation conflict from \(F\land\bigwedge_{c\in C}\neg c\).

notation.meaning: Partial assignment maintained by the checker

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States ordered RUP propagation hints; RAT subchecks use the same directed-chain predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the partial assignment \(\alpha\) by falsifying every literal of \(C\). Process the hinted identifiers \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) in order. At step \(j\), the referenced active clause \(D_{a_j}\) must either be falsified by \(\alpha\), which certifies conflict, or have exactly one unassigned literal while all its other literals are false, in which case that remaining literal is assigned true. A propagation hint sequence is valid only if this deterministic replay eventually reaches a falsified referenced clause. Thus the hints constitute a locally checkable RUP chain without searching the full formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation hints order clause references so a checker can replay unit assignments and reach a conflict without searching for antecedents.
knowledge_statements.title: LRAT Propagation Hints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate interpretation is plausible, but the exact ordered replay and terminal-conflict requirements require an authoritative LRAT checker or format source.

children.title: Hint-Consistency Requirements
children.top_down_role: Consistency obligations linking recorded hints to the active clause database.

assumptions_latex: The checker maintains an active map from clause identifiers to clauses.
A hint belongs to an addition with identifier \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hinted addition is accepted only when every reference and every local propagation or RAT check is consistent.

notation.meaning: Identifier of the clause being added

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects semantic well-formedness and replay requirements independently of concrete LRAT line syntax.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An LRAT hint list for identifier \(i\) is consistent relative to \(M_i\) only if every referenced identifier denotes an active earlier clause, no deleted or undefined identifier is used, and the references obey the format's required partition into propagation chains and RAT-resolvent subchecks. Each propagation chain must replay in order: every nonterminal referenced clause is unit under the accumulated assignment, and the terminal clause is falsified. For a RAT addition, the hinted complementary-pivot clauses must cover every required active occurrence, and each associated resolvent chain must conflict. Failure of any lookup, ordering, coverage, unit, or conflict check rejects the addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LRAT hints must reference active earlier clauses, replay valid unit chains, and, for RAT, cover and refute every required pivot resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Hint-Consistency Requirements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind matches the leaf, but deletion validity, hint partitioning, occurrence coverage, and RAT-chain requirements depend on the exact LRAT grammar and semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Checker-Oriented Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational acceptance criterion for an LRAT refutation checked against an initial CNF formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_0\) be a CNF formula and let \(P\) be an LRAT trace. A checker maintains an active clause map \(D\), initially containing the clauses of \(F_0\). It accepts an addition \((i,C,H)\) only when \(i\) is fresh and the identifier sequence \(H\) validates either reverse unit propagation for \(C\), or the required asymmetric-tautology resolvents for a designated pivot of \(C\), using active clauses. A deletion removes only the specified active identifiers. The trace is an accepted refutation exactly when every record passes these checks and some accepted addition has \(C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LRAT refutation is accepted by replaying identified additions and deletions, validating every supplied propagation or pivot hint, and finally deriving the empty clause.
assumptions_latex: \(F_0\) is a finite CNF formula.
Every referenced identifier denotes a currently active clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is accepted }\Longleftrightarrow\text{ all records validate and an accepted record adds }\varnothing.\)

notation.meaning: active map from clause identifiers to clauses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits checker-oriented validation, and the statement is internally coherent, but no citation supports the exact LRAT addition, RAT-hint, deletion, freshness, or acceptance semantics. Those format-specific details cannot be accepted without an inspectable LRAT specification locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Certified LRAT Checkers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness contract for an implementation whose LRAT acceptance function is formally verified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite CNF formula, let \(P\) be an LRAT trace, and let \(\operatorname{check}(F,P)\) be an executable checker proved to refine the formal LRAT transition relation. Suppose each accepted clause addition is justified by a sound reverse-unit-propagation or resolution-asymmetric-tautology check over the active database, and deletions do not assert new clauses. Then checker acceptance is a sound unsatisfiability certificate: \[\operatorname{check}(F,P)=\operatorname{accept}\;\Longrightarrow\;F\text{ is unsatisfiable}.\] No completeness claim follows: an unsatisfiable formula may be paired with a malformed, unsupported, or checker-incompatible trace that is rejected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formally verified LRAT checker is sound: accepting a trace that derives the empty clause certifies that the input CNF is unsatisfiable.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(P\) are finite.
\(\operatorname{check}\) refines the formal LRAT transition relation.
The formal RUP and RAT validation rules are sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}(F,P)=\operatorname{accept}\Longrightarrow F\text{ is unsatisfiable}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the certified-checker leaf and the one-way soundness conclusion is appropriately limited. However, no particular certified checker or formal soundness theorem is cited, so the refinement premise and resulting unsatisfiability guarantee lack inspectable support.

children.title: Direct LRAT Generation
children.top_down_role: Native production of LRAT records by a solver or proof-producing component.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct LRAT Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online production of checker-ready LRAT records by a conflict-driven SAT solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a CNF formula \(F_0\) with distinct initial clause identifiers. Initialize the active map \(D\) with those clauses and an empty trace \(P\). Whenever the solver learns a clause \(C\), assign a fresh identifier \(i\), extract from the conflict analysis an ordered hint list \(H\) that validates \(C\) by the LRAT RUP or RAT rule over \(D\), append \((i,C,H)\) to \(P\), and insert \(i\mapsto C\) into \(D\). Emit identified deletion records when clauses are retired. Stop with an UNSAT certificate only after appending a valid addition of the empty clause; output \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver emits each learned clause with a fresh identifier and complete LRAT hints, tracks deletions, and terminates the certificate by adding the empty clause.
assumptions_latex: The solver exposes sufficient conflict-analysis dependencies to construct LRAT hints.
Initial and learned clauses receive unique identifiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is output only after every emitted addition has a checker-oriented justification and the final derivation contains \(\varnothing\).\)

notation.meaning: LRAT hint list for an addition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits direct LRAT generation, but the claim that conflict analysis supplies complete ordered LRAT RUP or RAT hints, together with the deletion and identifier discipline, is implementation-specific and uncited.

children.title: DRAT-to-LRAT Elaboration
children.top_down_role: Conversion of less explicit DRAT evidence into LRAT records.

knowledge_statements.title: DRAT-to-LRAT Elaboration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Offline conversion of a valid DRAT refutation into an explicitly hinted LRAT refutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an identified CNF formula \(F_0\) and a DRAT trace \(Q\). Initialize an active clause database \(D\) and an empty LRAT trace \(P\). Replay \(Q\) in order. For every addition of \(C\), determine a RUP justification or a RAT pivot and, for each active clause containing the complementary pivot, construct an ordered unit-propagation hint chain for the corresponding resolvent. Assign a fresh identifier and append the resulting LRAT addition to \(P\). Translate deletions to active identifiers. Reject if any required justification cannot be reconstructed. Otherwise output \(P\) after the empty clause is elaborated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elaborator replays DRAT, reconstructs explicit propagation hints and pivot obligations for each addition, translates deletions, and outputs LRAT or reports failure.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) uses DRAT additions and deletions over the clauses reachable from \(F_0\).
The elaborator can index active clauses by literals and reconstruct unit propagation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{elaborate}(F_0,Q)=P\Longrightarrow P\text{ is an LRAT refutation of }F_0.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role matches the elaboration leaf, but the reconstruction of every RAT resolvent obligation, the treatment of DRAT deletions, and the conditional correctness conclusion require a cited elaborator specification or correctness result.

children.title: Generation–Elaboration Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Producer overhead, elaborator cost, and checker simplicity across LRAT production routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Generation–Elaboration Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource tradeoff between solver-side LRAT construction and postprocessing of a weaker proof log.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a solver run \(S\), compare direct generation \(G(S)\) with weak-log generation followed by elaboration \(E(Q(S))\). Direct generation records dependency information while it is available, but adds solver-side bookkeeping and may constrain clause deletion or identifier management. Post hoc elaboration keeps the solver logger simpler, but must reconstruct propagation and RAT obligations from the trace and active clause history. If both routes succeed and their outputs pass a sound LRAT checker, both certify unsatisfiability of the same input; neither route has an unconditional dominance in runtime, peak memory, or certificate size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct LRAT logging spends work inside the solver; later elaboration reconstructs missing evidence. Both can yield equivalent certificates, with workload and resource use shifted between stages.
assumptions_latex: Both routes process the same CNF formula and sound solver derivation.
Each produced LRAT trace is checked independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{accept}(G(S))\lor\operatorname{accept}(E(Q(S)))\Longrightarrow F\text{ is unsatisfiable},\) with no universal resource ordering between the routes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits a tradeoff leaf. The qualitative workload shift is plausible, but the bookkeeping, deletion constraints, and absence of universal runtime, memory, or certificate-size dominance are implementation-dependent claims with no cited evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver–Elaborator Communication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface invariant connecting FRAT-producing solvers to proof elaborators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) emit a FRAT stream \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)\) and let \(E\) elaborate it. The communication interface must preserve enough state to replay the solver's clause database: every semantic clause record carries a stable identifier, additions identify their clause and any available justification, deletions identify the removed clause, and finalization exposes the claimed contradiction. Extension records must be framed so that \(E\) can either interpret or safely skip them. If replay reaches an unknown identifier, reuses an active identifier ambiguously, or lacks evidence needed to reconstruct an addition, elaboration must fail rather than manufacture a justification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FRAT communication uses stable clause identities, replayable additions and deletions, optional hints, and safely framed extensions; inconsistent or insufficient information causes elaboration failure.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a finite sequence of framed FRAT records.
\(E\) implements the agreed record and identifier conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(R)=P\Longrightarrow P\text{ replays the semantic clause evolution reported by }S.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role is suitable for a solver-elaborator interface invariant, but stable identifier rules, finalization behavior, extension framing, safe skipping, and mandatory failure behavior are format-specific and need an authoritative FRAT specification locator.

children.title: Identified Proof Records
children.top_down_role: FRAT records equipped with stable identifiers for reference and lifecycle tracking.

knowledge_statements.title: Identified Proof Records
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clause-identity discipline for replaying FRAT additions, deletions, and references.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An identified proof state is a partial map \(D:I\rightharpoonup\mathcal C\) from identifiers to clauses. An addition record \((\mathsf a,i,C,H)\) is well formed when \(i\notin\operatorname{dom}(D)\); its state transition is \(D'=D\cup\{i\mapsto C\}\), after any required validation using hint payload \(H\). A deletion record \((\mathsf d,i)\) is well formed when \(i\in\operatorname{dom}(D)\), and yields \(D'=D\setminus\{i\}\). Any record referencing \(i\) must do so while \(i\) is active. Thus clause identity, rather than textual clause equality, determines record linkage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FRAT records give clauses stable identifiers: additions create active mappings, deletions remove them, and references are valid only while their identifiers remain active.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is an identifier set and \(\mathcal C\) is the set of finite clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) evolves by fresh identified additions and active identified deletions.

notation.meaning: partial map of active clause identifiers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits identified proof records, but the proposed partial-map semantics assumes freshness, active-identifier deletion, and identity-based linkage conventions that must be checked against the actual FRAT format, especially its identifier-reuse rules.

children.title: Extensible Proof Records
children.top_down_role: FRAT record structures supporting additional information and future record classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Extensible Proof Records
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Framed FRAT record representation permitting optional metadata without changing core proof semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a FRAT stream as \(R=r_1\cdots r_m\), where each record has an opcode and a finitely delimited payload. Core opcodes induce transitions of the identified clause state \(D\); an extension opcode carries a payload whose boundary is recoverable without interpreting its contents. For a consumer supporting extension set \(K\), projection \(\pi_K(R)\) retains all core records and supported extensions and skips unsupported, explicitly ignorable extensions. The representation is extensible when \(\pi_K(R)\) remains syntactically parseable and induces the same core clause-state transitions as \(R\) whenever skipped records have no core semantic effect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A FRAT stream is extensible when records are unambiguously framed and unsupported ignorable records can be skipped without changing core clause-state transitions.
assumptions_latex: Every record boundary is uniquely recoverable.
Extensions declared ignorable do not add, delete, or reinterpret core clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{core}}(\pi_K(R))=T_{\mathrm{core}}(R).\)

notation.meaning: projection understood by a consumer supporting extensions in K

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits extensible records, but the opcode-and-delimited-payload model, the class of ignorable extensions, and preservation of core transitions under projection are abstract assumptions not tied to an inspectable FRAT format specification.

children.title: Extension Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Interoperability considerations for consumers facing optional or newly introduced record content.

knowledge_statements.title: Extension Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservative compatibility condition for FRAT producers, extensions, and consumers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a FRAT stream, \(X\) an extension record class, and \(C\) a consumer that does not implement \(X\). The extension is backward-compatible for \(C\) precisely when: each \(X\)-record has an unambiguous boundary; its opcode cannot be confused with a core opcode; skipping it leaves identifier scope and the active clause map unchanged; and no later core record requires its payload for parsing or semantic validation. Under these conditions, deleting all \(X\)-records commutes with core replay: \[\operatorname{coreReplay}(R)=\operatorname{coreReplay}(R\setminus X).\] Extensions failing any condition require explicit consumer support or rejection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsupported FRAT extension is safely skippable only when framing stays unambiguous and removing it preserves identifier scope, clause state, parsing, and core validation.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is well framed under the producer's format.
\(C\) implements all core FRAT records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\text{ is safely skippable}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{coreReplay}(R)=\operatorname{coreReplay}(R\setminus X)\) under the stated framing conditions.

notation.meaning: consumer lacking support for the extension

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits extension compatibility, but the stated conditions are asserted to be necessary and sufficient without format evidence. In particular, equality of core replay and semantic independence from skipped payloads require precise parser and validator semantics from the FRAT specification.

children.title: Forward FRAT Processing
children.top_down_role: Proof processing in production order using accumulating record state.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward FRAT Processing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single forward replay of FRAT records while constructing checker-ready proof information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a CNF formula \(F_0\) and a FRAT stream \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)\). Initialize the active identified database \(D\) from \(F_0\) and an empty output trace \(P\). For \(k=1,\ldots,m\), parse \(r_k\): install a valid addition after checking or reconstructing its hints against the current \(D\), apply an identified deletion, process supported metadata, and skip only extensions declared ignorable. Append the corresponding checker-ready record to \(P\). Reject on malformed framing, invalid identifiers, or an unjustifiable addition. Output \(P\) only if replay derives the empty clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward processing scans FRAT in production order, updates the active database, elaborates each addition immediately, translates deletions, and outputs a refutation after deriving the empty clause.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is available in production order.
Required justifications can be checked or reconstructed from the current state and retained metadata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{forward}(F_0,R)=P\Longrightarrow P\text{ is a checker-ready refutation of }F_0.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits forward FRAT processing. Whether additions can be justified immediately from current state and retained metadata, which extensions may be skipped, and what checker-ready output is produced are format- and implementation-specific claims needing a cited source.

children.title: Backward FRAT Processing
children.top_down_role: Reverse proof traversal focused on records relevant to the final result.

knowledge_statements.title: Backward FRAT Processing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse dependency analysis for trimming FRAT before forward checker-ready emission.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an identified CNF formula \(F_0\) and a stored FRAT stream \(R\) ending in a claimed empty clause. Initialize the needed set \(N\) with the identifier of that clause. Traverse \(R\) backward: when an addition of identifier \(i\in N\) is encountered, retain it and add every clause identifier required by its supplied or reconstructed justification to \(N\); account for deletions and restorations so references are resolved in the appropriate historical state. Discard additions not marked needed. Finally replay retained records forward, complete their LRAT hints, and output \(P\); reject if any dependency or justification cannot be resolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backward processing starts from the empty clause, marks transitive proof dependencies in reverse, discards irrelevant additions, then replays retained records forward to emit LRAT.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is stored or reverse-readable and preserves clause identities.
The claimed empty-clause record and its dependencies can be resolved historically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{backward}(F_0,R)=P\Longrightarrow P\text{ is a dependency-trimmed checker-ready refutation of }F_0.\)

notation.meaning: set of clause identifiers marked necessary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits backward FRAT processing, but reverse dependency marking across deletions and restorations is technically delicate. The historical-state rules and the claim that the result is dependency-trimmed and checker-ready require an authoritative algorithm description or correctness result.

children.title: Directional Processing Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Memory, dependency, and trimming differences between traversal directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Processing Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational comparison of forward replay and backward dependency-directed FRAT processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) contain \(m\) records and let \(R_N\) be the records retained by backward dependency analysis from the final contradiction. Forward processing can consume \(R\) in arrival order and begin elaboration before the stream ends, but it examines every record and may elaborate records irrelevant to the contradiction. Backward processing can restrict final elaboration to \(R_N\), where \(|R_N|\le m\), but requires reverse access or prior storage plus a subsequent forward emission pass. Thus backward trimming cannot increase the number of retained records, while neither direction universally minimizes runtime or peak memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward processing supports streaming but touches all records. Backward processing can trim irrelevant records, yet needs reverse access or storage and another forward pass; resource dominance is implementation-dependent.
assumptions_latex: Both regimes preserve the same core FRAT semantics.
Backward marking retains every transitive dependency of the final contradiction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|R_N|\le |R|\), but no unconditional ordering of runtime or peak memory follows.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role matches the tradeoff leaf, and the cardinality inequality follows from defining the retained records as a subtrace. The streaming, storage, extra-pass, runtime, and peak-memory comparisons remain implementation-dependent and have no cited support.

knowledge_statements.title: FRAT-to-LRAT Elaboration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elaboration of an accepted FRAT refutation into an explicitly hinted LRAT refutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a CNF formula \(F\) and a well-formed FRAT refutation \(T\), replay \(T\) while maintaining the active clause database. For every clause-addition record, reconstruct an ordered list of active clause identifiers witnessing the required reverse-unit-propagation or resolution-asymmetric-tautology check, and emit the corresponding LRAT addition; translate deletions using the identifiers assigned in the output. Preserve the initial clauses and finish by emitting a justified empty clause. The output is an LRAT refutation \(L\) satisfying \(\operatorname{check}_{\mathrm{LRAT}}(F,L)=\mathsf{accept}\); elaboration fails rather than emitting \(L\) if any required justification cannot be reconstructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replay the FRAT trace, reconstruct explicit checking hints for every addition, translate deletions and identifiers, and emit LRAT only when the final empty clause is fully justified.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula with stable input-clause identifiers.
\(T\) is a well-formed FRAT trace ending in a justified empty clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}_{\mathrm{LRAT}}(F,L)=\mathsf{accept}\).
review_flags: FRAT/LRAT format specification and elaborator reference required
exact handling of RAT hints and identifier conventions needs source confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf, but no citation supports the precise FRAT replay, RAT-hint reconstruction, identifier handling, or LRAT acceptance guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: CDCL Proof Emission
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clause-level proof logging by a CDCL solver during search and conflict analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the active proof database with the clauses of \(F\). Whenever conflict analysis learns a clause \(C\), emit an addition record for \(C\) together with antecedents or propagation hints sufficient for the selected proof checker to validate \(F_t\vdash C\), where \(F_t\) is the active database immediately before the addition. Clause removals may emit deletion records but cannot serve as logical inferences. If root-level propagation derives a conflict, emit the empty clause \(\bot\) with its justification and terminate. The emitted trace \(P\) is a refutation certificate precisely when every addition is accepted and its final derived clause is \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CDCL solver logs every learned clause with checkable antecedents, optionally logs deletions, and terminates a refutation by emitting a justified empty clause.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
Every emitted inference uses the active clause database at its emission point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}(F,P)=\mathsf{accept}\) whenever all additions, including the final \(\bot\), validate.

notation.meaning: active clause database at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits CDCL proof emission, but the claim abstracts over proof systems whose required hints and inference rules differ. No authoritative source is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplification Proof Emission
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification discipline for preprocessing and inprocessing transformations of CNF formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_k\) be the clause databases produced by simplification. For each transition \(F_i\mapsto F_{i+1}\), emit proof records whose accepted interpretation establishes the soundness required by the certification goal: additions must be justified by the active proof rule, and deletions must not be treated as derived consequences. If the goal is an unsatisfiability certificate, the combined simplification and search trace must derive \(\bot\) from \(F_0\), even when search operates only on \(F_k\). Thus a simplification is certifiable only when every inference needed to connect the original instance to the terminal contradiction is represented or reconstructible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each preprocessing or inprocessing change must be logged so that a checker can connect the original CNF, not merely the simplified CNF, to the contradiction.
assumptions_latex: \(F_0\) is the original CNF and each \(F_i\) is finite.
The chosen proof system specifies accepted addition and deletion records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}(F_0,P)=\mathsf{accept}\) only if the emitted trace connects \(F_0\) to a justified \(\bot\).

notation.meaning: clause database after simplification stage i

review_flags: source required for proof-producing SAT simplification rules
specific proof format not fixed by node context

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits simplification proof emission, but certification requirements for additions, deletions, preprocessing, and inprocessing depend on the proof format and require a specific source.

children.title: Proof Trimming
children.top_down_role: Removal of proof material irrelevant to the final certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof Trimming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward dependency trimming of a clause refutation with explicit inference dependencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a validated refutation \(P=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\) with terminal empty-clause step \(s_m\), initialize \(R=\{s_m\}\). Repeatedly add to \(R\) every premise step named by a retained inference, until closure. Output the retained steps in their original relative order, retaining every required input clause and adjusting deletion records or identifiers as needed. If each inference depends only on its named premises, the resulting trace \(P|_R\) remains a valid refutation, and every omitted derived step lies outside the transitive dependency cone of the terminal contradiction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from the empty clause, retain its transitive inference dependencies, preserve their order, and discard all proof steps irrelevant to the final contradiction.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a validated finite refutation with explicit, complete dependencies.
The terminal step \(s_m\) derives the empty clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}(F,P|_R)=\mathsf{accept}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The backward-trimming algorithm is plausible, but no source supports its preservation guarantee. The conclusion also uses F without introducing it, and identifier/deletion adjustments are proof-format dependent.

children.title: Proof Compression
children.top_down_role: Reduction of proof representation size while retaining checkability.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic preservation criterion for replacing proof fragments by smaller checkable fragments.
