knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=A\cdot Q\cdot B\) be a validated refutation, where the proof fragment \(Q\) transforms an active database \(D\) into an interface state exposing clauses \(E\) used by \(B\). A replacement fragment \(Q'\) is a valid compression when it is checkable from \(D\), exposes every clause in \(E\) with compatible identifiers and lifetimes, and leaves all premises required by \(B\) available. Under these conditions, \(P'=A\cdot Q'\cdot B\) is a valid refutation. It is a strict size compression when the selected encoding measure satisfies \(\lvert Q'\rvert<\lvert Q\rvert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shorter proof fragment may replace a longer one only if it is checkable and preserves every clause, identifier, and lifetime required downstream.
assumptions_latex: \(P=A\cdot Q\cdot B\) is a validated refutation.
Dependencies of the suffix \(B\) are explicit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}(F,P')=\mathsf{accept}\), and strict compression additionally requires \(\lvert Q'\rvert<\lvert Q\rvert\).

notation.meaning: active database at the fragment boundary

review_flags: size measure depends on proof representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preservation criterion is suitable for proof compression, but F and the encoding measure are not fully introduced, and the stated interface conditions require proof-format-specific validation and citation.

children.title: Proof Reordering
children.top_down_role: Rearrangement of proof records subject to dependency constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof Reordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency and clause-lifetime condition under which proof steps may be permuted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For proof steps \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}\), define \(s_i\prec s_j\) whenever \(s_j\) uses the clause introduced by \(s_i\), or whenever moving a deletion before \(s_j\) would remove a clause required by \(s_j\). A permutation \(\pi\) is an admissible proof reordering exactly when it is a linear extension of \(\prec\), preserves the placement of input declarations, and places each deletion after the last retained use of its clause. If inference validity depends only on the available named premises, every admissible reordering preserves checker acceptance and the terminal empty clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof steps may be reordered only topologically: every producer precedes its consumers, and every deletion follows the last use of its clause.
assumptions_latex: All inference dependencies and clause deletions are explicit.
Inference validity is invariant under unrelated active clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ admissible}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{check}(F,\pi(P))=\mathsf{accept}\).
review_flags: some proof systems are sensitive to additional active clauses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits proof reordering, but P is undefined and the 'exactly when' characterization may omit format-specific ordering constraints. A source is required to establish necessity and sufficiency.

children.title: Proof-Transformation Interactions
children.top_down_role: Compatibility and tradeoffs among trimming, compression, and reordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Transformation Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional boundary for trimming, compression, reordering, and identifier rewriting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1,\ldots,T_r\) be proof transformations. Individual soundness of each \(T_i\) does not ensure that the syntactic composition is accepted: after every stage, clause identifiers, dependency hints, active-clause lifetimes, and the distinguished terminal derivation must match the next stage's input contract. Composition is sound when each transformed trace is validated or when a proved interface invariant guarantees these conditions. Failure can occur, for example, if trimming removes a clause still named by a compressed fragment, or reordering moves a deletion before the clause's final use; the resulting trace may be rejected despite every local rewrite pattern being sound in isolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof transformations compose safely only when dependencies, identifiers, lifetimes, and the terminal contradiction remain consistent across every transformation boundary.
assumptions_latex: Each \(T_i\) is locally sound on traces satisfying its declared precondition.
Proof traces use identifiers and may contain deletion records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{Inv}_i(T_i(P))\) is required for compositional acceptance; local soundness alone is insufficient.

notation.meaning: interface invariant required after stage i

review_flags: source required for transformation-composition failure modes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but Inv_i is not defined mathematically, P is not introduced, and the displayed conjunction does not itself express compatibility between consecutive transformation interfaces. Sources are needed for the asserted failure modes.

children.title: Proof Elaboration
children.top_down_role: Enrichment of proof records with information required by a stricter checker.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof Elaboration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstruction of omitted proof details into a checker-ready certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an original CNF \(F\) and a coarse trace \(P\), replay its records against an active clause database. For every under-specified addition of a clause \(C\), search for and record a finite witness \(h_C\) accepted by the target proof rule, including ordered propagation or antecedent information where required. Remap identifiers, materialize implicit steps, and preserve deletion lifetimes. Output the elaborated trace \(E(P)\) only after every record and the terminal empty clause validate; otherwise report elaboration failure. Successful elaboration satisfies \(\operatorname{check}_{\mathrm{target}}(F,E(P))=\mathsf{accept}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elaboration replays a coarse trace, reconstructs every omitted inference witness, remaps identifiers, and emits a detailed certificate only after complete validation.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF formula.
\(P\) identifies its clause additions and terminal contradiction unambiguously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(P)\neq\mathsf{failure}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{check}_{\mathrm{target}}(F,E(P))=\mathsf{accept}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits proof elaboration, but the reconstruction and acceptance guarantee is parameterized by an unspecified target proof rule and has no supporting citation.

children.title: Proof-Format Translation
children.top_down_role: Conversion between certificate representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Format Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantics-preserving conversion between source and target SAT proof formats.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a source-format trace \(P_S\) for CNF \(F\), parse each record under the source semantics, maintain a map from live source clause identifiers to target identifiers, and emit a target-format derivation implementing the same accepted inference or a finite simulation of it. Translate deletions only after all mapped uses, and require the translated terminal record to derive the empty clause. The translator returns \(P_T\) only if the target checker accepts it. Hence successful translation guarantees \(\operatorname{check}_T(F,P_T)=\mathsf{accept}\), while unsupported source rules or unrepresentable state transitions cause explicit failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translate each source proof record into a target inference or simulation, preserving identifiers, lifetimes, and the final contradiction; reject unsupported constructs.
assumptions_latex: \(P_S\) is well formed under the source-format semantics.
Every translated source inference has a sound target-format simulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{translate}_{S\to T}(P_S)=P_T\Longrightarrow\operatorname{check}_T(F,P_T)=\mathsf{accept}\).
review_flags: source and target formats are unspecified

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits proof-format translation, but no concrete source and target semantics or citation establishes the claimed simulations, deletion handling, and acceptance guarantee.

children.title: Translation-Fidelity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Preservation limits and unsupported features across proof-format conversions.

knowledge_statements.title: Translation-Fidelity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits on claims that a translated proof preserves source-format meaning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A translation \(\tau:S\to T\) is refutation-faithful on a class \(\mathcal P\) only if, for every \(P\in\mathcal P\) accepted for \(F\) under source semantics, \(\tau(P)\) is defined and accepted for the same \(F\) under target semantics. This guarantee is unavailable when the target cannot soundly simulate a source inference, when preprocessing changes the certified input without a reconstruction witness, or when identifier and deletion semantics cannot be preserved. Target acceptance alone certifies unsatisfiability of \(F\); it does not by itself establish step correspondence, reversibility, preservation of proof size, or preservation of proof-derived annotations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successful target checking proves unsatisfiability, but stronger fidelity claims fail without simulations for source rules, input reconstruction, and preserved state semantics.
assumptions_latex: Source and target formats have explicit acceptance semantics.
\(\tau\) is a partial translation procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{check}_T(F,\tau(P))=\mathsf{accept}\) does not imply structural, reversible, or size-preserving fidelity without additional invariants.

notation.meaning: partial translation from source to target format

review_flags: boundary depends on the chosen proof formats

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but the fidelity limits depend on concrete source and target semantics and are unsupported by any cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsatisfiable-Core Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction of an unsatisfiable input-clause subset from a dependency-complete refutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{C_1,\ldots,C_n\}\) and let \(P\) be a validated refutation with explicit inference dependencies. Starting from the terminal empty clause, compute the transitive closure of premise dependencies. Return \(U\subseteq F\) consisting exactly of the input clauses reached by this closure. Restricting \(P\) to reached derivation steps yields a refutation from \(U\), so \(U\) is unsatisfiable. The procedure does not generally guarantee that \(U\) is inclusion-minimal or has minimum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trace dependencies backward from the empty clause and return the reached input clauses; they form an unsatisfiable core, though not necessarily a minimal one.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a validated refutation of the finite CNF \(F\).
Every inference dependency used by \(P\) is explicit and complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U\subseteq F\) and \(U\models\bot\).

notation.meaning: input CNF viewed as a set of clauses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits unsatisfiable-core extraction and correctly distinguishes a core from a minimal core, but the restriction argument depends on complete proof dependencies and requires an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Core Workflow Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion-based interface for producing a subset-minimal unsatisfiable core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an unsatisfiable finite clause set \(U_0\), preferably obtained from a proof, and a SAT interface that returns either a satisfying assignment or a checked refutation. Set \(U:=U_0\). For each candidate clause \(C\in U\), query \(U\setminus\{C\}\): if it is unsatisfiable with an accepted certificate, replace \(U\) by \(U\setminus\{C\}\); if it is satisfiable, retain \(C\). Revisit clauses whenever the scheduling policy requires it, and stop only after every retained clause has a satisfiable deletion test. Output \(U\), its refutation, and the deletion-test results. Then \(U\) is subset-minimal unsatisfiable, not necessarily minimum-cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly test whether each core clause can be deleted, requiring certified UNSAT or a model; stop when every single deletion makes the set satisfiable.
assumptions_latex: \(U_0\) is a finite unsatisfiable clause set.
Each SAT-interface answer is accompanied by a checkable model or refutation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U\models\bot\) and \(\forall C\in U,\ U\setminus\{C\}\not\models\bot\).
review_flags: minimum-cardinality and subset-minimality must remain distinguished

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deletion-based algorithm fits the workflow-interface leaf and correctly targets subset minimality rather than minimum cardinality, but no source supports the scheduling, certification, and termination claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolant-Extraction Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface contract for extracting a Craig interpolant from a checked propositional refutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given CNF formulas \(A\) and \(B\) and a checked refutation \(\pi\) of \(A\land B\), an interpolant-extraction interface returns a formula \(I\) or reports that \(\pi\)'s proof rules are unsupported. A successful result must satisfy \[\operatorname{Var}(I)\subseteq\operatorname{Var}(A)\cap\operatorname{Var}(B),\qquad A\models I,\qquad B\models\neg I.\] The interface output is \((I,M)\), where \(M\) maps each subformula of \(I\) to the proof node and extraction rule that produced it; validation accepts only if the three displayed conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From a checked refutation of A with B, return a Craig interpolant over shared variables plus provenance, or explicitly reject unsupported proof rules.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are propositional CNF formulas.
\(\pi\) is a checker-accepted refutation of \(A\land B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(I)\subseteq\operatorname{Var}(A)\cap\operatorname{Var}(B)\), \(A\models I\), and \(B\models\neg I\).

notation.meaning: provenance map from interpolant components to proof nodes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the extraction-interface container and states the Craig conditions correctly, but no citation supports the proof-system-dependent extraction rules or the stronger subformula-level provenance-map contract.

children.title: Explanation Extraction
children.top_down_role: Derivation of human-facing or system-facing explanatory artifacts from proofs.

knowledge_statements.title: Explanation Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proof-based extraction of an input-clause explanation for a derived clause or contradiction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\) be a CNF formula and let \(D\) be a clause derived at node \(v\) of a checked proof DAG \(P\). Traverse backward from \(v\), following every antecedent edge required by the recorded inference, and collect the reached input clauses into \(E\subseteq F\). Return \(E\) together with the induced derivation of \(D\). A valid extracted explanation satisfies \(E\models D\); when \(D=\bot\), it satisfies \(E\models\bot\). No inclusion-minimality is implied unless a separate minimization phase succeeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backward proof traversal returns input clauses sufficient to derive the selected clause or contradiction, without claiming that the explanation is minimal.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a checked proof DAG whose leaves identify clauses of \(F\).
Every visited inference records all antecedents required by its proof rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \(E\subseteq F\) satisfies \(E\models D\).

notation.meaning: extracted set of explanatory input clauses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm matches Explanation Extraction and its nonminimality qualification is appropriate, but soundness depends on the proof rules and antecedent semantics, for which no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Dependency Extraction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of premise, clause, or decision dependencies represented by a proof.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency Extraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction of proof-node and input-clause dependencies from a checked proof DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a checked proof DAG \(P=(V,E_P)\) and selected node \(t\in V\), initialize \(R=\{t\}\) and repeatedly add every recorded antecedent of each node in \(R\) until closure. Return the induced dependency subgraph \(P[R]\) and the leaf set \(L=R\cap V_{\mathrm{in}}\). Each directed edge \((u,v)\in E_P\) means that the inference producing \(v\) consumes \(u\). Thus every directed path from an input node to \(t\) records a syntactic proof dependency; no semantic necessity or minimality is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute the backward-reachable proof subgraph and its input leaves; its edges record actual inference use, not necessarily indispensable semantic dependence.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a finite checked proof DAG.
Each noninput node records its complete antecedent list.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is exactly the set of nodes from which \(t\) is reachable in \(P\), including \(t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The backward-closure algorithm fits Dependency Extraction and distinguishes syntactic from semantic dependence, but the proof-DAG and edge-orientation conventions lack cited support.

children.title: Explanation–Dependency Relations
children.top_down_role: Use of proof dependencies to structure or constrain extracted explanations.

knowledge_statements.title: Explanation–Dependency Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between proof explanations, syntactic dependency closures, and semantic sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the backward dependency closure of a checked proof node deriving \(D\), and let \(L=R\cap V_{\mathrm{in}}\) be its input leaves. Then \(L\) is an explanation extracted from that derivation and satisfies \(L\models D\). Any explanation obtained by deleting leaves and rechecking the induced derivation is a subset of \(L\). However, a semantically sufficient explanation \(E\subseteq F\) need not be contained in \(L\), because a different derivation of \(D\) may use different input clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proof’s dependency leaves form a sufficient explanation, but they need not be minimal or include explanations arising from different derivations.
assumptions_latex: The proof DAG is sound and checker-accepted.
\(R\) contains every antecedent recursively required to derive \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\models D\), while proof dependency and semantic necessity need not coincide.

notation.meaning: input leaves of the dependency closure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the relation container and is plausible under sound, complete antecedent recording, but no source establishes the explanation convention or the asserted relationship between dependency leaves and semantic sufficiency.

children.title: Proof-Size Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Storage and processing pressure caused by large certificate volume.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Size Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource boundary caused by certificates whose length dominates generation, storage, or checking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_n\) be an encoded SAT instance and let \(\pi_n\) be its emitted certificate, with lengths \(N_n=|F_n|\) and \(L_n=|\pi_n|\) bits. In any explicit certificate pipeline, writing, retaining, or fully reading \(\pi_n\) requires \(\Omega(L_n)\) bit operations and, if retained, \(\Omega(L_n)\) bits of storage. Consequently, whenever \(L_n\) exceeds the available transfer, storage, or checking budget, end-to-end certification fails even if solving \(F_n\) itself remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit certificate of length L imposes linear reading or writing work and linear retained storage, so oversized proofs can defeat certification after solving succeeds.
assumptions_latex: Certificates are represented explicitly as bit strings.
Successful checking requires consuming the complete certificate or an equivalent amount of authenticated information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit certification incurs \(\Omega(L_n)\) certificate-access work and may fail when \(L_n\) exceeds a resource budget.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but the linear access and storage claims depend on the explicit representation, retention, streaming, compression, and authentication model and have no supporting citation.

children.title: Proof I/O Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Throughput limits caused by proof serialization, transfer, and persistent storage.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof I/O Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: I/O lower bound for explicit sequential transmission and checking of SAT certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an explicit certificate contain \(L\) bits and let the sustained producer-to-checker bandwidth be \(B>0\) bits per second. If every certificate bit must cross that channel before acceptance, then certificate transfer time satisfies \[T_{\mathrm{io}}\geq L/B.\] If the producer emits at rate \(B_p\) and the checker consumes at rate \(B_c\), a bounded-buffer pipeline has steady-state throughput at most \(\min\{B_p,B,B_c\}\). Thus faster proof inference cannot reduce end-to-end time below the transfer bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transmitting an explicit L-bit proof over bandwidth B takes at least L/B time, and pipeline throughput is limited by its slowest stage.
assumptions_latex: The certificate is transmitted explicitly without an independently checkable compressed substitute.
Acceptance occurs only after all required certificate bits are received.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{io}}\geq L/B\) and steady-state throughput is at most \(\min\{B_p,B,B_c\}\).

notation.meaning: channel bandwidth in bits per second

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits Proof I/O Bottlenecks and the formulas are correct under the stated explicit-transfer model, but no source with a specific locator supports that model or its throughput conclusion.

children.title: Size–Throughput Interactions
children.top_down_role: Coupling between proof volume and sustained proof-processing throughput.

knowledge_statements.title: Size–Throughput Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: End-to-end certificate rate under proof-size and finite-throughput constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For certificates \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k\) with total encoded size \(S=\sum_{i=1}^k|\pi_i|\), suppose generation, transfer, and checking sustain rates \(r_g,r_t,r_c>0\) bits per second. Any pipeline that explicitly processes every certificate bit has completion time \[T\geq S/\min\{r_g,r_t,r_c\}.\] Hence its certificate throughput satisfies \(k/T\leq k\min\{r_g,r_t,r_c\}/S\). Increasing average certificate size therefore lowers the maximum certificate rate unless the limiting bit-processing rate increases proportionally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For explicit proofs, total size divided by the slowest bit-processing rate lower-bounds completion time; larger average proofs reduce maximum certificate throughput.
assumptions_latex: Every required certificate bit is generated, transferred, and checked.
The stated rates are sustained effective rates over the workload.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\geq S/\min\{r_g,r_t,r_c\}\) and \(k/T\leq k\min\{r_g,r_t,r_c\}/S\).

notation.meaning: generation, transfer, and checking bit rates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity bound fits the size–throughput leaf and follows under sustained effective rates for stages that each process all S bits, but the pipeline assumptions and bound lack an inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Native Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust boundary when solver-native inference lacks a sound translation into checker-supported rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a solver derive a conclusion \(C\) from premises \(\Gamma\) using a native rule \(r\). Let \(\mathcal R\) be the checker's supported rule set. Certification is incomplete at this step if \(r\notin\mathcal R\) and the producer supplies neither a derivation of \(C\) from \(\Gamma\) using \(\mathcal R\) nor a separately checked extension validating \(r\). The checker must reject or return unsupported; accepting \(C\) solely because the producer labels the step as \(r\) enlarges the trusted computing base to include that native reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A native solver inference is uncertified unless translated into supported rules or validated by a checked extension; trusting its label moves reasoning into the trusted base.
assumptions_latex: The checker accepts only inferences justified by its declared rule set \(\mathcal R\).
The native step claims that \(\Gamma\) entails \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a supported derivation or checked extension, the step cannot contribute to a checker-certified conclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and statement match Unsupported Native Reasoning, but the checker-extension and trusted-computing-base claims require a cited proof-format or certified-checking source.

children.title: Checker Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Divergent validation behavior among proof checkers.

knowledge_statements.title: Checker Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance ambiguity caused by underspecified inference semantics rather than byte parsing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an input formula \(F\), a parsed certificate object \(P\), and two checker semantics \(V_1,V_2:\mathcal F\times\mathcal P\to\{0,1\}\) that both conform to the published rule description. Checker ambiguity occurs when \[V_1(F,P)\neq V_2(F,P).\] It arises, for example, when side conditions, deletion effects, integer overflow behavior, or treatment of unavailable antecedents are unspecified. In that case the certificate format does not determine a unique acceptance predicate, so checker acceptance alone is not portable evidence of certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Checker ambiguity exists when two conforming implementations assign different acceptance results to the same formula and already-parsed certificate.
assumptions_latex: Both checkers receive identical mathematical input and parsed certificate objects.
Both semantics satisfy all explicitly published checking requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(V_1(F,P)\neq V_2(F,P)\), the specification fails to define a unique certificate-validity predicate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary formulation cleanly separates checker semantics from parsing, but conformity to the published rule description is not formalized or supported by a cited specification source.

children.title: Parser Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Divergent interpretation of proof syntax, tokens, or record boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Parser Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique conversion of identical certificate bytes into checker-level proof objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\in\{0,1\}^*\) be certificate bytes and let \(p_1,p_2:\{0,1\}^*\rightharpoonup\mathcal P\) be parsers conforming to the same published syntax. Parser ambiguity occurs if both parsers accept \(b\) but \(p_1(b)\neq p_2(b)\), or if exactly one parser accepts \(b\). When the resulting objects differ in clauses, identifiers, integers, or step boundaries, a common checker predicate may yield different outcomes. A portable certificate language therefore requires a unique parse or an explicit rejection rule for every byte string.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parser ambiguity occurs when conforming parsers interpret the same bytes differently or disagree on whether those bytes are syntactically valid.
assumptions_latex: The parsers claim conformance to one certificate syntax.
Parser output determines the proof object supplied to checking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A byte string with nonunique conformance behavior lacks a portable certificate interpretation.

notation.meaning: partial parser from bytes to proof objects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits Parser Ambiguity and correctly treats differing parses or acceptance domains as nonportable behavior, but the syntax-conformance and byte-level interpretation model has no citation.

children.title: Format Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Underspecified certificate semantics or edge-case handling.

knowledge_statements.title: Format Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specification-level ambiguity admitting multiple incompatible syntactic or semantic interpretations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a certificate-format specification \(S\) denote a set \(\operatorname{Impl}(S)\) of conforming parser-checker pairs. For each \((p,V)\in\operatorname{Impl}(S)\), define the total observable result \(R_{p,V}(F,b)\) to be rejection when \(p(b)\) is undefined and otherwise \(V(F,p(b))\). The format is unambiguous only if, for every input \(F\), byte string \(b\), and implementations \((p_1,V_1),(p_2,V_2)\in\operatorname{Impl}(S)\), one has \[R_{p_1,V_1}(F,b)=R_{p_2,V_2}(F,b).\] A counterexample \((F,b)\) establishes format ambiguity and prevents implementation-independent certification for that instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A format is ambiguous if two conforming parser-checker pairs can disagree on one input and certificate byte string, counting parse failure as rejection.
assumptions_latex: Conformance to \(S\) is defined independently of the tested implementations.
Parse failure has the observable result rejection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Disagreement on some \((F,b)\) shows that \(S\) does not define implementation-independent certificate acceptance.

notation.meaning: conforming checker predicate on parsed proof objects
total observable parser-checker result, with parse failure treated as rejection

children.title: Cross-Implementation Disagreement
children.top_down_role: Certificate acceptance differences arising across independent implementations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Implementation Disagreement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A differential witness showing nonportable certificate acceptance across purportedly conforming implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For certificate implementations \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), define \(R_i(F,b)\in\{\mathrm{accept},\mathrm{reject},\mathrm{error}\}\) as the observable result on formula \(F\) and certificate bytes \(b\). A cross-implementation disagreement witness is a tuple \((F,b,I_1,I_2)\) satisfying \[R_1(F,b)\neq R_2(F,b).\] If both implementations claim conformance to the same deterministic specification, the witness refutes at least one of: both conformance claims, determinacy of the specification, or equality of the implementations' environmental assumptions. It does not by itself identify which alternative failed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One formula and certificate producing different results in two purportedly conforming implementations witnesses a conformance, specification, or environment mismatch.
assumptions_latex: \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) claim conformance to the same deterministic certificate specification.
Both runs use the recorded formula, certificate bytes, and declared environment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1(F,b)\neq R_2(F,b)\) disproves joint conformance under identical specified assumptions or exposes specification nondeterminacy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits this witness-oriented leaf, and the conclusion appropriately leaves the cause unresolved, but the differential-validation framework and equivalence of environmental assumptions lack cited support and formalization.

assumptions_latex: The checker receives a formula encoding \(F\) and a purported certificate \(P\).
All accepted inputs are interpreted by fixed parsing, preprocessing, and proof-calculus semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance certifies unsatisfiability only conditionally on the correctness of every trusted component establishing \(\operatorname{Accept}(F,P)\Rightarrow\operatorname{UNSAT}(F)\).

notation.meaning: SAT instance under the checker's declared encoding semantics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional soundness boundary for SAT certificate checkers and their trusted implementation components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) comprise the input parser, formula and certificate semantics, preprocessing reconstruction, proof-rule kernel, and implementation mechanisms on which acceptance depends. The intended soundness condition is \[\forall F\,\forall P,\qquad \operatorname{Accept}_{T}(F,P)\Longrightarrow \operatorname{UNSAT}(F).\] A successfully checked certificate establishes this conclusion only relative to the correctness of \(T\). If parsing changes \(F\), preprocessing lacks a checked reconstruction, the kernel admits an unsound inference, or implementation behavior violates the specified semantics, certificate acceptance alone does not establish \(\operatorname{UNSAT}(F)\). Thus the certificate does not certify the trusted computing base that interprets and checks it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate acceptance proves unsatisfiability only relative to the correctness of the parser, semantics, reconstruction, proof kernel, and implementation inside the trusted computing base.
knowledge_statements.title: Trusted-Computing-Base Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and conditional trusted-computing-base claim fit the leaf, but no inspectable SAT proof-checking source or locator supports the stated boundary.

children.title: Parallel Proof Assembly Gaps
children.top_down_role: Certificate omissions arising from concurrent solving, proof merging, or nondeterministic event ordering.

assumptions_latex: Each worker produces a locally checkable proof fragment for a common base formula and declared imported clauses.
Clause identifiers and worker contexts are intended to have a single global interpretation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local validity of all fragments implies global validity only when their dependencies admit a context-consistent, acyclic assembly order.

notation.meaning: proof fragment produced by worker i
directed dependency graph of imported and exported clauses

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global assembly condition for independently generated parallel SAT proof fragments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For worker fragments \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\), form a dependency graph \(G\) whose edge \(i\to j\) records that \(P_j\) imports a clause exported by \(P_i\). A sound assembled certificate requires that every imported clause be identified unambiguously, derived before its first use, and valid under the same formula and assumption context as its consumer. Equivalently, the imports must admit a global topological checking order, or the certificate format must provide a sound rule for cyclic dependencies. If fragments check only relative to unverified imports, then separate acceptance of every \(P_i\) does not imply that their union derives contradiction from \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel fragments are not a global proof unless imported clauses have unambiguous origins, compatible contexts, and a sound assembly order.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Proof Assembly Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited proof format supports the proposed worker-level dependency condition. The claimed equivalence between local import requirements and a topological order depends on whether fragments are atomic or may be interleaved.

children.title: Incremental Proof Continuity Gaps
children.top_down_role: Certificate discontinuities across successive solver queries or changing clause contexts.

assumptions_latex: Queries \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_m\) are issued to one incremental solver state.
Formula updates, assumptions, retained lemmas, and certificates may span query boundaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A certificate for query \(Q_t\) is continuous only if all state transitions and every retained lemma's validity at \(Q_t\) are checkable.

notation.meaning: retained checker or solver state after query t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate continuity across additions, removals, assumptions, and retained learned state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an incremental sequence \(F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_m\), proof continuity at transition \(t\to t+1\) requires a checkable update establishing the formula represented by \(S_{t+1}\) and the validity of every retained clause: \[\forall C\in L_{t+1},\qquad F_{t+1}\models C,\] unless the certificate explicitly records a context guard under which \(C\) is valid. A proof of \(\operatorname{UNSAT}(F_t)\) does not certify \(\operatorname{UNSAT}(F_{t+1})\), and an unchecked reset, deletion, assumption change, or lemma carryover breaks the certificate chain. Per-query conclusions are certified only when the checker can reconstruct each relevant transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental proofs remain continuous only when formula updates and carried lemmas are checked at every query boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Proof Continuity Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but incremental certificate semantics are uncited. The categorical statement that a proof for F_t does not certify F_{t+1} needs qualification because a valid proof may remain usable under some formula-strengthening transitions.

children.title: Cross-Regime Verification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Checker coverage limits shared by parallel or incremental certificate workflows.

assumptions_latex: A certificate pipeline changes proof calculus, formula representation, or native reasoning regime.
The regimes need not assign identical primitive meanings to certificate steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: End-to-end verification requires a checked semantic bridge for every regime transition; independent verification within each regime is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verification boundary between proof formats, encodings, preprocessors, and native constraint regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose verification moves from regime \(R_1\) to regime \(R_2\) through a translation \(\tau\). End-to-end soundness requires a checked bridge theorem appropriate to the claimed result, such as \[\operatorname{SAT}(X)\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{SAT}(\tau(X))\] for satisfiability preservation, or \[\operatorname{UNSAT}(\tau(X))\Longrightarrow\operatorname{UNSAT}(X)\] for backward transfer of an unsatisfiability certificate. The bridge must also map assumptions, clause identifiers, auxiliary variables, and conclusions consistently. Verification of steps internal to \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) does not cover an unchecked CNF conversion, preprocessing map, proof-format switch, or native-constraint inference between them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing encodings or proof systems requires a checked semantic bridge; separately valid proofs on either side do not certify the transition.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Regime Verification Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record appropriately describes a cross-regime failure boundary, but no inspectable source identifies the required preservation direction for the relevant translations and proof systems.

children.title: SAT Solver Evaluation Interface
children.top_down_role: Reusable solver interfaces, multi-query workflows, solver configuration, and evaluation methodology without absorbing neighboring application domains.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Chapters 11 and 12: runtime variation, automated configuration, and solver selection

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a CNF formula and \(A\) is a finite, consistent set of literals.
Assumptions affect the current query without becoming permanent clauses of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The query result is interpreted against \(F\land\bigwedge_{a\in A}a\), and an assumption core \(U\) must satisfy \(U\subseteq A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard incremental SAT semantics for temporary assumption literals and returned assumption cores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An assumption-literal query \(\operatorname{solve}(F,A)\) asks whether \[F_A:=F\land\bigwedge_{a\in A}a\] is satisfiable while leaving the permanent database \(F\) unchanged for later queries. A satisfiable response supplies an assignment satisfying \(F_A\). An unsatisfiable response asserts \(\operatorname{UNSAT}(F_A)\). If the interface returns an assumption core \(U\), correctness requires \(U\subseteq A\) and \(\operatorname{UNSAT}(F\land\bigwedge_{u\in U}u)\); minimality of \(U\) is an additional property and is not implied by the interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solving under assumptions means solving the permanent formula conjoined with temporary literals; a returned core is an unsatisfiable subset of those literals.
knowledge_statements.title: Assumption-Literal Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise and matches the assumption-literal interface leaf, but the temporary-assumption and returned-core API semantics have no cited authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Activation-Literal Encodings
children.top_down_role: Guard-based clause control for enabling or disabling portions of an incremental instance.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a clause over problem variables.
\(a\) is fresh and does not occur in \(C\) or elsewhere except as an activation control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The guarded clause \(\neg a\lor C\) enforces \(C\) under assumption \(a\) and becomes vacuous when \(a\) may be false.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-assumption convention for activating clauses through fresh guard variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent a conditionally active clause \(C\) by permanently adding \(
eg a\lor C\), where \(a\) is a fresh activation variable. Under the query assumption \(a\), \[a\land(
eg a\lor C)\equiv a\land C,\] so the guarded clause enforces \(C\). Without assumption \(a\), the solver may set \(a\) false, making \(
eg a\lor C\) true and removing its restriction on the problem variables. A family of clauses can share \(a\), thereby enabling or disabling the family through the assumption interface without deleting permanent clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Guarding a clause as not-a or C makes assumption a activate C, while allowing a to be false deactivates it.
knowledge_statements.title: Activation-Literal Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and positive-activation convention fit the leaf and are internally consistent, but no incremental-SAT encoding source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Context-Scoped Clause Encodings
children.top_down_role: Clause organization by query context, logical frame, or reversible problem scope.

assumptions_latex: Each context-scoped clause has a fresh activation variable occurring only negatively in clauses of its context.
A query assumes exactly the activation variables for contexts intended to be active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection onto problem variables yields precisely the conjunction of the base clauses and clauses belonging to active contexts.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guarded-clause representation of multiple selectable incremental contexts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For contexts \(j=1,\ldots,m\), assign a fresh activation variable \(a_j\) and store \[G:=F_0\land\bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}\ \bigwedge_{C\in\mathcal C_j}(\neg a_j\lor C).\] To activate the index set \(K\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), solve \(G\) under assumptions \(A_K=\{a_j:j\in K\}\). Because each unassumed \(a_j\) may be set false, projection of the satisfying assignments of \(G\land\bigwedge A_K\) onto the problem variables equals the satisfying assignments of \[F_0\land\bigwedge_{j\in K}\ \bigwedge_{C\in\mathcal C_j}C.\] This equivalence depends on freshness and restricted use of the activation variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fresh guards let one permanent clause database represent many contexts; assuming selected guards activates exactly their clause families after projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Context-Scoped Clause Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The guarded-context representation and projected-model claim are precise under the stated freshness restrictions, but they lack an inspectable supporting source and locator.

children.title: Context Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Validity limits encountered when activation states or incremental contexts change.

assumptions_latex: The permanent incremental database grows only by clause addition.
Temporary contexts are represented by fresh activation literals supplied as assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A context transition is sound only when retained clauses remain entailed by the new active query or carry guards recording their original context.

notation.meaning: active query formula in context K
clause retained across a context transition
old and new active context sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness boundary when activation assumptions change between incremental queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Changing the active context from \(K\) to \(K'\) changes the query formula from \(F_K\) to \(F_{K'}\), even though the guarded permanent database is unchanged. Any retained learned clause \(L\) used without a guard must satisfy \[F_{K'}\models L.\] Alternatively, a context-dependent consequence may be retained in discharged form, guarded by the assumptions on which its derivation depends. Simply dropping an activation assumption does not delete guarded clauses, but it can invalidate unguarded consequences derived only while that assumption was true. Hence context transition is a validity boundary for learned state and certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing activation assumptions changes the active formula, so retained learned clauses must be globally entailed or explicitly guarded by their derivation context.
knowledge_statements.title: Context Transition Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the treatment of context-dependent learned clauses depends on the solver's assumption-learning and guarding policy, for which no source or formal interface semantics is cited.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the permanent formula and \(A\) is the current assumption set.
The solver reports unsatisfiability and optionally returns literals drawn from \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid incremental core response is a set \(U\subseteq A\) satisfying \(\operatorname{UNSAT}(F\land\bigwedge_{u\in U}u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic contract and independent certification target for assumption-based unsatisfiable cores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incremental core interface for an unsatisfiable query \(\operatorname{solve}(F,A)\) may return \(U\subseteq A\). Its semantic contract is \[\operatorname{UNSAT}\!\left(F\land\bigwedge_{u\in U}u\right).\] Membership \(U\subseteq A\) is directly checkable, but unsatisfiability requires a proof certificate for the reduced query or another sound verification procedure. The interface need not return a subset-minimal or minimum-cardinality core unless that stronger guarantee is stated separately. Core literals must retain the same polarity, identity, and query-context interpretation used in the certified solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incremental core is a subset of the current assumptions whose conjunction with the permanent formula is independently certifiably unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Core Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic core condition is standard and precise, but no incremental-core API source is supplied. The selected certificate kind also requires source clarification because the record primarily specifies an interface contract and explicitly notes that the returned core alone does not certify unsatisfiability.

children.title: Reusable Solver State
children.top_down_role: Persistent solver information retained across related incremental queries.

assumptions_latex: An incremental solver retains clauses, activities, watches, or other internal data between queries.
Only retained clauses can constrain the logical solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Logical reuse is sound when every retained constraining clause is entailed by the next query formula, possibly through an explicit context guard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical validity condition for state retained by an incremental SAT solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_t\) be the clauses retained after query \(t\). Reusing the logical portion of the state for query \(t+1\) is sound if \[\forall C\in L_t,\qquad F_{t+1}\models C,\] where \(F_{t+1}\) includes the permanent database and the semantics of the new context. A clause depending on prior assumptions may instead be stored with those assumptions discharged as guards, provided the guarded clause follows from the permanent database. Heuristic data such as activities or restart counters may be reused without this entailment condition when it cannot exclude assignments or justify proof steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusable solver state may keep heuristics freely, but every retained clause that constrains search must follow from the new query or be context-guarded.
knowledge_statements.title: Reusable Solver State

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logical-reuse condition fits the leaf, but no authoritative source or precise solver-state model supports the distinction between constraining clauses and reusable nonlogical state.

children.title: Stale Learned-Clause Risks
children.top_down_role: Learned information whose relevance or validity is compromised by later context changes.

assumptions_latex: A learned clause is retained after clauses or assumptions supporting its derivation cease to be active.
The retained clause continues to participate in propagation or conflict detection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reuse can produce a false unsatisfiable result whenever the new query satisfies \(F_{t+1}\) but not the stale retained clause.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete unsoundness mechanism caused by retaining a clause after its supporting context disappears.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Take the old active formula \(F_t=(x)\), from which the clause \(L=(x)\) is valid and may be retained. Remove or deactivate the supporting clause and let the next query be \(F_{t+1}=(
eg x)\). Then \(F_{t+1}\) is satisfiable, but \[F_{t+1}\land L=(
eg x)\land(x)\] is unsatisfiable. Therefore a solver that retains \(L\) as an unconditional clause can incorrectly report unsatisfiability. The failure occurs because \(F_t\models L\) while \(F_{t+1}
ot\models L\); guarding \(L\) by its old context or discarding it prevents this particular stale-clause error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clause valid under an old context can contradict a satisfiable new query after its support is removed, causing a false unsatisfiable result.
knowledge_statements.title: Stale Learned-Clause Risks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly demonstrates unsound reuse after removal of support and fits a counterexample container, but no source establishes that this transition is within the intended incremental interface or learning model.

children.title: Cross-Query Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits governing which retained artifacts remain sound across incremental query transitions.

assumptions_latex: Queries \(t\) and \(t+1\) may differ in permanent clauses, assumptions, or active contexts.
Some logical clauses are candidates for reuse across the query boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cross-query reuse boundary is exactly the requirement \(F_{t+1}\models C\) for every unguarded retained clause \(C\).

notation.meaning: active formula of the next query

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary logical condition for carrying constraining clauses from one incremental query to another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each clause \(C\) carried from query \(t\) into query \(t+1\), unconditional reuse is sound precisely when \[F_{t+1}\models C.\] A sufficient implementation discipline is to retain only clauses entailed by a permanent formula common to both queries. If \(C\) was derived using temporary assumptions \(D\), it may cross the boundary in guarded form \(\bigvee_{d\in D}\neg d\lor C\) when that guarded clause is entailed by the permanent database. When neither unconditional entailment nor a valid guard is available, \(C\) must not constrain the next query or support its certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A retained clause may constrain the next query only if the new formula entails it or a valid guard records the assumptions supporting it.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Query Validity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the cross-query boundary leaf, but the claim that entailment is exactly necessary depends on whether soundness means preserving all models, preserving satisfiability status, or maintaining proof-valid learned clauses. No source fixes that intended notion.

children.title: Multi-Solution Interfaces
children.top_down_role: SAT-level enumeration interfaces only; counting and knowledge compilation remain external.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite propositional formula over variables \(V\).
A complete SAT call returns either a total satisfying assignment or \(\mathsf{UNSAT}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=\{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^{V}:\alpha\models F\}\), with each assignment occurring exactly once.

notation.meaning: The set of variables of the formula.
The accumulated output list of models.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: iterative SAT with full-assignment blocking is the standard finite model-enumeration interface
direct SAT model-enumeration source locator required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite propositional model enumeration using repeated SAT calls and full blocking clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(G:=F\) and \(L:=()\). Repeatedly invoke a complete SAT solver on \(G\). If it returns \(\mathsf{UNSAT}\), stop and output \(L\). Otherwise, for the returned total model \(\alpha:V\to\{0,1\}\), append \(\alpha\) to \(L\) and conjoin the blocking clause \[B_\alpha:=\bigvee_{v\in V:\alpha(v)=1}\neg v\;\vee\!\bigvee_{v\in V:\alpha(v)=0}v,\qquad G:=G\wedge B_\alpha.\] The clause excludes exactly \(\alpha\). Because \(V\) is finite and the solver is complete, termination occurs after all models of \(F\), and no model is emitted twice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the formula, output each satisfying assignment, and add a clause excluding exactly that assignment; termination with unsatisfiable status yields every model once.
knowledge_statements.title: Model Enumeration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and content kind fit the leaf, but no cited source supports the blocking-clause enumeration claim. The statement also contains proof-like justification, and the list L is equated with a set in the conclusion.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite propositional formula over variables \(V\).
\(P\subseteq V\) is the set of projection variables.
Each SAT result supplies a total satisfying assignment on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=\{\alpha|_P:\alpha\models F\}\), with every distinct projection occurring exactly once.

notation.meaning: Restriction of an assignment to the projection variables.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: projected enumeration blocks only the observed projection and thereby represents each equivalence class once
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration modulo equality on a designated finite set of projection variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(G:=F\) and \(L:=()\). When a SAT call on \(G\) returns a model \(\alpha\), emit \(p:=\alpha|_P\) and conjoin \[B_p:=\bigvee_{v\in P:p(v)=1}\neg v\;\vee\!\bigvee_{v\in P:p(v)=0}v,\qquad G:=G\wedge B_p.\] Stop when \(G\) is unsatisfiable. The clause \(B_p\) excludes every model whose restriction to \(P\) equals \(p\), while retaining models with any other projection. Thus the output contains exactly one representative value for every satisfiable projected assignment, independently of assignments to \(V\setminus P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each model, block its assignment only on the projection variables. The procedure emits each distinct satisfiable projection once and ignores differences on unprojected variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Model Enumeration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected-blocking algorithm fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but it has no inspectable citation. The explanatory correctness argument is proof-like, and L is introduced as a list but equated with a set.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) has finite variable set \(V\).
Each emitted object is either a total assignment on \(V\) or a projection on fixed \(P\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Mod}(F\wedge\bigwedge_{s\in S}B_s)=\operatorname{Mod}(F)\setminus\bigcup_{s\in S}E_s\).

notation.meaning: The set of already emitted assignments or projections.
The clause blocking emitted object s.
Models represented by emitted object s.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conjunction of complements of emitted assignment cubes gives exact exclusion and supports incremental enumeration
direct SAT blocking-clause management source locator required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic invariant for full or projected blocking clauses in incremental enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an emitted assignment \(s\) on coordinates \(Q\), where \(Q=V\) for full enumeration or \(Q=P\) for projected enumeration, define \[B_s:=\bigvee_{v\in Q:s(v)=1}\neg v\;\vee\!\bigvee_{v\in Q:s(v)=0}v\] and \(E_s:=\{\alpha\in\operatorname{Mod}(F):\alpha|_Q=s\}\). Maintaining \(G_S:=F\wedge\bigwedge_{s\in S}B_s\) gives the invariant \(\operatorname{Mod}(G_S)=\operatorname{Mod}(F)\setminus\bigcup_{s\in S}E_s\). Consequently, clauses may be added incrementally; deleting any active \(B_s\) forfeits exclusion of \(E_s\) unless another active clause already excludes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each active blocking clause removes exactly the models represented by one emitted assignment or projection; their conjunction preserves precisely the not-yet-blocked models.
knowledge_statements.title: Blocking-Clause Management

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The invariant is appropriate as a property of blocking-clause management, but no supporting source is cited. The deletion sentence is imprecise: other active clauses may exclude only part of E_s rather than preserve exclusion of all of E_s.

assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\) is a finite or compact configuration space.
\(D_{\mathrm{tr}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is a fixed training set.
\(c(\theta,x)\) is a measurable, capped performance cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\widehat R(\theta)\).

notation.meaning: The performance cost of a configuration on an instance.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: offline algorithm configuration is empirical optimization of parameter settings over a representative training set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical offline tuning of one SAT solver's parameter configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(D_{\mathrm{tr}}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), configuration space \(\Theta\), and nonnegative capped cost \(c\), define \[\widehat R(\theta):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(\theta,x_i).\] An offline configurator evaluates configurations under a declared experimental protocol and returns a configuration \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\widehat R(\theta)\), or the best evaluated configuration when exact minimization is unavailable. Solver seeds, cutoff rules, failed runs, and preprocessing choices are part of \(c\) and the protocol; the output is fixed before evaluation on held-out deployment instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Offline configuration chooses a fixed solver parameter setting that minimizes measured, capped cost on training instances under a declared evaluation protocol.
knowledge_statements.title: Offline Algorithm Configuration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits offline configuration, but the supplied assumptions do not ensure an empirical-risk minimizer exists on a compact configuration space; lower semicontinuity or an equivalent condition is missing. The exact-argmin conclusion also conflicts with the stated best-evaluated fallback. An authoritative configuration source is required.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\) is a finite solver portfolio.
\(\phi(x)\) is available before solving instance \(x\).
\(c(a,x)\) is the evaluation cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in\mathcal S}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(s(\phi(x_i)),x_i)\).

notation.meaning: A selector mapping features to a solver.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: per-instance selection minimizes empirical cost of a feature-based mapping into a finite solver portfolio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feature-based selection of one portfolio member for each SAT instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: From training data \(D=\{(x_i,c(a,x_i)):i\le n,\ a\in\mathcal A\}\), a selector-learning procedure chooses \[s^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in\mathcal S}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}c\bigl(s(\phi(x_i)),x_i\bigr),\] with ties and failed runs handled by a fixed rule. At deployment, compute \(z:=\phi(x)\), choose \(a:=s^*(z)\), run \(a\) under the prescribed resource limit, and return its result. Feature-computation cost must be included in \(c\) whenever it consumes the evaluated resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Learn a feature-based mapping from instances to portfolio members, then compute deployment features and run the selected solver while accounting for feature cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Per-Instance Solver Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feature-based selection procedure and algorithm kind fit the leaf, but no authoritative algorithm-selection citation is supplied. The assumptions do not ensure that the displayed argmin over the selector class is attained.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a finite set of candidate solvers or configurations.
\(D=(x_1,ldots,x_n)\) is an evaluation set with costs \(c(a,x_i)\).
The portfolio budget permits at most \(k\) members.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\subseteq\mathcal A,\ |P|\le k}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min_{a\in P}c(a,x_i)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: oracle-cost subset optimization formalizes complementary coverage in portfolio construction
authoritative SAT portfolio-design source locator required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-constrained portfolio construction under empirical virtual-best-solver cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty \(P\subseteq\mathcal A\), define its empirical oracle cost by \[\widehat R_{\mathrm{VBS}}(P):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min_{a\in P}c(a,x_i).\] Given a cardinality budget \(k\), portfolio design returns \(P^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\subseteq\mathcal A,\ 1\le |P|\le k}\widehat R_{\mathrm{VBS}}(P)\), or the best subset examined by a declared approximation procedure. Deployment additionally requires a selector or schedule; the virtual-best objective measures complementarity but does not itself specify which member runs on a new instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose at most k solvers whose per-instance best achievable training cost is minimal; a separate selector or schedule is still required for deployment.
knowledge_statements.title: Portfolio Design

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The virtual-best subset objective is relevant to portfolio design, but it lacks a supporting source. The assumption contains malformed LaTeX ('ldots'), and the conclusion permits P to be empty even though the minimum over an empty portfolio is undefined; the statement correctly requires 1 <= |P|.

children.title: Training-to-Deployment Distribution Shift
children.top_down_role: Performance degradation when operational instances differ from the configuration corpus.

assumptions_latex: Training and deployment instances follow distributions \(P_{\mathrm{tr}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{de}}\).
\(c(\theta,x)\) is integrable for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{tr}}\ne P_{\mathrm{de}}\) permits \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta}R_{\mathrm{tr}}(\theta)\ne\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta}R_{\mathrm{de}}(\theta)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unequal train and deployment distributions can reverse expected-cost rankings
authoritative distribution-shift source specialized to algorithm configuration required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of configuration transfer when expected performance is evaluated under a changed instance distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(R_j(\theta):=\mathbb E_{X\sim P_j}[c(\theta,X)]\) for \(j\in\{\mathrm{tr},\mathrm{de}\}\). Training-to-deployment shift occurs when \(P_{\mathrm{tr}}\ne P_{\mathrm{de}}\) on performance-relevant events. Without an invariance assumption linking these distributions, minimizing \(R_{\mathrm{tr}}\) need not minimize \(R_{\mathrm{de}}\). Concretely, for instances \(u,v\) and configurations \(a,b\), costs \(c(a,u)=c(b,v)=0\) and \(c(a,v)=c(b,u)=1\), concentration of \(P_{\mathrm{tr}}\) on \(u\) and \(P_{\mathrm{de}}\) on \(v\) reverses the uniquely optimal configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A change in the distribution of performance-relevant instances can reverse solver rankings, so the training-optimal configuration may be deployment-suboptimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Training-to-Deployment Distribution Shift

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and counterexample match distribution shift, but no inspectable source connects this formulation to algorithm configuration. The mathematical claim is plausible, yet source support is required before fixing the intended specialized scope.

children.title: Configuration Overfitting
children.top_down_role: Excessive specialization of solver settings to sampled instances or evaluation noise.

assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\) contains at least two candidate configurations.
Validation estimates \(\widehat R(\theta)\) contain sampling noise.
The same finite validation data guide selection and reported assessment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat R(\widehat\theta)-R(\widehat\theta)]\le 0\) can be strict for \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta}\widehat R(\theta)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adaptive minimization over noisy validation estimates creates optimistic selection bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive overfitting caused by repeated configuration selection on finite benchmark data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(\theta):=\mathbb E[c(\theta,X)]\) and let \(\widehat R(\theta)\) be its finite-sample estimate. If \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\widehat R(\theta)\) is selected and assessed on the same data, then even when every estimate is individually unbiased, selection can make \(\widehat R(\widehat\theta)\) optimistically biased for \(R(\widehat\theta)\). The failure intensifies as more configurations or adaptive tuning rounds exploit noise. An independent test set restores an unbiased assessment conditional on the completed selection procedure, but does not retroactively remove overfitting from configuration choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting and reporting the best of many noisy measurements on the same instances creates optimistic bias; independent final testing assesses the resulting configuration fairly.
knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Overfitting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon fits configuration overfitting, but the displayed expectation inequality requires explicit assumptions such as pointwise unbiased estimates, integrability, and a well-defined measurable selection rule. Those conditions are not included in the assumptions, and no authoritative source is cited.

children.title: Robust Configuration Validation
children.top_down_role: Evaluation designs that expose fragility across held-out families, seeds, or operating regimes.

assumptions_latex: Instances are partitioned into disjoint fitting, selection, and test units.
All preprocessing and configuration choices are fixed before test evaluation.
Dependence groups are kept within a single partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat R_{\mathrm{test}}(\widehat\theta)=|D_{\mathrm{test}}|^{-1}\sum_{x\in D_{\mathrm{test}}}c(\widehat\theta,x)\) is reserved for final assessment.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nested selection with an untouched test partition limits adaptive evaluation bias
authoritative robust algorithm-configuration validation source locator required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leakage-resistant validation protocol for selecting and assessing SAT configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition independent sampling units into \(D_{\mathrm{fit}}\), \(D_{\mathrm{sel}}\), and \(D_{\mathrm{test}}\), stratifying by declared provenance groups when needed. Fit candidate configurations using only \(D_{\mathrm{fit}}\); select \(\widehat\theta\) using \(D_{\mathrm{sel}}\), optionally by nested cross-validation wholly inside the non-test data. Freeze the configuration, preprocessing, cutoff, seed policy, and metric. Evaluate once on \(D_{\mathrm{test}}\) using \[\widehat R_{\mathrm{test}}(\widehat\theta):=\frac1{|D_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in D_{\mathrm{test}}}c(\widehat\theta,x).\] Report uncertainty over independent test units and disclose timeouts and failures under the prespecified cost rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tune, select, and test on separated dependence-aware partitions; freeze all choices before one final test evaluation and report uncertainty under a prespecified cost rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Configuration Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The validation protocol fits the leaf and algorithm kind, but it has no supporting citation. The conclusion presents a test-set estimate without specifying the sampling conditions under which its assessment or uncertainty claims are valid.

children.title: Industrial Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances derived from deployed systems, engineering workflows, or operational verification tasks.

assumptions_latex: Each benchmark instance has documented origin metadata.
The formula was generated from a practical application or operational workflow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\mathcal B_{\mathrm{industrial}}\iff \operatorname{origin}(b)\) is a documented practical application or operational process.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: SAT benchmark taxonomies classify industrial instances by provenance from practical applications
SAT competition or benchmark-taxonomy source locator required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provenance-based definition, independent of formula size, encoding family, or observed hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance \(b\) is an industrial SAT benchmark when its documented provenance traces the encoded decision problem to a practical application or operational process, such as verification, planning, scheduling, synthesis, or configuration. Formally, \(b\in\mathcal B_{\mathrm{industrial}}\) exactly when \(\operatorname{origin}(b)\) records such a source and the encoding lineage is identifiable. An instance is not industrial merely because its syntax resembles an application encoding, its variable-clause graph has similar statistics, or a generator was calibrated from industrial data without preserving application-instance provenance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An industrial benchmark is a SAT encoding with documented provenance from a practical application or operational process, not merely application-like syntax or statistics.
knowledge_statements.title: Industrial Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is the correct role, but the exact boundary of the industrial benchmark category is a community taxonomy convention and requires a specific SAT competition or benchmark-taxonomy source. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Crafted Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Purpose-built instances emphasizing selected structural features or solver weaknesses.

assumptions_latex: Each benchmark instance has documented construction metadata.
The instance is deliberately designed rather than sampled from a declared random formula distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\mathcal B_{\mathrm{crafted}}\iff b\) is deliberately constructed to express a chosen combinatorial structure or solver challenge.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: SAT benchmark taxonomies distinguish deliberately constructed instances from industrial encodings and random samples
SAT competition or benchmark-taxonomy source locator required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provenance-based classification of deliberately constructed SAT instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance \(b\) is a crafted SAT benchmark when \(\operatorname{meta}(b)\) documents deliberate construction to encode a selected mathematical or combinatorial structure, exhibit a controlled property, or challenge a solver mechanism, without arising as a direct encoding of a particular operational application instance. Thus \(b\in\mathcal B_{\mathrm{crafted}}\) is determined by construction provenance, not by observed difficulty. A parameterized deterministic generator may produce crafted instances; reproducibility of that generator does not make its outputs random unless the benchmark definition also specifies probabilistic sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A crafted benchmark is deliberately constructed to encode a chosen structure, property, or solver challenge; classification depends on provenance rather than measured difficulty.
knowledge_statements.title: Crafted Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the crafted-benchmark leaf, but the proposed provenance boundary—especially exclusion of direct operational instances and treatment of deterministic generators—requires an authoritative taxonomy citation.

children.title: Random Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances sampled from specified distributions for controlled experimental study.

assumptions_latex: A probability distribution \(P_\eta\) over finite SAT formulas is explicitly specified.
The parameter value \(\eta\) and random seed or sampling mechanism are recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\mathcal B_{\mathrm{random}}(\eta)\iff b\sim P_\eta\) under the declared sampling experiment.

notation.meaning: A family of formula distributions indexed by parameters.
Random benchmarks generated at parameter eta.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: random SAT benchmarks are samples from an explicitly declared probability model
SAT benchmark-taxonomy or random-SAT source locator required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional definition of random SAT benchmarks with recorded generation parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a declared family of probability distributions \(\{P_\eta:\eta\in H\}\) on finite propositional formulas, a random SAT benchmark at parameter \(\eta\) is an outcome \(b\sim P_\eta\) of the specified sampling experiment. Its provenance record includes \(\eta\), the generator version, and sufficient seed or randomness information for audit or reproduction. Randomness is a property of the generation law, not of an individual formula's appearance. Mixtures, conditioning on satisfiability, duplicate removal, and post-generation filtering form part of the effective distribution and must therefore be reported.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random benchmark is sampled from an explicit formula distribution whose parameters, generator, randomness, conditioning, and filtering are documented.
knowledge_statements.title: Random Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distributional description is relevant, but the equivalence b in B_random(eta) iff b is sampled from P_eta conflates a formula value with its generation provenance; the same formula can lie in the support of several generators. A precise provenance-based formulation and an authoritative random-SAT or benchmark-taxonomy source are required.

children.title: Cross-Regime Benchmark Comparability
children.top_down_role: Limits on comparing solver results across industrial, crafted, or random instance populations.

assumptions_latex: Each benchmark instance belongs to exactly one provenance regime.
All solver runs use the same hardware, resource limits, solver version, and success criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Differences in the regime-level summaries are interpretable relative to the declared aggregation functional, but do not by themselves establish regime-independent solver superiority.

notation.meaning: benchmark instances in provenance regime r
observed performance of solver s on instance i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines comparability across industrial, crafted, and random SAT benchmark regimes.
