knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a set of provenance regimes and let \(B_r\) be the instances sampled from regime \(r\in R\). A comparison is cross-regime comparable only if every observation \(Y_{s,i}\) is produced under a common protocol, the sampling rule within each \(B_r\) is disclosed, and the same functional \(G\) is applied within every regime. Results must be reported as \(G(\{Y_{s,i}:i\in B_r\})\) for each \(r\), with any pooled value using explicit nonnegative weights \(w_r\) satisfying \(\sum_{r\in R}w_r=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-regime comparison requires common experimental conditions, disclosed sampling, identical within-regime summaries, and explicit weights for any pooled result.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Regime Benchmark Comparability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the cross-regime comparability leaf and is internally coherent, but no inspectable source supports the proposed protocol requirements or aggregation rule.

children.title: Runtime Variability
children.top_down_role: Run-to-run performance dispersion caused by randomized search or execution conditions.

assumptions_latex: The SAT instance, solver configuration, hardware, and resource limits are fixed.
Repeated runs differ only through declared random seeds or controlled system noise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nondegenerate conditional distribution, equivalently \(\operatorname{Var}(T\mid I,C)>0\) when finite, constitutes runtime variability and requires repeated-run evaluation.

notation.meaning: runtime, including a declared timeout convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats runtime as a conditional random variable under controlled repeated runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed instance \(I\) and configuration \(C\), solver runtime is a random variable \(T\) induced by the seed and controlled execution noise. Runtime variability is present when the conditional law \(\mathcal L(T\mid I,C)\) is not a point mass. If its second moment exists, variability may be quantified by \(\operatorname{Var}(T\mid I,C)\); otherwise it must be described through quantiles or tail probabilities rather than variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime variability is the nondegeneracy of repeated-run runtime under a fixed instance and configuration; heavy tails may make variance inappropriate.
knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Variability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly characterizes repeated-run variability by a nondegenerate conditional runtime law, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Heavy-Tailed Runtime Distributions
children.top_down_role: Runtime populations in which rare, exceptionally long runs materially affect evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tailed Runtime Distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the regularly varying subclass of heavy-tailed runtime distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A runtime distribution has a regularly varying survival tail with index \(\alpha>0\) when there exists a slowly varying function \(L\), meaning \(L(ct)/L(t)\to 1\) for every \(c>0\), such that \[\Pr(T>t)=t^{-\alpha}L(t)\] for all sufficiently large \(t\). Every such distribution is heavy-tailed and satisfies \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda T}]=\infty\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularly varying runtime distribution has a polynomially decaying survival tail and no finite positive exponential moment; it is a specific class of heavy-tailed runtime distributions.
assumptions_latex: The runtime \(T\) is a nonnegative random variable under a fixed instance and solver configuration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(p>\alpha\), \(\mathbb E[T^p]=\infty\); at \(p=\alpha\), finiteness depends on the slowly varying factor \(L\).

children.title: Seed-Sensitive Performance
children.top_down_role: Solver rankings or aggregate results that depend strongly on random-seed selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Seed-Sensitive Performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines sensitivity to randomized solver seeds under a controlled protocol while distinguishing seed effects from other execution noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\sim P_S\) be the declared random seed and let \(Y\) be the resulting runtime or other declared performance measure. Performance is seed-sensitive when \(S\) and \(Y\) are not independent; equivalently, there exist measurable sets \(A\) of seeds and \(B\) of performance values such that \[\Pr(S\in A,Y\in B)\ne \Pr(S\in A)\Pr(Y\in B).\] If \(Y=f(S)\) almost surely for a measurable deterministic function \(f\), this condition is equivalent to \(Y\) being nonconstant with positive probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Performance is seed-sensitive when the performance distribution depends on the sampled seed. Overall runtime variance alone does not establish seed sensitivity if other execution noise is present.
assumptions_latex: The instance, solver version, parameters, hardware, and resource limits are fixed.
Seeds are sampled from a declared probability distribution \(P_S\).
Any execution randomness other than the seed is either controlled or represented in the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A single-seed result is not a seed-averaged estimate when \(S\) and \(Y\) are dependent.

notation.meaning: runtime or another declared performance measure

children.title: Robust Runtime Summaries
children.top_down_role: Performance summaries suited to variable, censored, or heavy-tailed runtime observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Runtime Summaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies quantile- and survival-based runtime summaries while accounting explicitly for timeout censoring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For runtime distribution function \(F(t)=\Pr(T\le t)\), define the population quantile \(q_p=\inf\{t:F(t)\ge p\}\). A robust runtime report declares a set of estimable quantiles, including \(q_{0.5}\) when identifiable, an interquantile spread when both endpoint quantiles are identifiable, and the timeout survival probability \(\Pr(T>\tau)\). When runs are right-censored, quantiles are estimated only under a declared censoring model and method; a quantile beyond the identifiable range is reported as bounded or not estimable. For multiple instances, seed-level summaries and instance-level aggregation are reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust runtime reporting uses identifiable medians, interquantile spreads, and timeout probabilities, explicitly accounting for censoring and separating seed-level from instance-level aggregation.
assumptions_latex: Repeated runtimes are sampled under one fixed instance and configuration.
Timeouts are retained as right-censored observations.
Any estimator for censored data states its censoring assumptions and estimation method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These summaries do not require finite runtime moments, but censoring can prevent some quantiles from being identified.

children.title: CPU-Time Limits
children.top_down_role: Evaluation under bounded processor time with explicit timeout handling.

assumptions_latex: CPU consumption is measured by a declared clock and attribution rule.
The same limit and enforcement mechanism apply to all compared runs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A terminated run supplies only the right-censored observation \(T>L\), unless the solver produced a valid result before termination.

notation.meaning: latent CPU time to solver completion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines per-run CPU-time censoring for controlled SAT evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a CPU-time limit \(L>0\), a run records \(X=\min(T,L)\) and completion indicator \(\delta=\mathbf 1\{T\le L\}\), where \(T\) is the CPU time required for completion without the limit. The limit is comparable across solvers only when the measured CPU components, treatment of parallel threads, and enforcement rule are identical and disclosed. A run with \(\delta=0\) is a timeout, not a completed runtime equal to \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CPU limit produces a completion time when solved and a right-censored timeout otherwise; clock attribution and parallel accounting must be common.
knowledge_statements.title: CPU-Time Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition gives a coherent administrative CPU-time censoring record and appropriately distinguishes a timeout from completion at the cutoff, but it has no protocol or survival-analysis source with a locator.

children.title: Memory Limits
children.top_down_role: Evaluation under bounded memory with explicit exhaustion outcomes.

assumptions_latex: Memory use is measured by a declared metric and sampling mechanism.
The same limit and enforcement mechanism apply to all compared runs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A memory-terminated run certifies only that the enforced memory threshold was reached; it does not reveal the memory required for eventual completion.

notation.meaning: measured memory usage at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines memory-bounded termination under an explicitly declared usage metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an enforced memory limit \(M>0\) and measured usage process \(U(t)\), define \(\tau_M=\inf\{t:U(t)>M\}\). The run is memory-terminated if \(\tau_M\) occurs before valid solver completion. Comparability requires a common definition of \(U\), including whether it measures resident, virtual, peak, process-tree, or aggregate parallel memory, and a common treatment of allocator, operating-system, and verifier memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A memory limit stops a run when a declared usage measure exceeds its threshold; comparisons require identical metrics, scope, and enforcement.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the memory-limit leaf and correctly requires a declared memory metric and enforcement scope, but no inspectable source supports the protocol.

children.title: Anytime Progress Reporting
children.top_down_role: Reporting of incumbent results, intermediate status, or useful progress before termination.

assumptions_latex: The solver emits timestamped incumbent or status records.
Every claimed solution or bound has a declared validation rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trace permits evaluation at every budget \(t\le L\); only validated records may improve the reported curve.

notation.meaning: best validated quality available by time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Models progress as a validated, timestamped trace over the available resource horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An anytime report is a trace \(\mathcal T=((t_k,q_k,v_k))_{k=0}^m\) with \(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le L\), where \(q_k\) is a claimed quality or status and \(v_k\in\{0,1\}\) records validation. For an ordered quality measure to be maximized, define \(Q(t)=\max\{q_k:t_k\le t,\ v_k=1\}\), using a declared null value if the set is empty. Thus \(Q(t)\) is nondecreasing and determined solely by information available by time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anytime reporting is a timestamped trace whose validated records define the best certified progress available at each resource budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Anytime Progress Reporting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent for an ordered optimization-quality trace, but ordinary SAT is a decision problem and does not automatically supply such an ordered quality measure. A SAT-specific source is needed to establish which validated progress records and ordering are intended.

children.title: Censored Outcome Accounting
children.top_down_role: Treatment of runs terminated by resource budgets before a conclusive solver result.

knowledge_statements.title: Censored Outcome Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents completed runs, administratively right-censored timeouts, and other noncompletion causes without conflating their statistical meanings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For run \(i\), record its observed elapsed time \(X_i\) and an outcome label \(O_i\) distinguishing validated completion, time cutoff, memory termination, crash, and external interruption. If a predetermined time cutoff \(C_i\) is reached before completion, record \(X_i=C_i\) and \(O_i=\mathrm{timeout}\); this supplies the right-censoring information \(T_i>C_i\). If \(O_i=\mathrm{complete}\), record the observed completion time \(T_i=X_i\). Memory termination, crash, and interruption remain separate outcomes and are treated as right-censoring observations only when an explicitly stated model justifies that interpretation. Solved counts include only validated completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Administrative timeouts provide right-censored completion-time information, while memory failures, crashes, and interruptions must remain separately labeled unless a model justifies treating them as censoring.
assumptions_latex: Each administratively timed run has a latent completion time \(T_i\) and a predetermined time cutoff \(C_i\).
Every noncompletion reason is recorded explicitly.
A declared validation rule determines whether a completion is counted as solved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A timeout contributes \(T_i>C_i\), not an exact runtime \(T_i=C_i\); other failure causes do not automatically provide the same censoring information.

notation.meaning: latent completion time of run i
predetermined administrative time cutoff of run i
observed elapsed time of run i
recorded completion or noncompletion outcome category

assumptions_latex: Each solver output has a declared claim type and corresponding checker.
Checker time, memory, and outcome are measured under a fixed protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only accepted claims contribute to certified success; solver and verification costs remain separately reportable and may also be combined by a declared end-to-end metric.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires evaluation to include independent validation and its resource cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every run claiming satisfiable or unsatisfiable status, let \(V=1\) exactly when the designated checker accepts the associated model, proof, or certificate, and let \(V=0\) otherwise. Certified success is the event that the claimed status is correct according to this validation rule and \(V=1\). Evaluation reports solver cost \(C_s\), verification cost \(C_v\), checker failures, and, when end-to-end cost is desired, the declared combination \(C_s+C_v\) for additive resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Verification-aware evaluation counts only checker-accepted claims and reports solver cost, checker cost, failures, and any declared end-to-end total.
knowledge_statements.title: Verification-Aware Evaluation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits verification-aware evaluation and separates solver, checker, and end-to-end costs, but no SAT certification-evaluation source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Benchmark Selection Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion caused by instance collections that favor particular solver capabilities or research histories.

assumptions_latex: A target population of SAT instances and a benchmark-selection mechanism are conceptually distinguished.
Solver performance may vary across instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark mean estimates the selected-population mean, not generally the target-population mean; equality requires representative selection or a justified correction.

notation.meaning: performance of a fixed solver on x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the estimand failure caused by nonrepresentative benchmark selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\sim P\) denote a target instance and let its inclusion probability be \(\pi(X)\). The selected benchmark distribution is \(P_B(dx)=\pi(x)P(dx)/\mathbb E_P[\pi(X)]\) when the denominator is positive. Therefore \[\mathbb E_{P_B}[Y(X)]=\frac{\mathbb E_P[\pi(X)Y(X)]}{\mathbb E_P[\pi(X)]},\] which differs from \(\mathbb E_P[Y(X)]\) whenever selection is associated with performance in a way not removed by weighting or design.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonrepresentative selection changes the evaluated instance distribution, so benchmark averages need not estimate performance on the intended target population.
knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Selection Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary formula correctly describes the distribution induced by inclusion weighting and its changed estimand, but the record lacks an inspectable benchmark-selection or sampling source.

children.title: Benchmark Family Leakage
children.top_down_role: Contamination between tuning, training, validation, or test partitions through related instances.

assumptions_latex: Every instance has a benchmark-family label.
Training or configuration data and evaluation data are intended to represent unseen families.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Instance-wise evaluation is contaminated for family-generalization claims whenever a family intersects both sides; splitting by family removes this direct overlap.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines leakage relative to an evaluation claim about unseen benchmark families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Benchmark family leakage occurs when \[\{g(x):x\in D_{\mathrm{tr}}\}\cap\{g(x):x\in D_{\mathrm{te}}\}\ne\varnothing,\] while evaluation is interpreted as performance on unseen families. Because related instances from the same generator, application, or transformation lineage may share predictive structure, an instance-level split does not identify family-level generalization. A family-disjoint split instead requires the displayed intersection to be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Family leakage occurs when related benchmark families appear in both development and test data despite a claim of generalization to unseen families.
knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Family Leakage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary definition matches a claim of generalization to unseen benchmark families and correctly distinguishes instance-wise from family-disjoint splitting, but no SAT-specific leakage source with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Family-Aware Data Splits
children.top_down_role: Partitioning practices that keep related benchmark families within controlled evaluation boundaries.

assumptions_latex: The finite benchmark set is \(B\), and \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(B\) encoding common instance family or generation provenance.
The designated training, validation, and test subsets \(B_{\mathrm{tr}},B_{\mathrm{val}},B_{\mathrm{te}}\subseteq B\) are pairwise disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall i\ne j,\quad \pi(B_i)\cap\pi(B_j)=\varnothing.\]

notation.meaning: Equivalence class, interpreted as the benchmark family containing instance \(b\).
Set of families represented in a subset \(S\subseteq B\).
The three data partitions, indexed by \(i\in\{\mathrm{tr},\mathrm{val},\mathrm{te}\}\).

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses SAT benchmark family splitting or contamination control.
A domain-specific benchmark-evaluation source is required to validate the chosen family-equivalence formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Group-disjoint splitting for finite SAT benchmark collections with an explicit family equivalence relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A split \((B_{\mathrm{tr}},B_{\mathrm{val}},B_{\mathrm{te}})\) is family-aware with respect to \(\sim\) if it partitions \(B\) and no equivalence class is represented in more than one part. Explicitly, it satisfies
\[B=B_{\mathrm{tr}}\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_{\mathrm{val}}\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_{\mathrm{te}}\]
and
\[\pi(B_{\mathrm{tr}})\cap\pi(B_{\mathrm{val}})=\pi(B_{\mathrm{tr}})\cap\pi(B_{\mathrm{te}})=\pi(B_{\mathrm{val}})\cap\pi(B_{\mathrm{te}})=\varnothing.\]
Thus every family is assigned wholly to one partition, although a partition may contain multiple families.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A benchmark split is family-aware when every instance family is assigned wholly to training, validation, or test, so no family occurs in two partitions.
knowledge_statements.title: Family-Aware Data Splits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent, notation is introduced, plain text matches the LaTeX, and content_kind fits the leaf. However, no citation supports treating family-aware SAT benchmark splitting through the stated provenance equivalence relation; the formulation therefore requires a specific inspectable source.

children.title: Duplicate Instance Contamination
children.top_down_role: Exact or near-duplicate instances that inflate apparent generalization or performance stability.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark set \(B\) is partitioned into training and test sets \(B_{\mathrm{tr}}\) and \(B_{\mathrm{te}}\).
A canonicalization map \(c:B\to C\) identifies instances regarded as duplicates, including syntactically identical copies as a special case.
Evaluation loss \(\ell\) takes values in \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[c(B_{\mathrm{tr}})\cap c(B_{\mathrm{te}})\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{the test set is not duplicate-disjoint from the training set}.\]

notation.meaning: Canonical representation used to determine duplicate equivalence.

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports duplicate contamination in SAT benchmark evaluation.
The canonicalization criterion is application-dependent and requires a domain-specific source or review decision.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duplicate leakage defined relative to an explicit canonicalization map; semantic equivalence is outside this local formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Duplicate-instance contamination occurs when
\[c(B_{\mathrm{tr}})\cap c(B_{\mathrm{te}})\ne\varnothing.\]
In that case, test performance need not measure performance on previously unseen canonical instances. Concretely, let \(b\in B_{\mathrm{tr}}\) and \(b'\in B_{\mathrm{te}}\) satisfy \(c(b)=c(b')\). A procedure that memorizes the observed outcome for \(c(b)\) can have \(\ell(b')=0\), while a new instance \(u\) with \(c(u)\ne c(b)\) may have \(\ell(u)=1\). Hence zero contaminated-test loss alone imposes no nontrivial upper bound below \(1\) on loss for new canonical instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A test set is duplicate-contaminated when it shares a canonical instance with training; perfect contaminated-test performance can coexist with maximal loss on genuinely new instances.
knowledge_statements.title: Duplicate Instance Contamination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The overlap condition appropriately describes a duplicate-contamination failure boundary, but no source supports the SAT-specific canonicalization criterion or the claimed generalization failure. Moreover, the domain of the loss and the outcome memorized by the procedure are not defined, so the maximal-loss example cannot be reliably validated without a sourced, precise formulation.
